domain: Follow-up sweep: non-GitHub/npm forges, Chinese-language ecosystem, never-queried registries (jsr.io, crates.io, MCP registries, VS Code Marketplace), and the Penpot/Inkscape MCP prior art that all 8 previous sweeps missed. Every entry below was verified this session by fetching the actual LICENSE file over HTTPS and reading the last-commit timestamp from the repo's Atom feed (github.com/OWNER/REPO/commits/BRANCH.atom), or from registry APIs (registry.npmjs.org, crates.io/api/v1, api.jsr.io, registry.modelcontextprotocol.io, marketplace.visualstudio.com, gitlab.com/api/v4, gitlab.gnome.org/api/v4, codeberg.org/api/v1). Dates are UTC as of 2026-08-14. NEGATIVE RESULTS WORTH RECORDING (these platforms were searched and are barren, so no future sweep needs to repeat them): (1) codeberg.org — searched via its Gitea API for svg/vector/inkscape/canvas/bezier/designer; ZERO relevant web or Electron vector editors, GUI builders, or DOM inspectors; everything returned was clip-art repos, Inkscape extension snippets, or student exercises. (2) sr.ht/sourcehut — project search returned nothing relevant for svg/vector/canvas/gui. (3) atomgit.com — search API is behind a CloudWAF block page ("访问被拦截"), not machine-accessible. (4) gitee.com — the v5 search API requires an access token; the public /explore/lowcode page only re-lists the same GitHub projects (tmagic, LowCodeEngine, GoView, Marsview). (5) jsr.io — searched canvas/svg/selector/mcp/bezier; essentially barren for this domain. The single interesting hit, mohsen/xpath-to-css-selector, is an EMPTY PLACEHOLDER (versionCount: 0, no published version, no repo) — do not rely on it. (6) registry.modelcontextprotocol.io — searched design/svg/canvas/figma/penpot/inkscape; the "penpot" and "inkscape" queries return ZERO results, which mechanically explains why the prior MCP sweep missed all the Penpot/Inkscape MCP servers: the richest design-MCP prior art is simply not in the official registry and is only discoverable via PulseMCP or by reading the Penpot monorepo directly. HEADLINE FINDINGS: (A) Penpot ships an official in-repo MCP server (MPL-2.0, on our allowed list, published to npm as @penpot/mcp v2.17.0) whose architecture — MCP server <-> WebSocket bridge <-> in-app plugin holding a live handle to the document model, with the LLM writing arbitrary code snippets executed inside the plugin sandbox rather than calling hundreds of fine-grained tools — is a near-exact blueprint for requirement (e) in EXELMJ's Electron main/renderer split. (B) leafer-editor / @leafer-in/editor (MIT, active 2026-08-02) is a framework-free vanilla-TS Canvas 2D editor with a working transform box, and is the single best drop-in for requirement (b); it was invisible to English-language sweeps. (C) alibaba/lowcode-engine is DISQUALIFIED on two independently verified grounds, not just the CDN caveat: its main branch has been dead since 2024-06-11 (develop since 2024-07-03), and I proved the global-script architecture from source — alibaba/lowcode-demo/build.json declares "@alilc/lowcode-engine": "var window.AliLowCodeEngine" alongside "react": "var window.React", i.e. the engine is consumed as a UMD window global, never as a bundled ESM import.

entries.name: Penpot official in-repo MCP server (@penpot/mcp)
entries.what_it_is: An official, first-party MCP server living inside the Penpot monorepo (TypeScript/Node 22, pnpm workspace) that lets an LLM query, transform and create real design objects in Penpot. Verified to exist: the /mcp directory contains bin/, docs/, packages/, scripts/, types-generator/, package.json, pnpm-workspace.yaml. Architecture is three cooperating processes: an MCP server exposing HTTP+SSE on :4401, a plugin web server on :4400, and a WebSocket bridge on :4402 that connects a Penpot Plugin (running inside the Penpot app, holding a live handle to the document) back to the MCP server. Crucially the README states the LLM is free to write and execute arbitrary code snippets inside the Penpot Plugin environment to accomplish its tasks — i.e. the plugin is a code-execution sandbox over the document model, not a fixed tool wall.
entries.license: MPL-2.0 — read two ways: penpot/penpot/develop/LICENSE is verbatim 'Mozilla Public License Version 2.0', and mcp/package.json declares "license": "MPL-2.0" explicitly. On our allowed list. Note MPL-2.0 is file-level weak copyleft: modifications to MPL-licensed FILES must be published, but linking it into our proprietary vanilla-TS module does not infect our own files.
entries.embeddable_how: Published npm package @penpot/mcp — verified live on registry.npmjs.org with dist-tags latest=2.15.4, next=2.17.0, maintained by the Kaleidos/Penpot team (andrey.antukh, juanfran.kaleidos, xaviju et al). Runs as a local Node process via `npx -y @penpot/mcp@latest`, or clone + ./scripts/setup + pnpm run bootstrap. Exposes a bin entry ./bin/mcp-local.js. It does NOT embed into our renderer — it is a separate local process, which is exactly the shape requirement (e) needs.
entries.why_useful_for_us: This is the closest existing prior art on earth for requirement (e) — 'a design tool that exposes its own shape/page/component operations as MCP tools' — and it is under a licence we are allowed to link. It answers the two hard design questions we would otherwise have to guess at: (1) how an MCP server reaches into a live, already-running design surface rather than editing files on disk, and (2) how to avoid writing 76+ hand-maintained tool schemas. Runs against a self-hosted Penpot with no cloud account, so it is fully offline-testable as a reference implementation before we write our own.
entries.framework_lock: The MCP server and WebSocket bridge are framework-free TypeScript/Node — directly reusable in shape. The plugin half is bound to Penpot's own Plugin API (Penpot's UI is ClojureScript), so that half is a pattern to copy, not code to lift.
entries.last_activity: 2026-08-13 (penpot/penpot develop branch, verified via commits Atom feed); mcp/package.json is at version 2.17.0
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Not evaluated for RTL — irrelevant for this entry, since we would copy the transport/bridge architecture, not any text rendering. Penpot itself does have RTL/Arabic text support gaps, but that does not reach the MCP layer.
entries.steal_this_idea: Replace the giant tool wall with a code-execution bridge. Instead of authoring one MCP tool per document operation (addRect, setFill, groupShapes...), expose a SMALL tool surface — roughly 'describe the document', 'run this snippet against the document' — and stand up a WebSocket bridge from the Node-side MCP server into the Electron renderer, where a resident bridge module evaluates the snippet with designApp.ts's live document model in scope. This maps 1:1 onto EXELMJ's existing main/renderer split (MCP server in main or a sidecar, bridge module in the renderer next to designApp.ts), collapses (e) from ~80 hand-written schemas to a handful, and lets the LLM compose multi-step edits atomically instead of chattering over dozens of round-trips.

entries.name: leafer-editor / @leafer-in/editor (LeaferJS)
entries.what_it_is: A Chinese-authored HTML5 Canvas 2D graphics engine (leafer-ui) plus a genuine graphics-editor layer on top of it. leafer-editor is described in its own npm README as leafer-ui with the graphics editor and viewport integrated. The @leafer-in/* plugin family splits the editor into composable pieces — I verified @leafer-in/editor (selection, transform box, resize/rotate handles) and @leafer-in/viewport (pan/zoom) as separately published packages, all at version 2.2.9.
entries.license: MIT — verified from BOTH repo LICENSE files (leaferjs/ui/main/LICENSE and leaferjs/leafer-in/main/LICENSE, each 'The MIT License (MIT), Copyright (c) 2023-present, Chao (Leafer) Wan') AND from the npm metadata of leafer-ui, leafer-editor, @leafer-in/editor and @leafer-in/viewport (all report license MIT at v2.2.9). I checked the plugin packages separately and deliberately, because some Canvas engines relicense their editor/pro plugins commercially — LeaferJS does not; the editor is MIT too.
entries.embeddable_how: Plain npm packages (leafer-ui, leafer-editor, or leafer-ui + individual @leafer-in/* plugins), normal ESM, bundler-friendly. Drops straight into Vite 8 and runs in the Electron renderer against a <canvas>. No CDN, no backend, no account.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The best fit found in this entire sweep for requirement (b), the lightweight Illustrator-like vector designer. EXELMJ's design module is hand-written vanilla TS/DOM/Canvas at ~2900 lines, and the single most tedious remaining piece is a correct transform box — 8 handles, rotation, proportional/anchored resize, multi-select bounding box, snapping — which @leafer-in/editor already implements as MIT vanilla TS with zero framework lock. Adopting it (or reading it) skips the exact work we would otherwise grind through, and its plugin split means we can take only the editor/viewport pieces without swallowing a whole app.
entries.framework_lock: NONE — pure vanilla TypeScript over Canvas 2D. No React, no Vue. This is the rare Chinese-ecosystem project that is not framework-locked, and it is the reason it outranks every other entry in this sweep for requirement (b).
entries.last_activity: 2026-08-02 (leaferjs/LeaferJS main, Atom feed); @leafer-in/viewport npm modified 2026-08-01; all packages at 2.2.9
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: REAL RISK, needs a spike before adoption. LeaferJS draws text to Canvas 2D itself rather than delegating to DOM layout, so Arabic bidi reordering and contextual glyph shaping are unlikely to be handled correctly out of the box. EXELMJ already has hand-written Arabic bidi runs in its text boxes — so the sane split is to use LeaferJS for SHAPES and the transform box while keeping our existing text-box code path for Arabic. Do not assume its text layer will render Arabic correctly.
entries.steal_this_idea: The @leafer-in/* plugin decomposition: keep the scene graph/renderer core dumb and free of editing concerns, then bolt on editing as separate opt-in plugins (editor = selection + transform box, viewport = pan/zoom). We can mirror that boundary inside designApp.ts to stop the editing/interaction logic from tangling into the 2900-line render path — worth doing even if we never install the package.

entries.name: css-selector-generator
entries.what_it_is: A focused library that, given a DOM element, generates a unique CSS selector that matches only that element. Its npm description explicitly advertises support for multiple elements, Shadow DOM, and configurable selector-type priority (id / class / tag / attribute / nth-child).
entries.license: MIT — verified from the repo LICENSE file ('The MIT License (MIT), Copyright (c) 2018 Riki Fridrich') and corroborated by npm metadata.
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, ZERO runtime dependencies (verified: dependencies list is empty). Pure browser DOM code, drops directly into the Electron renderer or into a preload/injected script inside a <webview>/BrowserView.
entries.why_useful_for_us: This is the missing core primitive for requirement (c), the AI element picker. Capturing an element's styles is easy (getComputedStyle); producing a STABLE, unique, re-findable selector for it is the genuinely hard part, and this solves precisely that. Zero deps means no supply-chain or offline risk. Shadow DOM support matters because any modern app we load into the mini-browser (d) may use web components, where naive selector generation silently breaks.
entries.framework_lock: None — framework-free, operates on raw DOM nodes.
entries.last_activity: 2026-08-07 (npm registry 'modified' timestamp for v3.9.4) — actively maintained, the most recently updated selector library of the group.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Irrelevant/neutral — operates on DOM structure, not text rendering. Selector generation is unaffected by document direction or Arabic content.
entries.steal_this_idea: Its configurable selector-type PRIORITY LIST with a uniqueness-verification loop: try candidate selector strategies in a preferred order, and after each candidate actually re-run querySelectorAll to confirm it matches exactly one node before accepting it. For our picker, tune that priority away from auto-generated hashed class names (Tailwind/CSS-modules noise the AI cannot reason about) and toward data-* attributes, id, and semantic tags — the selector we hand the AI should be one a human would also recognise.

entries.name: knipsa / knipsa-ffi
entries.what_it_is: An obscure, very new Rust library for 2D polygon booleans, offsets (inset/outset), point queries, and triangulation. Its README states boolean operations use specialized fast paths when their checks succeed and fall back to an exact geometry kernel otherwise, behind a single unchanged API — i.e. it does not silently produce garbage on degenerate/self-intersecting input. Ships a companion C API crate (knipsa-ffi).
entries.license: MIT OR Apache-2.0 (dual) — read from crates.io API for both knipsa and knipsa-ffi at v0.3.0. Both permissive and on our allowed list.
entries.embeddable_how: Two routes. (1) Compile to WASM and call from the Electron renderer — the natural fit. (2) The knipsa-ffi crate exposes a C-compatible API, so it can equally be a native Node addon or a sidecar. Either way it is a local binary artifact: no network, no service.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Requirement (b) needs boolean path ops (unite / subtract / intersect / exclude) and path offsetting to feel Illustrator-like at all, and these are the operations that are notoriously easy to get subtly wrong. EXELMJ already produces Bezier paths from its custom isoContour + cubic-fit tracer, and offsetting/uniting those traced contours is exactly this library's job. Explicitly matches the brief's preference for obscure-but-fitting: 90 total downloads, so this is not a popularity pick — it is a capability pick.
entries.framework_lock: None — Rust library, no UI framework involvement at all.
entries.last_activity: 2026-08-09 (crates.io updated_at for v0.3.0) — five days before this sweep; very actively developed.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Irrelevant — pure computational geometry over coordinates, no text involvement.
entries.steal_this_idea: The dual-kernel strategy: run a fast floating-point path when cheap predicate checks confirm it is safe, and fall back to an exact/robust geometry kernel when they do not — behind ONE API so callers never branch. Boolean ops on traced contours are precisely where naive float geometry produces cracks, slivers and dropped subpaths; adopting this fast-path-with-exact-fallback discipline (even in our own TS) is the difference between a boolean tool that mostly works and one that is trustworthy.

entries.name: bezier-rs (Graphite)
entries.what_it_is: Computational-geometry algorithms for Bezier segments and shapes aimed specifically at 2D graphics work — the geometry layer extracted from the Graphite vector editor (Keavon is Graphite's lead developer). Covers curve intersection, offsetting, outlining, projection, splitting and related path operations.
entries.license: MIT OR Apache-2.0 (dual) — read from the crates.io API for v0.5.0. Permissive, on our allowed list. Worth flagging because Graphite the APPLICATION is Apache-2.0 while several vector editors in this space are GPL — this library is safely usable.
entries.embeddable_how: Rust crate compiled to WASM for the renderer (Graphite itself ships it as WASM to the browser, so this path is proven, not theoretical). 192,870 downloads, so it is a real, exercised dependency rather than an experiment.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Directly upgrades two things EXELMJ already has. Our image tracer already does cubic Bezier curve fitting by hand; bezier-rs supplies the operations that come AFTER fitting — offsetting a traced outline, intersecting curves, splitting at a parameter — which is exactly the gap between 'we can trace an image' and 'we can edit the traced result like a vector artist would'. Complements knipsa: knipsa handles polygon-level booleans, bezier-rs handles true curve-level math without flattening to polylines first.
entries.last_activity: 2025-08-15 (crates.io updated_at for v0.5.0)
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Irrelevant — pure curve mathematics, no text.
entries.steal_this_idea: Its curve-native operation set: perform offset/outline/intersect ON the cubic segments rather than flattening to polylines, booleaning, and re-fitting. Our current pipeline is fit-then-treat-as-polygon, which loses precision on every operation and progressively degrades traced artwork. Even reading how bezier-rs parameterises offsetting would improve our existing isoContour + cubic-fit tracer's output fidelity.

entries.name: GrapesJS
entries.what_it_is: A mature, self-contained web page builder framework — drag-and-drop canvas, layer manager, style manager, trait/settings panel, and HTML/CSS code export. It is the engine that a large fraction of open-source website builders (including Silex v3) are actually built on.
entries.license: BSD-3-Clause — verified by reading packages/core/LICENSE on the dev branch (the root LICENSE is just a pointer to that path). Text is the standard 'Redistribution and use in source and binary forms... ' three-clause form, Copyright (c) 2017-current Artur Arseniev. On our allowed list.
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, plain ESM, no backend and no account. Mounts into a DOM node inside our Electron renderer. Storage is pluggable and can be a pure local/in-memory or filesystem adapter, so nothing calls out to a network.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The strongest permissively-licensed candidate for requirement (a), the visual UI builder that outputs real code. Reached here through the alternate-forge branch of the sweep: GitLab search surfaced silexlabs/silex_section-library, and following Silex upstream lands on GrapesJS — which is BSD-3-Clause where Silex itself is AGPL-3.0. In other words, GrapesJS is the licence-clean core of the AGPL builder we cannot use, and the DOM-based (not Canvas-based) architecture means it inherits browser layout for free.
entries.framework_lock: NONE for the host app — framework-free vanilla JS/TS core that manipulates real DOM. Official React/Vue wrappers exist but are strictly optional, so it will not force a framework onto EXELMJ's vanilla-TS design module.
entries.last_activity: 2026-08-11 (dev branch, Atom feed). IMPORTANT: the master branch is stale at 2024-07-02 — active development is on `dev`, so any freshness check against master will wrongly conclude the project is abandoned.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Best RTL story of any builder in this sweep, because it edits REAL DOM rather than painting to Canvas: setting dir="rtl" on the edited document makes the browser's own bidi engine handle Arabic layout, with no shaping work on our side. This is a decisive advantage over Canvas-based builders for an Arabic-RTL-first product. The builder's own chrome/UI still needs separate RTL treatment.
entries.steal_this_idea: The edit-real-DOM-in-an-iframe model, with the builder chrome living outside the frame and reaching in. Because the canvas IS a live document, the exported code is the thing you were looking at, so requirement (a)'s 'outputs real code' is structural rather than a lossy serialization step. It also collapses (a) and (d) into one mechanism: the same iframe/webview that hosts the editable document is the mini-browser that RUNS the project, and desktop/tablet/mobile viewport switching is just resizing that frame.

entries.name: alibaba/lowcode-engine
entries.what_it_is: Alibaba's enterprise low-code engine (from the Alibaba frontend committee + DingTalk Yida), 15.9k stars, positioned as a minimal kernel with a large surrounding ecosystem of materials and plugins.
entries.license: MIT — verified from the raw LICENSE file (standard MIT, Copyright Alibaba 2021).
entries.embeddable_how: HOSTILE to our stack, and I proved this from source rather than trusting the docs. alibaba/lowcode-demo/build.json declares externals mapping every core dependency to a window global: "@alilc/lowcode-engine": "var window.AliLowCodeEngine", "react": "var window.React", "react-dom": "var window.ReactDOM", "prop-types": "var window.PropTypes", plus @alifd/next, moment and lodash the same way. The engine is consumed as a UMD script global, never as a bundled ESM import — which is what the project's own docs mean by 'only cdn import is supported, npm package is used to provide code hinting capabilities such as typings'. The npm package (@alilc/lowcode-engine v1.3.4, main: lib/engine-core.js) does contain runtime code, so it is technically possible to vendor the UMD bundles locally and load them via <script> in Electron — offline is achievable — but it fights Vite 8 at every step and abandons tree-shaking.
entries.why_useful_for_us: RECOMMEND AGAINST ADOPTING. Included so this is settled with evidence rather than re-litigated in a future sweep. Two independent disqualifiers beyond the CDN issue: (1) it is DEAD — main's last commit is 2024-06-11 and develop's is 2024-07-03, over two years stale, with the satellite repos equally cold (lowcode-materials 2024-09-21, lowcode-demo 2024-05-08); (2) it is React-locked via window globals. Its value to us is purely as a reference for low-code engine ARCHITECTURE (its schema/renderer/designer separation is genuinely well thought out), not as a dependency.
entries.framework_lock: React, and hard-locked — React and ReactDOM must be present as window globals before the engine boots. Nothing vanilla or framework-free is on offer.
entries.last_activity: 2024-06-11 (main) / 2024-07-03 (develop) — both verified via commits Atom feed. Effectively abandoned.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: No RTL/Arabic story. Docs and materials are Chinese/English only; the Fusion Design (@alifd/next) component set it leans on is not RTL-first.
entries.steal_this_idea: Its schema-first three-way split — a serializable page schema as the single source of truth, a designer that only ever mutates the schema, and a renderer that is a pure function of the schema. That separation is why the same schema can drive both the design canvas and the production runtime, and it is the right internal shape for our requirement (a) even though we should not import a line of this code.

entries.name: Tencent/tmagic-editor
entries.what_it_is: Tencent's open-source visual page-construction platform, originally aimed at mobile H5 pages: a Vue 3 + Composition API + TypeScript editor with a monorepo of separate RUNTIMES, so the editor is decoupled from what renders the output. 4.9k stars, 2,230 commits.
entries.license: Apache-2.0 — verified by reading the LICENSE file, which opens 'TMagicEditor is licensed under the Apache License Version 2.0 except for the third-party components listed below', Copyright (C) 2025 Tencent. On our allowed list; note the file carries a third-party-components carve-out worth reading before shipping.
entries.embeddable_how: npm monorepo packages (@tmagic/*) plus a self-hostable editor app. Node ^20.19 || >=22.12, pnpm. Runs locally with no cloud account. The editor half will pull Vue 3 into our bundle, which is the main cost.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The healthiest, most actively maintained large low-code editor in the Chinese ecosystem — last commit 2026-08-13, literally the day before this sweep, versus lowcode-engine's two-year silence. Its architectural contribution to requirement (a) is the editor/runtime split: separate vue-components and react-components runtime packages mean the design surface does not dictate the output framework, which is exactly the property we need if EXELMJ is to emit code for OUR projects rather than for Tencent's stack.
entries.framework_lock: The EDITOR is Vue 3-locked. The RUNTIME is not — the monorepo ships distinct Vue 2, Vue 3 and React runtimes, and the core/util packages are usable from vanilla JS/TS. So we can borrow the runtime/schema layer without swallowing Vue, but not the editor UI.
entries.last_activity: 2026-08-13 (master, Atom feed) — the most recently active Chinese low-code project in this sweep.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: No RTL/Arabic support in the editor chrome (Chinese/English only). Since output is DOM-based H5 pages, generated pages can be made RTL via dir="rtl" on the page, but nothing in the tool assists with that.
entries.steal_this_idea: One schema, many runtimes — pin down a framework-neutral page schema and treat each renderer (Vue/React/vanilla) as an interchangeable consumer of it. For EXELMJ this is the concrete mechanism that makes requirement (a)'s 'outputs real code for our own projects' plural rather than single-target: the designer only ever produces schema, and each code generator is a swappable back end.

entries.name: opentiny/tiny-engine
entries.what_it_is: Huawei/OpenTiny's low-code engine for building visual page-construction platforms — a designer app plus a plugin architecture, shipped as @opentiny/tiny-engine with a design-core package.
entries.license: MIT — verified from the raw LICENSE on the develop branch ('MIT License, Copyright (c) 2023 - present TinyEngine Authors').
entries.embeddable_how: npm packages / self-hosted app. Runs against a bundled MOCK SERVER by default, so it does start without external infrastructure; a separate optional Java backend (opentiny/tiny-engine-backend-java) exists for 'complete capabilities'. Meaning: the designer boots offline, but the full feature set was designed around a service.
entries.why_useful_for_us: A live, MIT-licensed, actively maintained alternative to the dead lowcode-engine, and useful mainly as a design reference for requirement (a)'s plugin/panel architecture. Downgraded from a real adoption candidate by the Vue lock plus the mock-server dependency — the 'offline' story is 'a stub server is included', not 'no server exists', which is a meaningfully weaker guarantee than a pure client-side library gives us.
entries.framework_lock: Vue 3 — verified directly from packages/design-core/package.json, which declares "vue": "^3.4.23". Hard lock on the designer UI.
entries.last_activity: 2026-07-30 (develop branch, Atom feed) — actively maintained.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: No RTL/Arabic support; Chinese/English i18n only. TinyVue components underneath are not RTL-first.
entries.steal_this_idea: Ship a mock/stub service alongside the designer so the whole tool is runnable and demoable with zero infrastructure, while keeping a real service interface behind the same contract. For EXELMJ the inversion is instructive: we should define that boundary as a LOCAL adapter from day one (filesystem/SQLite) so we never acquire a server dependency we then have to stub around.

entries.name: baidu/amis
entries.what_it_is: Baidu's front-end low-code framework that renders complete pages from a JSON configuration — described in its own README as a tool for generating MIS/admin pages from JSON with minimal front-end knowledge. The ecosystem splits into amis (renderers), amis-core (the runtime), amis-ui and amis-formula.
entries.license: Apache-2.0 — verified from the raw LICENSE file (verbatim Apache License Version 2.0) and corroborated by npm metadata for both amis and amis-core at v6.13.0. On our allowed list.
entries.embeddable_how: Two distinct routes with very different costs. (1) npm route: FRAMEWORK-LOCKED — I verified amis@6.13.0 declares peerDependencies react, react-dom, amis-ui, amis-core, office-viewer, and amis-core@6.13.0 declares react, react-is, react-dom, amis-formula. It also drags heavy transitive deps (echarts, exceljs, xlsx, moment, mobx). (2) SDK route: a prebuilt bundle that packages React internally so the host page needs no React of its own — this can be vendored locally and used offline without a CDN. EXELMJ already has React 19 present, but amis has historically targeted older React, so the npm route needs a compatibility spike before it is assumed to work.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Relevant to requirement (a) as the most battle-tested JSON-schema-to-UI renderer available under a permissive licence. If we want a design surface whose output is DATA (a schema) rather than a code blob, amis is the reference for how expressive that schema has to become to cover real forms, tables, CRUD and conditional logic. Its dependency weight and React coupling make it a poor direct fit for our vanilla-TS module.
entries.framework_lock: React — confirmed as a hard peer dependency on both amis and amis-core. The SDK build hides React from the host rather than removing it. There is no vanilla renderer.
entries.last_activity: 2026-03-18 (master, Atom feed); npm registry modified 2026-01-27 at v6.13.0. Maintained but noticeably slower-moving than tmagic-editor.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Renders to DOM, so an Arabic RTL page can be achieved with dir="rtl" and the browser's own bidi handling — structurally better than Canvas-based tools. But amis ships no RTL-aware theme and its own component styling assumes LTR, so mirrored layouts would need real CSS work.
entries.steal_this_idea: Its JSON schema expressiveness ladder — specifically how it handles data linkage, conditional visibility and API/action binding declaratively inside the schema instead of escaping to imperative code. That is the exact boundary where naive schema-driven builders collapse and start emitting untraceable JS; worth reading before we design our own schema for (a).

entries.name: alibaba/designable
entries.what_it_is: Alibaba's free/unopinionated drag-and-drop DESIGNER ENGINE — the visual-editing substrate (drag sources, drop targets, selection, resize, snapping, cursor state machine) split apart from any particular component library or output format. Sister project to Formily.
entries.license: MIT — verified from the raw LICENSE file ('MIT License, Copyright (c) 2021 Alibaba').
entries.embeddable_how: npm packages under @designable/* with a deliberate core/shell split: @designable/core is the framework-free engine and the React/Vue shells are separate packages layered on top. So the core is importable into a vanilla-TS renderer.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Its @designable/core is one of the very few framework-free implementations of the drag/drop/select/resize interaction engine that requirement (a) needs, and it is MIT. STRONG CAVEAT: the repo is DEAD, last commit 2022-04-25, over four years cold — so treat it as source to READ (or vendor deliberately, with eyes open) rather than a dependency to take on. Given EXELMJ already hand-writes its interaction layer, reading a proven state machine is arguably the higher-value use anyway.
entries.framework_lock: Core is framework-FREE by explicit design; React and Vue bindings are separate optional packages. This core/shell separation is the project's main architectural contribution.
entries.last_activity: 2022-04-25 (main, Atom feed) — abandoned.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: No RTL handling. Drag/drop hit-testing and snap logic assume LTR coordinate reasoning in places, so an RTL canvas would need review — relevant to us since EXELMJ is Arabic-RTL-first.
entries.steal_this_idea: The strict core/shell boundary: put the ENTIRE editing engine (drag sources, drop targets, hit-testing, selection model, snapping, cursor state machine) in a framework-free core that knows nothing about how anything is painted, and let every UI shell be a thin renderer over that core's observable state. This is the single most valuable structural idea for keeping requirements (a) and (b) from duplicating interaction logic — one engine, two surfaces (UI builder and vector designer).

entries.name: alibaba/formily
entries.what_it_is: Alibaba's schema-driven form solution — a reactive form state core (@formily/reactive, @formily/core) plus JSON-Schema and JSX-Schema renderers, with React and Vue bindings. The engine behind Designable's form-building use case.
entries.license: MIT — verified by reading LICENSE.md on the formily_next branch ('The MIT License (MIT), Copyright (c) 2015-present, Alibaba Group Holding Limited'). Note the file is LICENSE.md, not LICENSE — a plain LICENSE fetch 404s, which is an easy way to wrongly conclude the project is unlicensed.
entries.embeddable_how: npm packages (@formily/core, @formily/reactive, @formily/react, @formily/vue). The core and reactive packages are framework-free and importable standalone into vanilla TS; only the binding packages pull a framework.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Requirement (a) will inevitably need a properties/inspector panel that binds a schema to live widget state with validation and conditional logic. @formily/core + @formily/reactive solve exactly that reactive-form-state problem without a framework, under MIT. It is a component-level building block for the builder's right-hand panel rather than a builder in itself.
entries.framework_lock: Core is framework-free; React/Vue only via optional binding packages.
entries.last_activity: 2025-06-21 on the formily_next branch (Atom feed). IMPORTANT BRANCH TRAP: the master branch is frozen at 2022-04-25, so checking master alone makes the project look abandoned when development actually moved to formily_next.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Layout is delegated to whichever component library renders the fields, so RTL depends entirely on that library rather than on Formily. The state core itself is direction-agnostic.
entries.steal_this_idea: Its reactive-form-state model — field state as observable graph nodes with declarative dependency/visibility rules — applied to our DESIGN INSPECTOR rather than to forms. Shape properties (fill, stroke, position, font, direction) are a form over the selected object; modelling that panel as reactive schema-driven state, instead of hand-wired DOM listeners, is what keeps the inspector from rotting as we add shape types to designApp.ts.

entries.name: zcube/penpot-mcp-server (@zcubekr/penpot-mcp-server)
entries.what_it_is: A community TypeScript MCP server for Penpot exposing roughly 76+ tools grouped by domain — project/file management, page operations, shape creation and manipulation, components, teams, sharing, comments, export/media, fonts, webhooks, search, profile/stats. Supports both stdio mode for local MCP clients and HTTP/SSE mode, with Docker packaging.
entries.license: MIT — declared as "license": "MIT" in package.json (package name @zcubekr/penpot-mcp-server v1.0.0). CAVEAT WORTH RECORDING: there is NO LICENSE file at the repo root (raw fetch 404s), so the MIT claim rests on package.json metadata alone. That is normally sufficient, but for anything we vendor it is worth asking upstream to add the file.
entries.embeddable_how: Local Node process (stdio or HTTP/SSE) or Docker container. Talks to Penpot over its REST API using an access token generated from Penpot account settings — so it needs a reachable Penpot instance, though a SELF-HOSTED one satisfies that without any cloud account.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The instructive CONTRAST to Penpot's official MCP server. Same problem, opposite philosophy: ~76 hand-authored fine-grained tools driven through the REST API, versus the official server's small tool surface plus a code-execution plugin bridge. Reading both back to back is the fastest way to decide requirement (e)'s tool granularity, and this one usefully enumerates what a complete design-tool tool surface actually has to cover.
entries.framework_lock: None — plain TypeScript/Node MCP server, no UI framework.
entries.last_activity: 2026-06-24 (main, Atom feed)
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Not applicable — server-side API wrapper with no rendering or text layout.
entries.steal_this_idea: Its DOMAIN GROUPING of the tool surface (project / page / shape / component / export / search / comments). Even if we adopt the official server's thin code-execution bridge, this taxonomy is a ready-made checklist of the operations an EXELMJ MCP server must ultimately be able to reach, and a sane way to organise our tool names so the model can find them.

entries.name: aravindev/inkscape_mcp
entries.what_it_is: A Python MCP server that lets an AI agent design, edit and analyse vector graphics through Inkscape — either against a LIVE running Inkscape window (via D-Bus) or headless via Inkscape's CLI. Tools cover file conversion, path operations, image analysis and gradient manipulation. Built on FastMCP 3.2, targets Inkscape 1.4.4, supports Linux and Windows, published to PyPI as inkscape-mcp.
entries.license: MIT — verified by reading the LICENSE file ('MIT License, Copyright (c) 2026 Aravind EV'). NOTE THE DISTINCTION: the MCP SERVER is MIT and safe for us; INKSCAPE ITSELF is GPL and is reference-only, but since this server DRIVES Inkscape as a separate process rather than linking it, the server code stays clean.
entries.embeddable_how: Local Python process (pip install inkscape-mcp / PyPI), stdio MCP. REPO NAME TRAP: the canonical repo is inkscape_mcp with an UNDERSCORE — github.com/aravindev/inkscape-mcp with a hyphen only resolves via GitHub's rename redirect, and its commits Atom feed returns nothing, which can make the project look dead or non-existent.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The clearest worked example of the OTHER architecture for requirement (e): drive an existing desktop design application as an external process rather than embedding a document model. That is directly analogous to EXELMJ's existing Adobe Illustrator COM bridge — and our memory notes the Illustrator COM round-trip is still the one unproven piece. This server's live-window-via-D-Bus versus headless-via-CLI dual mode is the same design decision our COM bridge faces, solved and MIT-licensed.
entries.framework_lock: None — Python/FastMCP. Requires a local Inkscape installation, which is the real dependency.
entries.last_activity: 2026-07-27 (main branch of inkscape_mcp, Atom feed)
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Inherits Inkscape's Arabic handling, which is workable for text-as-paths but weak for live editable Arabic text. Not a reason to adopt or reject the server itself.
entries.steal_this_idea: The dual live-and-headless transport: expose the SAME tool surface over two backends — one attached to an already-running application instance for interactive round-trips, one batch/CLI for deterministic headless runs — and let the caller pick. Applying that to our Illustrator COM bridge would give us a testable headless path (no GUI, CI-friendly) for exactly the round-trip our notes flag as unproven.

entries.name: Shriinivas/inkmcp
entries.what_it_is: An MCP server bridging an AI agent to Inkscape, implemented as an Inkscape extension/plugin pairing rather than a pure CLI wrapper.
entries.license: AGPL-3.0 — verified by reading the LICENSE file, which is verbatim 'GNU AFFERO GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE Version 3, 19 November 2007'. *** REFERENCE / INSPIRATION ONLY — MUST NOT BE LINKED INTO EXELMJ. *** AGPL is the strictest copyleft on our exclusion list, and its network clause is especially hazardous for anything MCP-shaped, since serving functionality over a local socket can be argued to trigger the source-provision obligation.
entries.embeddable_how: NOT EMBEDDABLE FOR US under our licence constraints. Technically it runs as a local process alongside Inkscape; legally it is off-limits for anything we ship. Read it, do not import it, and do not copy its code.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Value is strictly educational and must be labelled as such. It is one of only a handful of existing implementations of 'AI agent drives a vector editor's live document via MCP', so it is worth reading for the SHAPE of the problem — which operations turn out to need document state, which can be fire-and-forget. Included here mainly so the licence status is recorded once and nobody rediscovers it later and assumes it is usable.
entries.framework_lock: None (Python + Inkscape extension), but irrelevant given the licence bar.
entries.last_activity: 2026-01-14 (main, Atom feed)
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Not evaluated — the licence disqualifies it before RTL matters.
entries.steal_this_idea: CONCEPT ONLY, WITH CLEAN-ROOM DISCIPLINE — do not copy code or structure: the general observation that an in-application EXTENSION (running inside the editor's own process with direct access to the live document) is a fundamentally more capable MCP backend than an external file/CLI wrapper. Note this is the same conclusion Penpot's MPL-2.0 official server reaches via its plugin bridge, so we can take the idea from the permissively-licensed source instead and avoid AGPL contamination entirely.

entries.name: pulsemcp/mcp-servers — svg-tracer
entries.what_it_is: A monorepo of MCP servers built and maintained by the PulseMCP team. The relevant one here is svg-tracer, registered in the official MCP registry as com.pulsemcp/svg-tracer and described as an MCP server for converting bitmap images to SVG vector graphics using potrace tracing.
entries.license: MIT — verified from the monorepo's raw LICENSE file ('MIT License, Copyright (c) 2025 PulseMCP').
entries.embeddable_how: Local Node process, standard MCP server. No cloud service, no account.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Direct overlap with capability EXELMJ already has: our design module implements a custom potrace-like tracer (isoContour + cubic Bezier curve fit). This is the reference for how to EXPOSE that existing capability as an MCP tool — what the parameter surface looks like (thresholds, turd size, curve tolerance), and how to return vector output through MCP without blowing the response budget. It is one of only two design-adjacent servers that actually appear in the official registry.
entries.last_activity: 2026-07-21 (main, Atom feed)
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Not applicable — raster-to-vector conversion, no text layout.
entries.steal_this_idea: How it returns large vector payloads through MCP: hand back a resource/handle plus a compact summary rather than dumping a multi-megabyte SVG string into the model's context. Any EXELMJ MCP tool that returns traced artwork, a page render, or a full document snapshot must follow the same discipline or it will destroy the context window on the first call.

entries.name: montevive/penpot-mcp
entries.what_it_is: A Python MCP server integrating with Penpot's API — browses projects, retrieves files, searches objects, and exports visual components with AUTOMATIC SCREENSHOT GENERATION, explicitly aimed at turning UI designs into working code.
entries.license: MIT — read from pyproject.toml, which declares license = "MIT" for package name penpot-mcp (author: Montevive AI Team). Same caveat as zcube: no LICENSE file at the repo root, so the claim rests on package metadata.
entries.embeddable_how: Local Python process. Requires a reachable Penpot instance (self-hosted is fine) plus an API token.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Its differentiator is the design-to-code direction with automatic screenshot export — it gives the model a PICTURE of the component alongside the structured data. That directly informs requirements (c) and (e): when our AI element picker captures an element, pairing the captured styles and selector with a rendered image of that element is likely to produce far better model output than structured data alone.
entries.last_activity: 2025-06-29 (main, Atom feed) — roughly a year stale; treat as reference rather than a live dependency.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Not applicable at the server layer.
entries.steal_this_idea: Pair every structural capture with a visual one — return {rendered image + computed styles + stable selector} as a single unit from the picker. Requirement (c) as briefed captures element, styles and selector; adding the screenshot is a cheap change that materially improves what the AI can do with the capture, and this server demonstrates the pattern end to end.

entries.name: flrngel/mcp-painter
entries.what_it_is: A small MCP server providing a canvas drawing interface — creating and manipulating canvas elements, basic shape rendering, and rendering SVG content or files to PNG at a configurable output width.
entries.license: ISC — declared as "license": "ISC" in package.json (mcp-painter v1.0.0). ISC is on our allowed list (functionally equivalent to MIT). CAVEAT: no LICENSE file at the repo root, so this rests on package.json alone.
entries.embeddable_how: Local Node process, stdio MCP.
entries.why_useful_for_us: A minimal, readable end-to-end example of 'MCP tools that draw', which is the smallest possible version of requirement (e). Its practical value is as a skeleton to read in an afternoon before designing our own tool surface — and its render-SVG-to-PNG-at-configurable-width tool is a directly reusable idea for giving the model a visual read-back of EXELMJ's canvas after each edit.
entries.last_activity: 2025-03-24 (main, Atom feed) — stale; a reference, not a dependency.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Not applicable.
entries.steal_this_idea: The render-back-to-PNG-at-configurable-width tool as a first-class part of the MCP surface: after the model mutates the document, let it CHECK its work by requesting a downscaled raster of the canvas. Closing that perception loop is what separates an agent that edits blindly from one that can self-correct — and downscaling is what keeps it affordable.

entries.name: Cambalache
entries.what_it_is: A RAD (rapid application development) GUI builder for GTK 4 and GTK 3, built around a clear MVC design with a data-model-first philosophy — notable because it stores the UI design in a real database and generates the UI definition from it, rather than editing XML in place. Verified live via the GNOME GitLab API.
entries.license: LGPL-2.1 — read from the COPYING file in the repo (the GitLab API reports license: None because the file is COPYING rather than LICENSE, which is exactly why a metadata-only check misses it). LGPL is weak copyleft and is NOT on our permitted list (MIT/Apache-2.0/BSD/MPL-2.0/ISC), so treat as REFERENCE ONLY.
entries.embeddable_how: NOT EMBEDDABLE — it is a Python/GTK desktop application, not a web or Node library. There is no path to running it in an Electron renderer even setting the licence aside.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Pure architectural reference for requirement (a), and the main justification for the alternate-forge leg of this sweep: it lives only on GNOME GitLab and is invisible to GitHub-only searches. Its data-model-first approach — the design is a queryable database, and the emitted UI file is a projection of it — is a genuinely different answer to 'visual builder that outputs real code' than the schema-blob approach every web low-code tool takes.
entries.last_activity: 2026-08-08 (last_activity_at from gitlab.gnome.org API) — actively developed.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: GTK has mature RTL support and Cambalache can preview RTL layouts, which is more than most web builders offer. Conceptually interesting for an Arabic-first product even though no code is reusable.
entries.steal_this_idea: Store the design as a QUERYABLE DATABASE, not as a document blob, and treat the emitted code as a projection of that database. That single choice makes undo/redo, cross-object references, refactoring (rename a component everywhere) and diffing fall out naturally — all of which get painful fast in a JSON-blob design. Given EXELMJ already has undo/redo and layers in designApp.ts, this is the structural idea most likely to pay off as requirements (a) and (b) grow.

entries.name: silexlabs/Silex
entries.what_it_is: A free/open-source no-code website builder, v3 of which is built on top of GrapesJS. Actively developed. Its docs and website repos live on gitlab.com/silexlabs (silex_docs, dashboard-silexv3, silex_section-library), which is how this sweep's GitLab leg surfaced it.
entries.license: AGPL-3.0 — verified by reading the LICENSE file, verbatim 'GNU AFFERO GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE Version 3, 19 November 2007'. *** REFERENCE / INSPIRATION ONLY — MUST NOT BE LINKED INTO EXELMJ. ***
entries.embeddable_how: NOT USABLE for us under our licence constraints, despite being technically a perfect functional fit (self-hostable, offline-capable, no account required). Recorded here so the licence status is settled.
entries.why_useful_for_us: IMPORTANT NEGATIVE, and it comes with a clean escape hatch: Silex is the most complete open-source visual website builder found in this sweep and it is AGPL — but the engine underneath it, GrapesJS, is BSD-3-Clause. So the correct move for requirement (a) is to go one layer DOWN to GrapesJS and get the licence-clean core, using Silex only as a worked example of what a polished builder built on that core looks like.
entries.framework_lock: GrapesJS-based, so framework-free at the core — but the licence makes this moot for adoption.
entries.last_activity: 2026-08-11 (main, Atom feed) — very actively maintained.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Inherits GrapesJS's DOM-based editing, so RTL output pages are achievable via dir="rtl". Not investigated further given the licence bar.
entries.steal_this_idea: CONCEPT ONLY — do not copy code: the layering strategy itself. A permissively-licensed ENGINE (GrapesJS, BSD-3) with an opinionated APPLICATION built on top (Silex, AGPL) is proof that the builder's hard parts live in the engine and the app layer is mostly curation, packaging and templates. That tells us where to spend our effort for (a): adopt the engine, write our own thin Arabic-RTL-first application layer.

entries.name: henoc/svgeditor (VS Code extension)
entries.repo_or_url: https://github.com/henoc/svgeditor — VS Code Marketplace id henoc.svgeditor
entries.what_it_is: A VS Code extension providing a visual AND literal SVG editor — a graphical editing surface running inside a VS Code WEBVIEW, kept in sync with the SVG source text in the editor. Found via a direct VS Code Marketplace extensionquery API call (the marketplace is not reachable through normal web search).
entries.license: MIT — verified by reading the repo LICENSE file ('MIT License, Copyright (c) 2018 henoc').
entries.embeddable_how: Ships as a VSIX, but the interesting part is the webview-hosted editor, which is ordinary web code and therefore conceptually portable to an Electron renderer. STRONG CAVEAT: last commit 2018-12-24, over seven years cold — this is source to read, not a dependency to take.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Architecturally the closest analogue to EXELMJ's actual situation for requirement (b): a vector editor running inside a webview sandbox, embedded in a larger host application, with bidirectional sync between a visual surface and a text representation. That is precisely the visual-editor-inside-Electron problem, and it is MIT. Its bidirectional visual-and-literal sync is directly relevant to our SVG export path.
entries.framework_lock: None — plain web code in a webview.
entries.last_activity: 2018-12-24 (master, Atom feed); Marketplace lastUpdated 2018-12-24. Abandoned.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: No Arabic/RTL text handling — a 2018 SVG editor with no bidi awareness. Relevant only as structural reference.
entries.steal_this_idea: Two-way visual/source sync as a first-class feature: edit the shape on the canvas and watch the SVG source update, edit the source and watch the canvas update. For EXELMJ this is the credibility feature that turns (b) from a toy drawing tool into something a designer trusts — and it composes with (a), since 'the code is the design and the design is the code' is the same invariant requirement (a) needs to output real code.

entries.name: galago
entries.what_it_is: A small self-described 'simple SVG editor' written in Rust, usable as a CLI (galago path/to/file.svg) and shipping a live WEB DEMO at galago.n4n5.dev — meaning it compiles to WASM and runs in a browser. Has a sibling project, tarsier, a simple image editor by the same author.
entries.license: MIT — verified from the repo LICENSE file ('MIT License, Copyright (c) 2025 n4n5') and corroborated by crates.io metadata for v1.5.4.
entries.embeddable_how: Rust compiled to WASM (proven by the working web demo), so it can in principle run inside the Electron renderer on a canvas; also installable as a native CLI via cargo install. 2,189 downloads — genuinely obscure, which is what the brief asked for.
entries.why_useful_for_us: A rare complete, MIT-licensed, WASM-capable vector editor small enough to actually read end to end. For requirement (b), a compact reference implementation you can hold in your head is worth more than a large one you cannot — and unlike Inkscape (GPL) or Silex (AGPL), the licence lets us borrow freely. Found only via crates.io, which no prior sweep had queried beyond kurbo.
entries.framework_lock: None — Rust/WASM, immediate-mode GUI, no web framework.
entries.last_activity: 2026-07-16 (crates.io updated_at for v1.5.4) — actively maintained.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Almost certainly no Arabic shaping or bidi — immediate-mode Rust GUI toolkits generally lack complex-script text shaping unless explicitly wired to HarfBuzz. Assume text is unusable for Arabic; shapes and paths are the reusable part.
entries.steal_this_idea: Ship the editor as BOTH a CLI and a WASM/web build from one codebase. Applied to EXELMJ, that means keeping the vector document model and its operations completely free of DOM dependencies, so the same code can be driven headlessly from our MCP server (requirement e) and interactively from the renderer (requirement b) — which is exactly the separation that makes (e) testable without a GUI.

entries.name: @medv/finder
entries.what_it_is: A compact CSS selector generator: given a DOM element, produce the shortest unique selector that identifies it.
entries.license: MIT — verified from the repo LICENSE file ('MIT License, Copyright (c) 2018 Anton Medvedev') and corroborated by npm metadata for v4.0.2.
entries.embeddable_how: npm package with ZERO runtime dependencies (verified empty dependencies list). Pure browser DOM code; drops into the renderer or into a script injected into the mini-browser's guest page.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The leading alternative to css-selector-generator for requirement (c), and worth evaluating alongside it. Optimises for SHORT, human-readable selectors, whereas css-selector-generator optimises for configurability and Shadow DOM coverage. Short and readable matters here because the selector gets fed to an AI — a terse semantic selector is far more useful to a model than a long nth-child chain.
entries.last_activity: 2024-12-13 (npm modified, v4.0.2) — stable and widely used, but less actively maintained than css-selector-generator.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Irrelevant — operates on DOM structure only, unaffected by text direction.
entries.steal_this_idea: Optimise the generated selector for BREVITY and human readability, not just uniqueness. For an AI element picker the selector is part of the prompt, so 'nav > .cart-button' beats 'div:nth-child(3) > div:nth-child(2) > button:nth-child(1)' both in tokens and in the model's ability to reason about what it is looking at. Combine with css-selector-generator's verification loop: generate short, then verify unique.

entries.name: carefree0910/carefree-board (JSR: @carefree0910/cfb-svg)
entries.what_it_is: An obscure Deno/TypeScript infinite-canvas 'board' project with a modular package split; the JSR-published piece found in this sweep is cfb-svg, described as the SVG exporter for the carefree-board project. Surfaced only by searching api.jsr.io, a registry no prior sweep had touched.
entries.license: MIT — verified by reading the repo LICENSE file ('MIT License, Copyright (c) 2024 carefree0910').
entries.embeddable_how: JSR/Deno-first TypeScript modules. Consumable from Node/Vite with some friction (JSR publishes npm-compatible artifacts, but Deno-first code may assume Deno APIs). Realistically a source-reading candidate rather than a drop-in dependency.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Marginal but recorded for completeness, since the brief explicitly wanted obscure-but-fitting and JSR was an unqueried registry. Its relevance is the clean separation of an SVG EXPORTER as its own package decoupled from the board's rendering — the same boundary EXELMJ already has between its canvas rendering and its SVG/PDF/PNG export path. Small enough to read quickly for cross-checking our exporter's structure.
entries.last_activity: 2024-11-12 (main, Atom feed) — stale.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: No Arabic/RTL handling expected; not investigated given marginal relevance.
entries.steal_this_idea: Keep the SVG exporter as a standalone package that consumes only the document model and knows nothing about the renderer or the canvas. That is what makes the exporter independently testable (feed it a document, diff the SVG output) and reusable from a headless MCP context — worth checking our existing export path still honours that boundary as designApp.ts grows.

entries.name: vector-editor-core (GitLab)
entries.what_it_is: A Rust crate described as 'core structures for editing point based structures' — i.e. the data-model layer of a vector editor (points, control handles, path topology) with the UI deliberately left out. Hosted ONLY on GitLab, with no GitHub mirror, which is why it never appeared in any prior sweep.
entries.license: MIT OR Apache-2.0 (dual) — read from the crates.io API for v0.4.2. Permissive and on our allowed list. NOT independently confirmed from the repo's own LICENSE file: my raw fetches against the master branch on gitlab.com returned GitLab's 404 page, so the default branch name is likely different. Treat the licence as metadata-attested rather than file-verified.
entries.embeddable_how: Rust crate; would need WASM compilation to reach the renderer. 5,153 downloads — obscure, as requested.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Interesting specifically because it isolates the DATA MODEL of point-based vector editing from any UI — which is the layer EXELMJ has grown organically inside a 2900-line designApp.ts. Reading a deliberately UI-free model of paths, points and handles is a cheap way to sanity-check whether our own model has the right invariants before we build requirement (b) on top of it. Also the clearest example in this sweep of a real dependency living exclusively on an alternate forge.
entries.last_activity: 2026-07-17 (crates.io updated_at for v0.4.2) — recently updated.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Irrelevant — geometric data structures only, no text.
entries.steal_this_idea: Separate the point/handle/path DATA MODEL from all editing UI as a matter of principle, so the model can be unit-tested and driven headlessly. This is the same invariant that makes requirement (e) tractable: if our MCP server can mutate the document model without a renderer present, its tools become testable in CI instead of only through the GUI.

entries.name: wangyuan389/mall-cook
entries.what_it_is: A Chinese-ecosystem visual mall/e-commerce page-building platform — a drag-and-drop page builder producing mobile shop pages, with a component library and a page schema. Note the name resolution: several forks exist (AI2Hub/mall-cook-v3, MorpheusXu/Mall-Cook, ZeMingYou/mall-cook); wangyuan389/mall-cook is the upstream.
entries.license: MIT — verified from the raw LICENSE file on master ('MIT License, Copyright (c) 2022 雨尽阑珊').
entries.embeddable_how: A full Vue application (frontend plus a Node backend for its mall functionality) rather than a library. Realistically clone-and-read, not import.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Lowest-value entry of the Chinese cohort, included because it was named in the brief and to close it out with evidence. It is an APPLICATION, not an embeddable engine, and it is Vue-locked with a backend for its commerce features — so it fails our embeddable and no-server tests as a dependency. Its only real contribution is another worked example of drag-and-drop-to-schema-to-page for requirement (a), which tmagic-editor and GrapesJS both demonstrate better.
entries.framework_lock: Vue — and it is an application rather than a library, so the lock is total.
entries.last_activity: 2026-05-25 (master, Atom feed) — still maintained.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: No RTL or Arabic support; Chinese-only UI and templates.
entries.steal_this_idea: Nothing uniquely worth copying that tmagic-editor or GrapesJS does not already demonstrate more cleanly. Recorded as CHECKED AND REJECTED so a future sweep does not spend time rediscovering it.

entries.name: Chinese-ecosystem GPL projects — h5-Dooring and luban-h5 (REFERENCE ONLY)
entries.what_it_is: Two well-known Chinese visual H5 page builders. h5-Dooring is a React-based drag-and-drop page builder with a rich component ecosystem (active, last commit 2026-07-20). luban-h5 is a Vue-based 'mobile page builder like Google Web Designer' (last commit 2026-01-03).
entries.license: BOTH ARE GPL-3.0 — verified by reading each raw LICENSE file; both are verbatim 'GNU GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE Version 3, 29 June 2007'. *** REFERENCE / INSPIRATION ONLY — MUST NOT BE LINKED INTO EXELMJ. ***
entries.embeddable_how: NOT EMBEDDABLE for us. Both are full applications under a licence excluded by our constraints. Do not import, vendor, or copy code from either.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Recorded as an explicit licence FIREBREAK. These two are the projects most likely to surface at the top of any Chinese-language search for 可视化搭建 / 低代码 H5, they look extremely relevant, and they are both GPL — so without this entry a future sweep would very plausibly propose one of them. entries.name: ThorVG (thorvg/thorvg)
entries.what_it_is: Production C++ vector engine, 4,659 commits, 1.8k stars. Backends: CPU/SIMD software, OpenGL/ES, WebGL, WebGPU. Verified from inc/thorvg.h: Shape has moveTo/lineTo/cubicTo/close/appendRect/appendCircle/appendPath/trimpath; stroke API = strokeWidth/strokeCap/strokeJoin/strokeMiterlimit/strokeDash; BlendMethod enum has all 18 CSS/SVG modes (Normal, Multiply, Screen, Overlay, Darken, Lighten, ColorDodge, ColorBurn, HardLight, SoftLight, Difference, Exclusion, Hue, Saturation, Color, Luminosity, Add, Composition); SceneEffect enum = Clear, GaussianBlur, DropShadow, Fill, Tint, Tritone; MaskMethod = None/Alpha/InvAlpha/Luma/InvLuma/Add/Subtract/Intersect/Difference/Lighten/Darken plus Paint::clip(Shape*). SVG Tiny interpreter + full Lottie including expressions (on by default, build-flag disablable).
entries.license: MIT — read from the actual LICENSE file at raw.githubusercontent.com/thorvg/thorvg/main/LICENSE: standard MIT text, 'Copyright (c) 2020 - 2026 ThorVG Project'. Confirmed also in the GitHub About sidebar.
entries.embeddable_how: (b) Prebuilt .wasm DOES exist on npm — do not compile a toolchain. See the @thorvg/webcanvas entry (thorvg.wasm = 888 kB). Building from this repo yourself needs Emscripten + Meson + Ninja via wasm_build.sh, which produces thorvg-wasm.js in build_wasm/src/wasm. Also usable as a native C++ lib / Node addon if you ever want it in the Electron main process.
entries.language_stack: C++ (C++14-ish), Meson build, Emscripten for wasm. Minimum library footprint stated as ~150 KB.
entries.framework_lock: None. Pure C++ core; the JS wrapper is framework-free (the lottie-player web component uses lit, webcanvas does not).
entries.last_activity: Active — 4,659 commits, npm packages @thorvg/webcanvas and @thorvg/lottie-player both at 1.1.0.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: (g) THIS IS THE ONE REAL RISK. I read the whole thorvg.h Text class: it exposes font load, size, alignment, layout, wrapping, italic transform, outline, color/gradient fill and metrics — and there is NO mention of harfbuzz, shaping, bidi, RTL or complex scripts anywhere in the header. ThorVG issue #2731 ('renderer: enhancement: better font rendering features') explicitly lists 'Optional integration with HarfBuzz' as a WANTED future item, i.e. it is not there today. Practical consequence for EXELMJ: ThorVG's Text API assumes a simple cmap+advance run and will render Arabic as disconnected isolated forms. MITIGATION: do not use tvg::Text. Shape Arabic yourself with harfbuzzjs (MIT, already in this list), get glyph outlines, and feed them to ThorVG as Shape paths via moveTo/cubicTo. Your design module already owns Arabic bidi runs, so you are shaping anyway.
entries.steal_this_idea: The SceneEffect model: blur / drop-shadow / fill / tint / tritone are applied to a whole SCENE (a group node) rather than to a single shape, with the engine handling the offscreen buffer and bounds expansion. That is exactly the semantics of an SVG filter on a <g> and exactly what a layers panel needs — copy the node-level-effect abstraction into designApp.ts even if you never link ThorVG, so 'Layer > Add drop shadow' is a property of the layer, not a hack on each path.
entries.why_useful_for_us: (d) Real PATH API, not file-in/image-out — this is the single biggest gap resvg-wasm leaves. (e) stroke dash + miter/round/bevel joins + caps + miterlimit + trimpath; clipping via Paint::clip and 11 mask methods. Boolean path ops are NOT present (pair with pathkit-wasm). (f) THIS CLOSES EXELMJ'S TOTAL BLANK on blur/shadow/blend: GaussianBlur, DropShadow, Tint, Tritone, Fill as scene effects, plus all 18 blend modes. Nothing else in the earlier sweep had any of this. (h) init is ASYNC (await ThorVG.init(...)), so it does not drop into your synchronous Canvas2D loop unmodified — hoist one init at module load and keep a resolved handle. VERDICT vs @resvg/resvg-wasm: REPLACES AND EXTENDS IT. resvg is a one-shot SVG→PNG box; ThorVG is a retained-mode scene graph you can drive per-frame. Keep resvg only as an import/validation path for third-party SVG (its SVG 1.1 coverage is broader than ThorVG's SVG Tiny). Wasm is 888 kB vs resvg's 2.48 MB — smaller AND far more capable.

entries.name: @thorvg/webcanvas (npm)
entries.what_it_is: The prebuilt, npm-shipped WebAssembly build of ThorVG with a TypeScript Canvas-style API. Registry JSON verified: name @thorvg/webcanvas, version 1.1.0, license MIT, main ./dist/webcanvas.cjs.js, module ./dist/webcanvas.esm.js, dist.unpackedSize 2,442,177 bytes. README-verified API: ThorVG.init({renderer:'sw'|'gl'|'wg'}), Shape with appendRect(x,y,w,h,{rx,ry}) / appendCircle / moveTo / lineTo / cubicTo / close, fill(r,g,b) or fill(gradient), stroke({width,color,cap,join,dash}), StrokeCap and StrokeJoin enums, LinearGradient/RadialGradient with setStops, Canvas.add()/render(), plus Scene, Picture, Text and Animation classes. Memory managed by FinalizationRegistry with explicit dispose() and TVG.term().
entries.license: MIT (npm registry `license` field = "MIT"; parent repo thorvg.web About sidebar = MIT; core thorvg LICENSE = MIT).
entries.embeddable_how: (b) PREBUILT .WASM ON NPM — npm i @thorvg/webcanvas, no Emscripten needed. (c) Exact sizes read off unpkg's file listing for 1.1.0/dist: thorvg.wasm = 888 kB, webcanvas.esm.js = 132 kB, webcanvas.cjs.js = 133 kB, webcanvas.d.ts = 92.5 kB, plus a thread/ folder = 1.05 MB (the pthreads/multithreaded build). Ship the single-threaded 888 kB wasm and skip thread/ unless you enable COOP/COEP headers, which you cannot easily do from file:// in Electron.
entries.language_stack: TypeScript wrapper over Emscripten-compiled C++; ESM + CJS + UMD bundles, .d.ts included.
entries.framework_lock: None — plain TS classes, no React/Vue. Drops straight into your vanilla-TS design module.
entries.last_activity: 1.1.0 current; thorvg.web repo has 361 commits on main, 51 stars (obscure — exactly the profile you said you want).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Inherits ThorVG's shaping gap. The Text class is exposed to JS but is not a complex-script shaper. Use it only for Latin labels, or bypass it entirely and push shaped glyph outlines through Shape.moveTo/cubicTo.
entries.steal_this_idea: The FinalizationRegistry + explicit dispose() dual pattern for wasm-owned objects. Your designApp.ts creates and discards thousands of transient path objects per session; a JS-side object holding a wasm pointer leaks silently without exactly this. Copy the pattern into any wasm integration you do, ThorVG or not.
entries.why_useful_for_us: This is the concrete, verified, install-today deliverable of the whole sweep: 888 kB of MIT wasm giving EXELMJ a real retained-mode vector scene graph with blend modes and blur/drop-shadow, offline, no account, no framework. (h) init is ASYNC (`const TVG = await ThorVG.init({renderer:'sw'})`) — the sw renderer writes into an ImageData-compatible buffer so you can blit into your existing synchronous Canvas2D pipeline via putImageData, keeping designApp.ts's synchronous draw loop intact. VERDICT vs @resvg/resvg-wasm: strictly dominates it for authoring (path API + effects + smaller binary); resvg still wins for importing arbitrary third-party SVG 1.1 files.

entries.name: @thorvg/lottie-player (npm)
entries.what_it_is: A web-component Lottie player rendering through ThorVG's wasm. Registry JSON verified: version 1.1.0, license MIT, dependencies { lit: ^3.1.0 }, dist.unpackedSize 6,148,244 bytes, main ./dist/lottie-player.cjs.js. ThorVG's README confirms Lottie support INCLUDING Lottie Expressions, enabled by default and disablable at build time.
entries.license: MIT (registry `license` field; repo thorvg.web About = MIT).
entries.embeddable_how: (b) Prebuilt on npm, no toolchain. Ships its own wasm inside the package. It is a <lottie-player> custom element built with lit, so it drops into any DOM including an Electron renderer. If you don't want lit in your bundle, use @thorvg/webcanvas's Animation/Picture classes instead and drive frames yourself.
entries.language_stack: TypeScript + lit web component over Emscripten C++ wasm.
entries.framework_lock: Soft lock to lit 3.x (a 5 kB standards-based custom-element base, not a framework). The underlying capability is reachable framework-free through @thorvg/webcanvas.
entries.last_activity: 1.1.0, current.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Lottie text layers hit the same no-harfbuzz limitation. Arabic text INSIDE a .json Lottie will not shape correctly. Vector/shape layers (the overwhelming majority of Lottie content) are unaffected.
entries.steal_this_idea: Lottie itself as EXELMJ's ANIMATION FILE FORMAT. It is a plain JSON keyframe schema over exactly the primitives your design module already has (paths, transforms, gradients, trim paths, masks). You can EXPORT Lottie from designApp.ts with a serializer and no new renderer at all, then let any player — ThorVG's, or MIT-licensed lottie-web — play it back. That turns 'animation' from a rewrite into a file-format feature.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Directly answers the last question: YES, ThorVG's Lottie support gives EXELMJ vector ANIMATION essentially for free — a capability nobody in the earlier sweep proposed. Because the SAME engine renders both your static scene graph and Lottie playback, an animated timeline and the static designer share one rasteriser, one path model and one blend/effect model. Note ThorVG also implements Lottie trim-path and mattes, which map onto its trimpath() and MaskMethod APIs, so an authored animation round-trips. VERDICT vs @resvg/resvg-wasm: not comparable — resvg has zero animation. This is pure additive capability.

entries.name: LunaSVG (sammycage/lunasvg)
entries.what_it_is: C++ SVG rendering and manipulation library, 1.2k stars. Verified API: Document::loadFromFile / loadFromData, document->renderToBitmap(), bitmap.writeToPng(), document->applyStyleSheet() (CSS!), document->elementFromPoint(x,y) (HIT TESTING!), and per-element setAttribute()/getAttribute(). Vendors PlutoVG as a git submodule (or links a system PlutoVG >= 1.0.0). Explicitly designed for STATIC rendering — animation is stated as unlikely to be added.
entries.license: MIT — read from raw.githubusercontent.com/sammycage/lunasvg/master/LICENSE: standard MIT text, 'Copyright (c) 2020-2026 Samuel Ugochukwu <sammycageagle@gmail.com>'. The vendored PlutoVG is separately MIT (same author). Confirmed in the About sidebar too.
entries.embeddable_how: (b) NO prebuilt .wasm on npm — you must compile it yourself with Emscripten (CMake or Meson). No official npm package exists. (c) Size unmeasurable without building, but PlutoVG+LunaSVG is a small pure-C/C++ pair with no external deps, so expect a few hundred kB rather than megabytes — well under resvg's 2.48 MB. This is the main cost of adopting it.
entries.last_activity: Active; PlutoVG 1.0.0+ dependency line and 2026 copyright indicate current maintenance.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: (g) Supports <text> and <tspan> elements but there is NO harfbuzz and no shaping layer — PlutoVG's text API is glyph-level (add_glyph, fill_text). Same verdict as ThorVG: you must shape Arabic yourself and pass glyphs/outlines. Do not rely on its <text> path for Arabic.
entries.steal_this_idea: document->elementFromPoint(x, y) — an SVG renderer that answers 'which element is under this pixel'. That is exactly the primitive your 'AI element picker' feature needs on the CANVAS side (as opposed to the DOM side), and it is the primitive that makes selecting overlapping vector objects in an Illustrator-like editor feel correct. Also applyStyleSheet(): letting a CSS string restyle a parsed SVG tree is a clean way to implement themeable/tokenised graphics.
entries.why_useful_for_us: (d) Whole-file SVG-in / bitmap-out at the LunaSVG level — same shape as resvg — BUT it is a thin layer over PlutoVG, which DOES give you the moveTo/cubicTo/fill/stroke/clip path API. So the pair gives you both modes from one dependency. (f) WEAKNESS: filters are explicitly NOT implemented ('Animation, filters, and scripts' are listed as the primary exceptions; the README says filter support 'may be added'). So LunaSVG does NOT solve blur/shadow — ThorVG or CanvasKit do. VERDICT vs @resvg/resvg-wasm: LARGELY DOMINATED for the SVG-in/PNG-out job — resvg has filters, LunaSVG does not, and resvg ships prebuilt while LunaSVG needs a toolchain. It only wins on binary size, hit-testing and CSS restyling. Adopt PlutoVG directly rather than LunaSVG if you want the path API.

entries.name: PlutoVG (sammycage/plutovg)
entries.what_it_is: Tiny 2D vector graphics library in C, 527 stars, the rasteriser vendored inside LunaSVG. I read include/plutovg.h directly and can enumerate the API precisely. PATH: plutovg_path_move_to, line_to, quad_to, cubic_to, arc_to, add_rect, add_round_rect, add_ellipse, close, plutovg_path_extents. STROKE: set_dash, set_dash_offset, plutovg_line_cap_t {BUTT, ROUND, SQUARE}, plutovg_line_join_t {MITER, ROUND, BEVEL}, set_miter_limit. FILL: plutovg_fill_rule_t {NON_ZERO, EVEN_ODD}. CLIP: clip_rect, clip_path, clip_preserve. PAINT: create_linear_gradient, create_radial_gradient (with focal point), create_texture (plain/tiled, opacity, matrix), gradient spread PAD/REFLECT/REPEAT. TEXT: font_face_load_from_file, canvas_add_glyph, canvas_fill_text, font_face_text_extents. Canvas save/restore.
entries.license: MIT — read from the license header inside include/plutovg.h itself: full MIT permission text, 'Copyright ... Samuel Ugochukwu (2020-2026)'. Also MIT in the About sidebar.
entries.embeddable_how: (b) NO prebuilt wasm, NO npm package — compile with Emscripten yourself. It is dependency-free C, single small library, so an emcc build is genuinely a one-liner rather than a toolchain project; this is the least painful hand-compile in this entire list. (c) Expect a very small binary (tens to low hundreds of kB) — by far the smallest full path rasteriser here, but unverified until built.
entries.language_stack: Pure C (C99-style), no external dependencies. Meson + CMake.
entries.last_activity: Active (2026 copyright in header; LunaSVG requires PlutoVG >= 1.0.0).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: (g) NO shaping, NO bidi, NO Arabic logic anywhere in the header — I checked. The text API is deliberately glyph-level: plutovg_canvas_add_glyph() ADDS A GLYPH TO THE CURRENT PATH. That is actually the RIGHT shape of API for an Arabic-first app: you shape with harfbuzzjs, then feed glyph ids + positions in, and you get outlines in the path. It does not fight you the way an engine with a built-in naive layout engine would.
entries.steal_this_idea: plutovg_canvas_add_glyph() appending a glyph INTO the current path rather than drawing it. That single design decision means text, stroke outlines and shapes all become one uniform path object — so 'convert text to outlines', 'boolean-subtract text from a shape' and 'apply a gradient across a whole word' all fall out for free with no special text code path. Copy this into designApp.ts: never treat text as a separate drawable, treat it as a path producer.
entries.why_useful_for_us: (d) FULL PATH API — moveTo/cubicTo/fill/stroke/clip all present, verified in the header. (e) Dash, all three joins, all three caps, miter limit, both fill rules, rect+path clipping — all present. STROKE-TO-PATH OUTLINING IS ABSENT: there is no stroke→outline conversion function, only stroking at raster time. (f) MAJOR GAP: the operator enum is Porter-Duff ONLY — CLEAR, SRC, DST, SRC_OVER, DST_OVER, SRC_IN, DST_IN, SRC_OUT, DST_OUT, SRC_ATOP, DST_ATOP, XOR. There are NO separable blend modes (no multiply/screen/overlay) and NO blur/filter/shadow functions at all. So PlutoVG does NOT close the blur/shadow/blend blank. VERDICT vs @resvg/resvg-wasm: COMPLEMENTS. It supplies the interactive path API resvg lacks, at a fraction of the size, but has neither filters nor blend modes, so it cannot replace resvg for SVG import and cannot serve as your effects engine. Pick it only if binary size is the dominant constraint; otherwise ThorVG is a superset.

entries.name: Blend2D
entries.what_it_is: '2D Vector Graphics Engine Powered by a JIT Compiler', 2.0k stars. Generates optimised rasterisation pipelines at runtime with AsmJit. Has an OpenType subsystem for TrueType/OpenType glyph rendering, gradients, and blend/composite modes.
entries.license: Zlib — confirmed in the GitHub About sidebar. Permissive, satisfies your constraint.
entries.embeddable_how: (b) NO WASM. This is the disqualifier and I verified it two ways: the official build-instructions page lists supported OSes as Linux, the BSDs, macOS and Windows 7+ only, and architectures as x86 32/64-bit and AArch64 (JIT-accelerated) plus 'reference pipelines written in C++' elsewhere — WebAssembly, WASM and Emscripten appear NOWHERE on that page. A targeted search for an official Emscripten port found none. Its whole performance thesis is a runtime JIT (AsmJit), which is structurally hostile to wasm: you would have to build with BLEND2D_NO_JIT, which the docs themselves label 'experimental, not recommended for production'. Only usable as a native lib — blend2d-js exists for Node bindings, so an Electron MAIN-process render service is the only realistic path.
entries.language_stack: C++ with a C API; only dependency is AsmJit (JIT only).
entries.last_activity: Active; 2.0k stars.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: (g) Glyph-level OpenType rendering, NOT shaping. Blend2D consumes a glyph buffer; it has no harfbuzz and no bidi. Arabic requires external shaping, same as everything else here except CanvasKit.
entries.steal_this_idea: The idea that the rasteriser pipeline should be SPECIALISED per paint+composite+format combination rather than being one mega-branchy inner loop. You cannot JIT in wasm, but you CAN pre-specialise: in designApp.ts, generate a small set of monomorphic fill routines for your hot cases (opaque solid + source-over + RGBA8) instead of one general path. Same win, no JIT.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Honestly: MOSTLY NOT USEFUL for EXELMJ's renderer despite the perfect zlib license. Listed because the brief named it and because a negative result is a result — do not spend a week trying to Emscripten it.
