Risk: it is a single-maintainer project with a very promotional README, so benchmark the accuracy claims against lcms-wasm on our own profiles before trusting deltaE numbers.
entries.language_stack: JavaScript (main: src/main.js) with optional WASM scalar + SIMD kernels; webpack build for the browser bundle
entries.last_activity: v1.4.4 published 2026-05-02 — actively maintained (a second package, jscolorengine2 v1.0.8, was published 2025-11-03; clarify which line is canonical before adopting)
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: N/A
entries.steal_this_idea: Portable baked LUTs: build a transform once at deploy time, serialize the whole pipeline to JSON, and reconstruct it at runtime with Transform.fromJSON() — no profiles, no CMS, no pipeline build cost on the user's machine. For EXELMJ this means we can ship a handful of pre-baked sRGB<->CMYK LUT JSON files inside the app and get colour-managed preview with zero ICC files and zero startup cost. Also steal the LUT-free f64 escape hatch: fast quantised LUT for interactive preview, exact pipeline for final export.

entries.name: lcms-wasm
entries.what_it_is: Little-CMS (lcms2) compiled to WebAssembly — a reboot of yoya/lcms.js using WASM instead of ASM.js for better performance and memory growth. Exposes a low-level API that closely mirrors the C library (cmsOpenProfileFromMem, cmsGetProfileInfoASCII, cmsGetColorSpaceASCII, transforms). The repo's test/ folder contains two working demos: a CMYK->sRGB transform and an sRGB->CIE L*a*b* transform.
entries.license: MIT — verified from LICENSE.md in the repo (Matt DesLauriers 2024); the README explicitly states "The submodule (Little-CMS) is also MIT", and mm2/Little-CMS's own LICENSE confirms MIT (Marti Maria Saguer). Fully clean for linking.
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, zero dependencies, 579 KB unpacked for the ENTIRE package including the .wasm — remarkably small for a full CMS. ESM-first. In Vite you locate the wasm explicitly: `import wasmFileURI from 'lcms-wasm/dist/lcms.wasm?url'` then `instantiate({ locateFile: () => wasmFileURI })`. Works in web, Node and web workers.
entries.why_useful_for_us: YES, a permissive Little-CMS wasm build exists — this is the direct answer to that question. It is the conservative choice against jscolorengine: same engine the entire print industry validates against, MIT throughout, and only 579 KB. Use it in a Worker for CMYK soft-proof and for export-time conversion. Caveat straight from the README: the API is 'quite low-level', docs are unwritten (read the demos), and you must supply your own ICC files because the standard CMYK profiles are not redistributable — plan a UI for the user to point at their printer's profile.
entries.language_stack: C (Little-CMS) -> Emscripten -> WebAssembly, with a JS/ESM wrapper
entries.last_activity: v1.0.5 published 2025-01-08 — quiet but the underlying lcms2 is the industry standard and stable
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: N/A
entries.steal_this_idea: The `locateFile` indirection for wasm loading — it is the one pattern that makes an Emscripten module survive Vite/Electron packaging without a CDN, and it is the pattern EVERY wasm dependency in EXELMJ (loro, resvg, pdf.js worker) will need. Standardise on it once.

entries.name: Kittl/Little-CMS (wasm fork)
entries.what_it_is: A wasm fork of Little-CMS maintained by Kittl (a commercial browser-based design tool), providing JavaScript/TypeScript bindings to lcms2 compiled to WebAssembly for Node and browsers. It exists because a real browser design product needed CMYK and hit exactly the ceiling described in this task.
entries.license: MIT — verified, repo LICENSE is the MIT text (Marti Maria Saguer, 2023), same as upstream mm2/Little-CMS
entries.embeddable_how: Vendor/build from source. NOTE: no npm package is published under the name `littlecms` (registry returns "Not Found"), so this is a git-submodule-and-build dependency, not an npm install. Prefer lcms-wasm unless you need something Kittl's bindings expose that mattdesl's do not.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Second source for the same MIT lcms2 wasm capability, and — more valuably — existence proof plus reference implementation: a shipping commercial vector design tool concluded that compiling Little-CMS to wasm was the right answer for browser CMYK. Read their binding layer for the TypeScript surface they chose over the raw C API.
entries.last_activity: Fork of a 2023-era lcms2; activity not verified (GitHub API was rate-limited during this sweep) — treat the date as unverified
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: N/A
entries.steal_this_idea: Their TypeScript binding layer: which subset of the ~200-function lcms2 C API a real design tool actually needs. Copying that subset saves us designing the CMS wrapper from scratch.

entries.name: icc (lovell/icc)
entries.what_it_is: A tiny parser for International Color Consortium (ICC) profile headers and tags — reads the description, colour space, connection space, device class, manufacturer, copyright etc. out of an .icc/.icm buffer. It does NOT perform colour transforms.
entries.license: Apache-2.0
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, zero dependencies, 19 KB / 5 files. Trivially vendorable — it is essentially one file.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The cheap 90% solution for profile UI. When the user drops an ICC profile into EXELMJ we need to show its human name and colour space in the profile picker BEFORE deciding whether to spin up a 579 KB wasm CMS. 19 KB to read the header, and only instantiate lcms-wasm/jscolorengine when an actual transform is requested. From the sharp/libvips author, so the parsing is battle-tested.
entries.last_activity: v4.0.0 published 2026-04-23 — actively maintained
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: N/A
entries.steal_this_idea: The split itself: a 19 KB metadata reader in front of a multi-hundred-KB engine. Apply the same shape to PDF/AI/PSD import — sniff and describe the file cheaply, load the heavy parser only on confirm.

entries.name: colord
entries.what_it_is: A ~1.7 KB core colour manipulation/conversion library with an opt-in plugin architecture (a11y, cmyk, harmonies, hwb, lch, mix, names, xyz and others are separate plugins you register).
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, zero dependencies, 114 KB / 44 files unpacked, sideEffects:false, ESM+CJS+UMD. Small enough to vendor wholesale.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The floor option if bundle size ever becomes the deciding constraint for the colour picker chrome (hex/HSL/alpha manipulation only, no perceptual work). Its cmyk plugin is naive like chroma's, so it does not change the print story. Include here mainly so the shortlist has a genuine sub-2 KB rung.
entries.language_stack: TypeScript compiled to JS, no wasm
entries.last_activity: v2.9.3 published 2022-08-10 — DEAD but complete and vendorable; four years with no release, treat as frozen source we own
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: N/A
entries.steal_this_idea: The extend([pluginA, pluginB]) registration model that keeps the core at 1.7 KB — the same shape as culori's useMode but for behaviour rather than data. Good template for EXELMJ's design-module plugin surface.

entries.name: @thi.ng/color
entries.what_it_is: Karsten Schmidt's array-based colour package: colours are plain typed arrays (so they interoperate with vector maths and can be memory-mapped for GPU buffers), plus CSS parsing, conversions, transformations, DECLARATIVE THEME GENERATION and gradients.
entries.license: Apache-2.0
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, sideEffects:false, ESM-only, 275 KB / 221 files. CAVEAT: 13 sibling @thi.ng/* dependencies (api, math, arrays, binary, checks, errors, random, compare, compose, strings, vectors, defmulti, transducers) — small individually but it is a whole ecosystem entering the lockfile, not one library.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Genuinely obscure and genuinely fitting: the array-based representation means a colour is already in the layout a Canvas/WebGL buffer wants, with no boxing per pixel — relevant if the vector designer ever renders gradients on the GPU. The declarative theme generation feature (generate a coherent palette from constraints) is the most directly reusable piece for the swatch/token layer.
entries.last_activity: v5.8.31 published 2026-07-21 — very active (348 published versions)
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: N/A
entries.steal_this_idea: Colours as flat typed arrays with named-accessor proxies over them, rather than {r,g,b} objects. Zero-copy handoff to Canvas/WebGL and no GC pressure on a per-frame gradient repaint — the same argument @texel/color makes with its `out` parameters, taken one step further.

entries.name: @thi.ng/color-palettes
entries.what_it_is: A dataset of 200+ image-derived colour themes with composable query filters (find palettes by hue presence, contrast, saturation, number of dark/light entries, etc.).
entries.license: Apache-2.0
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, 103 KB / 13 files, sideEffects:false, ESM. Depends on @thi.ng/color plus a few small siblings. The palette data alone is trivially extractable if we do not want the ecosystem.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Fills the 'swatches' half of the colour requirement with actual curated content rather than machinery. A designer opening EXELMJ's vector module should find real palettes in the swatch panel on first launch, offline, with no cloud fetch. The composable query filters mean we can offer 'show me palettes with a warm dark and three cool mids' as a UI feature almost for free.
entries.last_activity: v1.5.62 published recently alongside the rest of the umbrella monorepo
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: N/A — palette data has no locale dimension
entries.steal_this_idea: Palettes as queryable data with composable predicates, instead of a flat hardcoded list. Ship the same idea in EXELMJ's swatch panel and the search box becomes a feature rather than a substring match.

entries.name: style-dictionary
entries.what_it_is: The build system for design tokens: takes token definitions (JSON/JSON5) through a parse -> transform -> format pipeline and emits CSS custom properties, SCSS, JS/TS constants, Android/iOS resources and more. Notably it already depends on colorjs.io internally for its colour transforms.
entries.license: Apache-2.0
entries.embeddable_how: Node process / build-time CLI, NOT a renderer dependency. 4.38 MB / 701 files with 13 dependencies (chalk, json5, prettier, commander, colorjs.io, tinycolor2, change-case, is-plain-obj, path-unified, @zip.js/zip.js, plus bundled-es-modules glob/memfs/deepmerge). Run it from our MCP server or a build script; never import it into the Electron renderer.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Relevant to deliverable (a) as much as (b): if the UI-builder is going to output REAL CODE for our own projects, the colour tokens the designer picks in EXELMJ have to leave as CSS variables / TS constants / Flutter or Android resources. This is the mature, permissive, fully offline pipeline for that, and it can run as an MCP tool. Its use of colorjs.io internally also means OKLCH tokens survive the transform chain.
entries.framework_lock: None for the output; the tool itself is Node-only
entries.last_activity: v5.5.1 published 2026-08-07 — very active
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Token names are ASCII by convention; no RTL implications. If we emit Arabic-facing CSS we should still generate logical properties (inline-start/inline-end) rather than left/right — that is our formatter's job, not the tool's.
entries.steal_this_idea: The parse -> transform -> format three-stage pipeline with a registry of named transforms and a 'transformGroup' per platform. That is exactly the architecture the UI-builder's code emitter needs so one design tree can produce vanilla TS, React and Flutter output without three separate codebases.

entries.name: loro-crdt
entries.what_it_is: A Rust CRDT framework compiled to wasm. VERIFIED FROM THE SHIPPED loro_wasm.d.ts: exports LoroDoc, LoroTree, LoroTreeNode, LoroMovableList, LoroList, LoroMap, LoroText, LoroCounter, UndoManager, VersionVector, Cursor, EphemeralStoreWasm, AwarenessWasm. LoroTreeNode has moveBefore(target), moveAfter(target), index(), createNode(parent, index) — a genuine MOVABLE TREE, not delete+reinsert. LoroDoc has checkout(frontiers), checkoutToLatest(), fork(), forkAt(frontiers), export(mode), travelChangeAncestors() — built-in version control and time travel. UndoManager has undo/redo/canUndo/canRedo/clear, setMaxUndoSteps, setMergeInterval, addExcludeOriginPrefix, topUndoValue/topRedoValue and onPush/onPop metadata callbacks.
entries.license: MIT — verified, repo LICENSE is the MIT text (Loro, 2023)
entries.embeddable_how: npm package. THE SIZE NUMBER THAT MATTERS: the npm 'unpackedSize' of 19.3 MB is misleading — it ships five build targets. The actual per-target payload is a ~3.18 MB .wasm plus ~270 KB of JS glue (bundler/, browser/, web/, nodejs/, and a 4.5 MB base64-inlined variant). Pick the `bundler` target for Vite/Electron and ship ~3.4 MB. Requires NO networking, NO sync server, NO account — the sync layer is entirely optional and separate.
entries.why_useful_for_us: This is the strongest single finding of this sweep for deliverable (b). A vector designer's document IS a movable tree of layers and groups, and loro gives us that tree, its history, branch/fork, checkout-to-any-past-version, and an undo stack in one MIT dependency with zero network. The UndoManager details are what sell it: setMergeInterval coalesces a 200-event drag into ONE undo step; addExcludeOriginPrefix keeps selection/viewport changes out of the undo stack (the single most common undo bug in design tools); onPush/onPop let us attach the selection state to each step so undo restores what was selected, not just what was drawn. Explicit tradeoff to weigh: ~3.2 MB wasm, and its undo is peer-local by design ('undo operations are local and cannot revert changes made by other peers') — irrelevant for single-user EXELMJ.
entries.last_activity: v1.14.1 published 2026-08-10 — extremely active (169 versions)
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: LoroText is a rich-text CRDT and is UTF-safe, but it will NOT do Arabic bidi/shaping for you — EXELMJ's existing bidi run logic in designApp.ts stays the authority. Store the logical string in loro, keep the visual runs derived.
entries.steal_this_idea: The three UndoManager knobs, whether or not we adopt the library: (1) a merge interval so continuous manipulation is one undoable step, (2) an origin-prefix exclusion list so non-document mutations (selection, zoom, tool state) never pollute the stack, (3) onPush/onPop metadata so each undo step carries the selection to restore. Our current hand-written undo/redo almost certainly lacks all three, and they are the difference between undo that feels professional and undo that feels broken.

entries.name: yjs
entries.what_it_is: The most widely deployed JS CRDT. Shared types Y.Map / Y.Array / Y.Text / Y.XmlFragment, plus Y.UndoManager with trackedOrigins and captureTimeout. Pure JavaScript — no wasm anywhere.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package with exactly ONE dependency (lib0). Real payload verified from the tarball: dist/yjs.mjs is 300 KB raw (roughly 30 KB gzipped), sideEffects:false. Networking is entirely opt-in — y-websocket / y-webrtc / y-indexeddb are SEPARATE packages; core yjs has no transport and works fully offline.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The lightweight alternative to loro when 3.2 MB of wasm is unacceptable: ~30 KB gz of pure JS, no wasm loading dance in Electron, and Y.UndoManager gives us trackedOrigins (same idea as loro's exclude-prefix) and captureTimeout (same idea as merge interval). The cost is the thing you asked about specifically: Yjs has NO movable-tree type. Reparenting a layer is delete+insert, which loses node identity and can duplicate a subtree if two operations ever race. For strictly single-user EXELMJ that race cannot happen, so this is a legitimate cheap pick — but it is a worse model of a layer tree.
entries.language_stack: Pure JavaScript ESM+CJS, no wasm, no native
entries.last_activity: v13.6.32 published 2026-08-04 — very active
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Y.Text handles UTF-16 offsets correctly but does no bidi; keep our own Arabic run logic.
entries.steal_this_idea: Y.UndoManager's trackedOrigins set: every transaction is tagged with an origin, and the undo manager only records transactions whose origin is in the tracked set. One Set membership test cleanly separates 'user drew something' from 'the app moved the viewport', with no per-call-site bookkeeping.

entries.name: @automerge/automerge
entries.what_it_is: Rust-core CRDT with a JS API, strong on rich history: getHistory(), view(heads), full change-by-change provenance, and binary document save/load.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package. HEAVIEST OPTION BY FAR — verified from the tarball: automerge_wasm_bg.wasm is 3.57 MB per target, and the package additionally ships base64-inlined variants at 4.76-4.90 MB each (dist/iife/iife.js is 4.90 MB), totalling 46.5 MB unpacked. Multiple entrypoints (nodejs / web / workerd / fullfat_base64). No networking required.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Include for completeness and because its history model is the most explicit of the three, but it is the wrong pick here: bigger wasm than loro, no movable-tree primitive, and its strengths (multi-device sync, conflict provenance) are exactly the strengths a single-user offline app does not need. If we ever want per-change authorship for an AI-assisted edit log, revisit it.
entries.last_activity: v3.4.1 published 2026-08-12 — very active
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: N/A
entries.steal_this_idea: The base64-inlined wasm build variant. It bloats the bundle but it removes wasm file-location problems entirely — a genuinely useful escape hatch to keep in mind for the Electron packaging step if locateFile/asar interactions become painful.

entries.name: mutative
entries.what_it_is: Immer-compatible structural-sharing immutable updates, faster, with an explicitly better patch story. VERIFIED FROM ITS README: `create(base, draft => {...}, {enablePatches: true})` returns `[state, patches, inversePatches]`, `apply(base, patches)` and `apply(state, inversePatches)` move forward and backward, and enablePatches accepts `{pathAsArray, arrayLengthAssignment}` — setting arrayLengthAssignment:false makes the output FULLY COMPLIANT with the JSON Patch spec (its comparison table claims this compliance where immer does not).
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, ZERO dependencies, 705 KB / 68 files unpacked (source + multiple builds; the runtime bundle is small). Pure JS, no wasm. Drop-in-ish for immer.
entries.why_useful_for_us: THE NON-CRDT ANSWER, and the one that satisfies the constraint you actually stated: single-user, offline, no sync server, no networking. A nested layer tree lives as a plain JS object; every edit goes through create(); you push the returned inversePatches onto an undo stack and the patches onto a redo stack; undo is apply(state, inversePatches.pop()). No wasm, no new document model, and it composes with EXELMJ's existing hand-written undo/redo rather than replacing it. Zero deps means zero supply-chain surface. Choose this over loro if the ~3.2 MB wasm or the document-model rewrite is judged too expensive.
entries.framework_lock: None (works with any state library, has a reducer helper)
entries.last_activity: v1.3.0 published 2025-09-21
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: N/A
entries.steal_this_idea: The `arrayLengthAssignment:false` option and why it exists: naive draft-diffing emits an array-length assignment op that is not valid JSON Patch, so strict compliance costs a little performance and they made it a flag rather than a silent default. If we ever persist our undo history to disk or send it over MCP, we want the strict mode — patches become a portable, inspectable, replayable format instead of an internal detail.

entries.name: immer
entries.what_it_is: The original copy-on-write draft library. With enablePatches(), produceWithPatches() returns [nextState, patches, inversePatches], and applyPatches() replays them in either direction.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, zero dependencies, sideEffects:false, ESM+CJS, 931 KB / 34 files unpacked (runtime bundle is a few KB gzipped). Pure JS.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The conservative sibling of mutative — same undo-via-inversePatches architecture, far larger install base, and by far the most documented. Difference that matters for us: immer's patch paths are arrays and it is NOT strictly RFC 6902 compliant (mutative's own comparison table calls this out), so if we ever want to hand a patch stream to an external tool or store it as a portable file format, mutative is the cleaner choice. If we only ever keep patches in memory, immer is fine and lower-risk.
entries.last_activity: v11.1.16 published 2026-08-05 — very active
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: N/A
entries.steal_this_idea: That patches must be an OPT-IN plugin (enablePatches()) rather than always-on, because recording them costs on every write. Same lesson for EXELMJ: record undo patches only while the design module is open, not for every app-wide state change.

entries.name: rfc6902
entries.what_it_is: A complete, standalone implementation of RFC 6902 JSON Patch and RFC 6901 JSON Pointer: createPatch(before, after), applyPatch(doc, patch), and createTests() for generating 'test' ops that make a patch fail loudly if applied to unexpected state.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, ZERO dependencies, 98 KB / 16 files. Pure JS. Small enough to vendor.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The library-free path to the same outcome as immer/mutative when we do NOT want to route edits through a draft function: snapshot the layer tree before and after, createPatch the difference, store patch + inverse. Slower than draft-based diffing on large trees but zero intrusion into existing code — which matters given designApp.ts is ~2900 lines of already-working vanilla TS that we would rather not restructure. Its createTests() is the piece nobody thinks of: guard ops that turn 'undo silently corrupted the document' into 'undo threw'.
entries.last_activity: v5.3.0 published 2026-07-23 — actively maintained
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: JSON Pointer escaping is ASCII-only; Arabic layer NAMES live in values not paths, so no encoding hazard. If we ever key objects by Arabic strings, remember pointer tokens escape only ~0 and ~1.
entries.steal_this_idea: createTests(): emit RFC 6902 'test' operations alongside the real ops so a patch refuses to apply to a document that has drifted. This is the cheapest possible integrity check on an undo stack and turns a whole class of silent corruption into a clean error.

entries.name: fast-json-patch
entries.what_it_is: RFC 6902 implementation with a distinctive duplex mode: observe(document) returns an observer that watches a plain mutable object and generate(observer) returns the patch of everything that changed since the last call — no drafts, no proxies-on-write, no snapshots.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, zero dependencies, 159 KB / 24 files, ESM+CJS. Vendorable.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The lowest-intrusion option of all for an existing imperative codebase: EXELMJ's design code can keep mutating its scene objects exactly as it does today, and we call generate(observer) at a commit boundary (mouseup, tool change) to harvest an undo patch. Nothing else here lets us add patch-based history without touching the mutation sites. Cost: dirty-checking is O(size of document) per generate, so it wants a bounded scene or a per-subtree observer.
entries.last_activity: v3.1.1 published 2022-03-24 — DEAD but complete and stable (RFC 6902 does not change); safe to vendor
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: N/A
entries.steal_this_idea: observe/generate as the commit boundary. Instead of instrumenting every mutation, define WHEN a change becomes undoable (mouseup, blur, tool switch) and harvest the diff there. That single decision is what makes undo granularity feel right, and it is orthogonal to which diff library we use.

entries.name: microdiff
entries.what_it_is: A very small, very fast deep object/array diff returning {type: CREATE|REMOVE|CHANGE, path: [...], value, oldValue}. Zero dependencies, no patch application — diff only.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, zero dependencies, 13.9 KB / 7 files unpacked — the smallest thing in this whole sweep. Vendor it as a single file.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Not an undo system, but the right primitive when we just need to know WHAT changed: dirty-region computation for canvas repaint, telling the AI element-picker (deliverable c) which properties a user actually edited, or driving incremental re-render of the layers panel. 14 KB for a correct, fast deep diff is the kind of dependency that never needs justifying.
entries.last_activity: v1.6.0 published 2026-08-02 — active
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: N/A
entries.steal_this_idea: Path-as-array (not JSON Pointer string) diff output. Array paths cost nothing to produce, are trivially walkable for dirty-marking a node in the layer tree, and only need stringifying at the serialization boundary.

entries.name: rbush
entries.what_it_is: Vladimir Agafonkin's high-performance 2D spatial index — an optimised R*-tree with bulk loading and bulk insertion. API: insert, load (bulk), remove, search(bbox), collides(bbox), clear, toJSON/fromJSON.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, ONE dependency (quickselect), 48.8 KB / 6 files, ESM. Trivially vendorable — the whole implementation is a single readable file.
entries.why_useful_for_us: THE pick for the live scene graph, and the direct answer to the hit-testing/marquee gap. Marquee selection becomes index.search({minX,minY,maxX,maxY}) instead of iterating every shape; click hit-testing becomes a search of a 1px box followed by exact geometry tests on the handful of candidates. Critically it is DYNAMIC: shapes are added, moved and deleted constantly in a designer, and rbush supports insert/remove without a rebuild. Its collides() is a short-circuiting 'does anything overlap' that is ideal for snap-guide detection.
entries.last_activity: v4.0.1 published 2024-08-21 — mature and stable rather than dead (mourner's libraries stay unchanged because they are finished)
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: N/A — pure geometry. Note that in an RTL layout the canvas coordinate system does NOT flip; only the chrome does. Keep the index in document coordinates and mirror at the view layer.
entries.steal_this_idea: The two-phase query discipline: cheap bbox prune via the index, then exact hit-test (bezier/stroke-width/transform-aware) on the survivors. Our current ~2900-line designApp.ts almost certainly does exact tests on everything; this one change is the difference between a canvas that stays responsive at 5000 objects and one that does not. Also steal bulk-load: building the tree from a sorted array is far faster than N inserts, which is what we want after a file import.

entries.name: flatbush
entries.what_it_is: A STATIC spatial index — a packed Hilbert R-tree. Verified from README: 'you can't add/remove items after initial indexing', 'faster indexing and search, with much lower memory footprint' than RBush, and the whole index is stored as a SINGLE ARRAY BUFFER so it can be transferred between threads or saved as a compact binary file. Usage is add() x N, finish(), then search(minX,minY,maxX,maxY) and neighbors(x,y,k).
entries.license: ISC
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, ONE dependency (flatqueue), 53.9 KB / 6 files, ESM, sideEffects:false. Vendorable.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The complement to rbush, not a competitor. Use it for anything frozen: an imported PDF/AI/DXF page with 50k paths, a locked layer, a reference/template layer, a font glyph outline cache. Two properties are worth the second dependency: the index IS an ArrayBuffer, so we can build it in a Worker and postMessage it with zero copy (keeps import of a huge PDF off the UI thread), and we can persist it next to the document so reopening a heavy file does not rebuild the index. neighbors() also gives us k-nearest for snapping to the closest anchor points.
entries.last_activity: v4.6.2 published 2026-06-09 — actively maintained
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: N/A
entries.steal_this_idea: Index-as-transferable-ArrayBuffer. Any derived acceleration structure EXELMJ builds (spatial index, glyph cache, tessellation) should be designed to live in a flat typed array so it can cross the Worker boundary for free and be memcpy'd to disk. That is an architectural constraint worth adopting even where we write the structure ourselves.

entries.name: kdbush
entries.what_it_is: A very fast STATIC 2D index for POINTS (not rectangles), based on a kd-tree, stored in flat typed arrays. range() and within() queries.
entries.license: ISC
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, ZERO dependencies, 39.1 KB / 7 files, ESM, sideEffects:false.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Rectangles are the wrong primitive for the thing a vector editor queries most often: ANCHOR POINTS and control handles. Snapping, 'select points inside marquee' in direct-selection mode, and 'which handle is under the cursor' are all point queries over potentially tens of thousands of bezier nodes. kdbush is the purpose-built structure for exactly that, at zero dependencies and 39 KB.
entries.last_activity: v4.1.0 published 2026-05-19 — actively maintained
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: N/A
entries.steal_this_idea: Separating the point index from the rectangle index instead of forcing degenerate zero-area rects into an R-tree. Two purpose-built indexes are smaller and faster than one general one, and the split maps cleanly onto the tool modes (selection tool -> rbush of bboxes, direct-selection tool -> kdbush of anchors).

entries.name: d3-quadtree
entries.what_it_is: Two-dimensional recursive spatial subdivision. Incremental (add/remove supported), with a visit(callback) traversal whose callback can return true to PRUNE an entire subtree, plus find(x, y, radius) for nearest-point search.
entries.license: ISC
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, ZERO dependencies, 43.4 KB / 20 files, ESM, sideEffects:false. Standalone — importing d3-quadtree does NOT pull in d3.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The quadtree alternative you asked for, and it fills the one gap rbush and kdbush leave: rbush is dynamic-but-rectangles, kdbush is points-but-static, d3-quadtree is points-AND-dynamic. Anchor points move constantly while dragging, so for live direct-selection editing this is arguably the better fit than kdbush. find(x,y,radius) is a ready-made 'snap to nearest anchor within N pixels'. Its prune-on-visit traversal is also the natural way to draw a debug overlay of the index.
entries.framework_lock: None — despite the d3- prefix it is an independent micro-package
entries.last_activity: v3.0.1 published 2021-06-05 — DEAD but complete and stable; d3 micro-packages are finished software, and it is 20 files we could vendor outright
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: N/A
entries.steal_this_idea: visit() with early subtree pruning via a boolean return. It is a tiny API that turns one traversal primitive into range search, nearest search, collision detection AND debug visualisation. Worth copying into whatever index we end up writing or wrapping.

entries.name: @timohausmann/quadtree-ts
entries.what_it_is: A TypeScript quadtree that indexes SHAPES rather than points: built-in Rectangle, Circle and Line primitives, each of which can be inserted and used as a retrieval query.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, ZERO dependencies, 99 KB / 13 files, ESM+CJS with real TS types.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The obscure-but-fitting entry for this layer. Line and Circle as first-class indexed primitives matter for a vector designer in a way they do not for a map library: a lasso/freehand selection is a polyline query, and a radius-based snap is a circle query. rbush would force both into bounding boxes and then over-fetch. Zero deps, proper TypeScript, and small enough to audit fully.
entries.last_activity: v2.3.0 published 2025-10-27 — maintained
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: N/A
entries.steal_this_idea: Making the QUERY a shape object of the same family as the indexed objects, so lasso/line/circle selection all go through one code path. That symmetry is what lets a designer add a new selection mode without touching the index.

entries.name: pdfjs-dist (mozilla/pdf.js)
entries.what_it_is: Mozilla's PDF parser and renderer. CRITICAL VERIFIED FINDING FOR IMPORT: the SVG backend is GONE — src/display/svg.js returns 404 on master, and issue #19417 ('SVG backend no longer available?') confirms SVGGraphics was deprecated from v2.15.349 and subsequently removed. The vector-import path is therefore page.getOperatorList() plus the OPS enum, which I confirmed is still exported from src/shared/util.js with the operators we need: moveTo:13, lineTo:14, curveTo:15, curveTo2:16, curveTo3:17, closePath:18, rectangle:19, stroke:20, fill:22, eoFill:23, fillStroke:24, clip:29, constructPath:91, setFillRGBColor:59, setStrokeRGBColor:58, paintImageXObject:85, plus the full text operator set (setFont:37, showText:44, setTextMatrix:42).
entries.license: Apache-2.0
entries.embeddable_how: npm package pdfjs-dist, ZERO runtime dependencies, 34.5 MB / 550 files unpacked (many build variants + the CMaps and standard fonts). Ships build/pdf.mjs plus a separate worker file — in Electron/Vite you must wire GlobalWorkerOptions.workerSrc explicitly. Runs fully offline once cMapUrl/standardFontDataUrl point at local copies.
entries.why_useful_for_us: This is the whole vector-IMPORT story and it is the mirror image of the pdf-lib export we already have. Because modern .ai files are PDFs, getOperatorList() gives us BOTH 'import a PDF as editable vectors' and a large part of 'import an Illustrator file'. Walking the operator list into our existing path model is mechanical: constructPath carries the subpath commands and coordinates, the transform stack comes from OPS.transform/save/restore, and fill/stroke colours come from setFillRGBColor/setStrokeRGBColor. The catch to budget for: we must implement the graphics-state machine ourselves now that SVGGraphics is gone — that is the real cost of this feature, roughly a few hundred lines.
entries.language_stack: JavaScript ESM + a Web Worker; optional wasm for some image codecs
entries.last_activity: v6.2.108 published 2026-07-28 — extremely active (1564 published versions)
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: HIGHLY RELEVANT: pdf.js has mature bidi handling in its text layer (it ships a bidi implementation) and handles Arabic/CJK via CMaps. If we import PDFs with Arabic text, pdf.js gives us correctly ordered logical text — but the operator list gives us VISUAL glyph runs with a text matrix per run. For editable Arabic text on import, take the text content from getTextContent() and the positioning from the operator list, and re-shape with our own bidi code rather than trusting glyph order.
entries.steal_this_idea: The operator-list intermediate representation itself: a flat typed array of opcode + args that is produced on a worker thread and consumed by a dumb, stateless replayer on the main thread. That is a better architecture than 'parse to an object tree then render' and it is exactly the shape EXELMJ's own scene renderer could adopt to move parsing off the UI thread. Even if we never import a PDF, read src/display/canvas.js for how a complete PDF graphics state machine is structured — it is the reference implementation for clip stacks, soft masks and pattern fills.

entries.name: @opendesign/illustrator-parser-pdfcpu
entries.what_it_is: An Adobe Illustrator (.ai) file parser targeting both Node.js and the browser via WebAssembly, built on pdfcpu (a Go PDF library) compiled to wasm. Extracts artboards and the Illustrator PRIVATE data embedded inside the PDF container — i.e. it reaches the Illustrator-specific structures, not just the PDF compatibility layer.
entries.license: Apache-2.0 — verified, repo LICENSE is the Apache License 2.0 text (Copyright 2022 Ceros, Inc.)

This gives us .ai import on machines where Illustrator is NOT installed and on the non-Windows path, closing the gap the COM bridge leaves. Realistic plan: use this to extract artboards and structure, and pdf.js getOperatorList for the actual path geometry.

entries.last_activity: v1.1.2 published 2023-02-09 (npm metadata modified 2024-07-02) — DEAD but complete; the .ai container format is stable so a frozen parser degrades slowly. Open Design Dev shut down, so assume no upstream fixes.

That means our EXISTING pdf-lib/pdf.js competence already gets us most of .ai import, and the private-data extraction is the only genuinely new work. Do not budget .ai import as a from-scratch format.

entries.name: svgo
entries.what_it_is: The standard SVG optimiser: a plugin pipeline over an SVG AST that removes metadata, collapses groups, merges and rounds paths, converts shapes to paths, minifies transforms and styles.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package with 7 dependencies (sax, csso, css-tree, css-what, commander, css-select, picocolors), 1.46 MB / 154 files. VERIFIED: package.json exports declares a `./browser` subpath mapping to dist/svgo.browser.js — so `import { optimize } from 'svgo/browser'` works in the Electron RENDERER, not just Node. Also ships a CLI.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Two jobs, and the second is the one the sweep missed. (1) Output optimisation: run our SVG export through optimize() so files are small and clean. (2) IMPORT NORMALISATION: run incoming SVGs through a custom plugin preset (convertShapeToPath, convertTransform, inlineStyles, convertStyleToAttrs) so our importer only ever sees paths with baked transforms and presentation attributes — that removes an enormous amount of special-casing from the import code. Its AST is also a perfectly good SVG parser in its own right.
entries.language_stack: JavaScript ESM + CJS builds; browser bundle provided
entries.last_activity: v4.0.2 published 2026-07-11 — actively maintained
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: CAUTION: SVGO plugins can rewrite or drop <text> attributes and merge text nodes. For Arabic SVG content, disable text-touching plugins on import or you will lose direction/unicode-bidi and xml:space information that our bidi runs depend on.
entries.steal_this_idea: Using an optimiser as a NORMALISER on the import path. Configure a preset whose only job is to reduce SVG's many ways of saying the same thing down to one canonical form before our parser sees it. This is the highest leverage-per-line trick available for SVG import and it needs no new code from us.

entries.name: svgson
entries.what_it_is: Turns SVG source into a simple JSON AST ({name, type, value, attributes, children}) and back again via stringify — a round-trippable SVG-to-AST layer.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, 2 dependencies (xml-reader, deep-rename-keys), 49.2 KB / 7 files, ESM+CJS. Small enough to vendor if the two deps are unwanted.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The lightest honest answer for SVG-to-AST when we do not want SVGO's 7 dependencies and CSS machinery. Its round-trip property (parse -> mutate -> stringify) is what makes it useful for import: read an SVG, walk the tree building our own shape objects, and if anything is unsupported, keep the original node so re-export is lossless. It also runs in the renderer with no DOM dependency, which matters if we ever import in a Worker.
entries.last_activity: v5.3.1 published 2023-07-17 — quiet/semi-dead but complete; SVG's syntax is not changing
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Preserves attributes verbatim, so direction/unicode-bidi/xml:space on <text> survive the round trip — better behaved than SVGO for Arabic content.
entries.steal_this_idea: Lossless round-trip as an import invariant: keep the untouched source node attached to every imported object so that anything we cannot model is preserved on export instead of silently dropped. That single rule is what separates an importer users trust from one they do not.

entries.name: svg-parser
entries.what_it_is: Rich Harris's minimal SVG-to-JSON parser producing a hast-like AST ({type, tagName, properties, children}). No dependencies, no DOM, no validation — just structure.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, ZERO dependencies, 48.9 KB / 9 files, ESM+UMD. The actual implementation is one small file — the ideal vendor candidate.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The zero-dependency floor for SVG-to-AST, and the right pick if the only thing we need is structure. Because the output is hast-shaped it composes with the unified/rehype ecosystem if the UI-builder side (deliverable a) ever wants to treat SVG and HTML through one pipeline. Being dependency-free and one file, we can vendor it into src/design/ and never think about it again.
entries.last_activity: v2.0.4 published 2020-02-29 — DEAD but complete and vendorable; six years untouched, which for a syntax parser of a frozen format is fine
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Attribute-preserving, no text transformation — safe for Arabic content.
entries.steal_this_idea: hast-compatible output shape. Choosing an AST shape that an existing ecosystem already understands costs nothing at write time and buys interoperability later. Worth applying to whatever AST the UI-builder emits.

entries.name: parse5
entries.what_it_is: A spec-compliant HTML5 parser and serializer — the same parser used by jsdom. Produces a real DOM-like tree with correct HTML5 error recovery, and can serialize back.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, ONE dependency (entities), 337 KB / 33 files, ESM. Runs in Node and the browser.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Listed in the brief under SVG-to-AST, but it is the WRONG tool for SVG (SVG is XML; parse5 applies HTML5 foreign-content rules and will mangle case-sensitive SVG attributes like viewBox unless handled carefully). It is however the RIGHT tool for deliverable (a) and (c): parsing captured HTML from the AI element picker, and parsing/serializing the HTML the UI-builder emits, with correct error recovery on real-world malformed markup. Use svgson or svg-parser for SVG and parse5 for HTML — do not use one for both.
entries.last_activity: v8.0.1 published 2026-04-19 — actively maintained
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Fully Unicode-correct and preserves dir/lang attributes; the right foundation for round-tripping Arabic RTL markup in the UI-builder.
entries.steal_this_idea: Its tree ADAPTER interface: the parser is decoupled from the tree representation, so you can parse straight into YOUR node type instead of building a DOM and then converting. If the UI-builder needs HTML in its own component model, parse directly into it and skip an entire intermediate tree.

entries.name: openfig-core
entries.what_it_is: An isomorphic .fig file parser — reads Figma's binary format in both Node.js and browsers. Decodes the Kiwi-encoded scenegraph out of the compressed .fig container. Part of the OpenFig project (openfig.org), which also ships openfig-cli for rendering and asset export.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, 3 small dependencies (fzstd for Zstandard, fflate for deflate, kiwi-schema for the binary decode), 488 KB / 8 files, ESM+CJS. Genuinely browser-capable, so it can run inside the Electron renderer or a Worker. Fully offline — parses the local file, no Figma API, no account.
entries.why_useful_for_us: This is the .fig answer and it is BRAND NEW — published 2026-08-01, i.e. it did not exist during earlier sweeps, which is why every prior search surfaced only the unlicensed fig-kiwi. MIT, isomorphic, small dependency set, and no Figma REST API dependency means no cloud account and no rate limits. For a design tool aimed at real designers, 'open the .fig my client sent me' is a headline feature. Risk to state plainly: v0.4.1, days old, one organisation, and Figma can change the format — pin the version and vendor a copy.
entries.language_stack: TypeScript -> JS (ESM + CJS), pure JS decoders (no wasm in core)
entries.last_activity: v0.4.1 published 2026-08-01 — brand new and actively developed (11 versions already)
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Figma stores text as logical strings with its own bidi/direction settings; expect to map those onto EXELMJ's existing Arabic run model rather than getting shaped runs.
entries.steal_this_idea: The container recipe, which is reusable even if we write our own parser: a .fig is a compressed container (zstd via fzstd, deflate via fflate) wrapping a Kiwi-encoded message whose SCHEMA IS EMBEDDED IN THE FILE ITSELF. That self-describing-schema trick is why third parties can decode .fig at all, and it is a genuinely good idea for EXELMJ's own document format — embed the schema and old files stay readable forever.

entries.name: openfig-cli
entries.what_it_is: The OpenFig toolchain around openfig-core: parses .fig and .deck files and RENDERS them, exporting assets. Its dependency list is revealing — @resvg/resvg-wasm for SVG rasterisation, pdf-lib for PDF output, ssim.js for visual-regression comparison, playwright-core for browser rendering, node-html-parser, @foxglove/wasm-zstd, and @modelcontextprotocol/sdk.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: Node CLI / local process, 7.05 MB / 87 files with heavy dependencies (playwright-core, sharp). NOT a renderer dependency — run it as a subprocess or behind our MCP server. Note it already bundles @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, i.e. it ships as an MCP server itself.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Two distinct reasons. First, it is a working reference for the whole .fig -> render -> export -> PDF pipeline we would otherwise design blind. Second and more interesting for deliverable (e): it is an existing MIT MCP server for design files, so it is both a competitor to study and something we could compose with rather than reimplement. Its use of ssim.js also hands us the pattern for verifying our own renderer against a reference — structural-similarity diffing of rendered output.
entries.language_stack: TypeScript/Node.js; pulls wasm (resvg, zstd) and a headless browser (playwright-core)
entries.framework_lock: None for us; internally uses playwright
entries.last_activity: v0.6.0 published 2026-08-02 — brand new, active
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Rendering fidelity for Arabic depends on resvg/playwright font handling; verify with an Arabic test file before trusting it.
entries.steal_this_idea: ssim.js as a RENDERER TEST HARNESS: render a document, compare against a golden PNG with structural similarity, fail the build on regression. EXELMJ's design module has no such safety net today, and this is the cheapest way to stop a refactor of designApp.ts from silently breaking rendering. Steal the technique regardless of .fig support.

entries.name: fig-kiwi
entries.what_it_is: The widely-cited .fig reader/writer: parses Figma's binary format for .fig files and also for the text/html pasteboard payload Figma puts on the clipboard, with TypeScript definitions derived from the Kiwi schema embedded in the file.
entries.license: NONE — DO NOT LINK. VERIFIED: the published package.json has NO license field at all (the registry returns undefined), it has exactly ONE published version (0.0.1, 2022-07-05), and third-party mirrors report 'License: None'. Absent an explicit grant, default copyright applies and we have no right to redistribute it. REFERENCE / INSPIRATION ONLY, and it must be labelled as such anywhere it appears in our docs.
entries.embeddable_how: NOT EMBEDDABLE under our constraints. Read it to understand the format; use openfig-core (MIT) for anything we ship.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Included specifically so nobody later finds it in a search, sees 'MIT-ish npm package', and vendors it. It is the package most blog posts point at for .fig parsing and it is the one we cannot use. Its clipboard-parsing capability is the genuinely distinct feature — decoding what Figma writes to the system clipboard would let a user copy in Figma and paste into EXELMJ — but that capability would have to be reimplemented from the format, not copied from this code.
entries.language_stack: TypeScript -> JS; deps pako, buffer, kiwi-schema
entries.last_activity: v0.0.1 published 2022-07-05, single version, never updated — dead AND legally unusable
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: N/A
entries.steal_this_idea: The IDEA only, cleanly reimplemented: Figma's clipboard payload is decodable, so 'copy in Figma, paste into EXELMJ' is technically achievable via the text/html clipboard flavour rather than requiring a file at all. That is a differentiating feature nobody expects from a local desktop app.

entries.name: kiwi-schema
entries.what_it_is: Evan Wallace's schema-based binary encoding format for trees of data — similar in spirit to Protocol Buffers but simpler, with compiled encoders/decoders and forward/backward compatible schema evolution. It is the primitive underneath Figma's .fig format and clipboard payloads.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, ZERO dependencies, 244 KB / 20 files, ESM+CJS. Can compile a schema at runtime (which is how .fig decoding works, since the schema travels inside the file) or generate code ahead of time.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Two uses. Defensively, it is the licensed primitive we would build on if openfig-core ever became unmaintained and we had to write our own .fig decoder — the unlicensed fig-kiwi is not needed because the actual codec is MIT. Offensively, it is a strong candidate for EXELMJ's OWN document format: a compact binary tree encoding with schema evolution beats JSON for a vector document with tens of thousands of nodes, and unlike Protobuf it has no toolchain to install.
entries.language_stack: JavaScript/TypeScript, zero deps; also has Rust/C++/Skew implementations upstream
entries.last_activity: v0.5.0 published 2023-08-11 — stable/quiet; the format is finished, and it is from the author of esbuild and Figma's original engine
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Strings are UTF-8; Arabic content is safe. Encoding is byte-order agnostic.
entries.steal_this_idea: Embedding the SCHEMA inside the FILE so the file is self-describing and old documents remain decodable by future versions without a migration table. For an app whose users will accumulate years of .exelmj documents, that single decision prevents the entire class of 'cannot open old file' bugs — and Kiwi shows it costs only a few KB per file.

entries.name: dxf (skymakerolof/dxf)
entries.what_it_is: A DXF parser for Node and the browser that goes beyond parsing: it interprets entities (including block references, arcs, ellipses, splines, LWPOLYLINE) and can convert a DXF to SVG paths or polylines.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, 3 dependencies (vecks, lodash, commander), 535 KB / 111 files, CJS main. Browser-capable. The lodash dependency is the main bundle concern for a renderer import; consider running it in the Node/main process and passing geometry to the renderer.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The ACTIVELY MAINTAINED DXF option (published 2025-09-01 versus dxf-parser's 2021), and the one that actually produces geometry rather than just a token tree. DXF import matters for the Arabic-market audience EXELMJ targets: signage, laser cutting, CNC and architectural work all move as DXF, and none of the other design tools in this space import it. Its spline and arc tessellation is the hard part and it already has it.
entries.last_activity: v5.3.1 published 2025-09-01 — maintained
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: DXF TEXT/MTEXT encoding is a real hazard: older DXF files use ANSI codepages (e.g. CP1256 for Arabic) rather than UTF-8, and DXF has its own %%u style control codes. Expect to detect $DWGCODEPAGE from the header and transcode; do not assume UTF-8.
entries.steal_this_idea: Its entity-interpretation layer sitting ON TOP of a dumb group-code parser. Parse DXF's flat group-code stream into records first, then interpret records into geometry in a separate pass. Same two-layer split is the right shape for any of our importers, and it makes the interpretation layer testable without file fixtures.

entries.name: dxf-parser
entries.what_it_is: Parses DXF files into a plain, readable JS object graph (header variables, tables, blocks, entities) without interpreting geometry.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, ONE dependency (loglevel), 193 KB / 70 files, ESM+CJS.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The lower-level complement to `dxf`: when we want the raw structure and intend to write our own geometry interpretation (likely, since we already have curve-fitting code from the image tracer), this is the cleaner starting point and has fewer dependencies. Also the better choice if we ever need to READ metadata (layers, line types, units, $INSUNITS) without pulling geometry.
entries.last_activity: v1.1.2 published 2021-11-12 — DEAD but complete and vendorable; DXF is a documented, slow-moving format so a frozen parser stays useful
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Same codepage caveat as `dxf` — check $DWGCODEPAGE before decoding Arabic TEXT/MTEXT.
entries.steal_this_idea: Reading its handling of the DXF group-code stream is the fastest way to understand the format; the file is short and the format's oddities (paired code/value lines, section markers, nested blocks) become obvious in about twenty minutes.

entries.name: @dxfjs/parser
entries.what_it_is: A modern TypeScript DXF parser with zero runtime dependencies, ESM-first, from the dxfjs organisation (which also publishes a DXF writer).
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, ZERO dependencies, 517 KB / 10 files, ESM + CJS with TypeScript types.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The zero-dependency, TypeScript-native DXF option — the best fit stylistically for a vanilla-TS codebase, since it introduces neither lodash nor loglevel. Its sibling writer package would also give us DXF EXPORT, which would be genuinely differentiating for the CNC/signage audience. Weigh against `dxf`'s superior geometry interpretation and much more recent activity.
entries.last_activity: v0.3.2 published 2023-09-29 — semi-dead (three years quiet) but complete and dependency-free, so vendoring is low risk
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Same DXF codepage caveat applies.
entries.steal_this_idea: Being a zero-dependency TypeScript parser for a legacy format is itself the lesson: for file formats, dependencies buy very little and cost forever. Prefer vendoring a dependency-free parser we can read end to end over a maintained one with a dependency tree.

entries.name: @lottiefiles/lottie-js
entries.what_it_is: An object MODEL for Lottie JSON in JavaScript/TypeScript — parses a .json Lottie into typed Animation/Layer/Shape/Property objects and serializes back. It is a data model, NOT a renderer.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, 841 KB / 10 files, ESM+CJS. Its declared dependencies are odd (cross-fetch plus two typedoc plugins listed as runtime deps — almost certainly a packaging mistake) so audit before installing; the core model itself is dependency-light and vendorable.
entries.why_useful_for_us: THE RIGHT LOTTIE LIBRARY FOR IMPORT, which is the distinction the brief is really asking about. lottie-web and dotlottie-web PLAY Lottie files; only this one gives us a structured tree we can walk to turn Lottie shape layers into EXELMJ vector objects. Since Lottie's shape model is bezier paths, fills, strokes, gradients and transforms, the mapping onto our existing shape model is close to direct — this is the cheapest path to 'import an After Effects animation as editable vectors'.
entries.last_activity: v0.4.2 published some time ago — quiet/semi-dead but the Lottie schema is stable and the package is complete
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Lottie text layers carry raw strings plus font references; Arabic text would need re-shaping through our own pipeline, and Lottie's per-character animation model does not map cleanly onto Arabic contextual forms. Treat Arabic text-in-Lottie as import-as-outlines.
entries.steal_this_idea: Modelling an animation format as PROPERTIES THAT ARE EITHER STATIC OR KEYFRAMED, uniformly, at every node. If EXELMJ ever animates anything, that single uniform representation (value | keyframe-list) is the design decision that keeps the renderer simple.

entries.name: @lottiefiles/dotlottie-web
entries.what_it_is: A Lottie and dotLottie PLAYER for the web, rendering via the ThorVG engine compiled to WebAssembly. Canvas-based, with playback control, segments and theming.
entries.license: MIT (ThorVG itself is also MIT — verified from thorvg/thorvg LICENSE)
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, ZERO dependencies, 7.1 MB / 30 files (dominated by the ThorVG wasm), sideEffects:false, ESM+CJS. Runs fully offline once the wasm is bundled locally.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The playback half of Lottie support, and the most actively maintained package in this entire sweep (published 2026-08-13 — yesterday). If EXELMJ's mini-browser (deliverable d) previews projects that contain Lottie animations, or if the designer needs to preview an imported animation before flattening it to vectors, this renders it correctly with no cloud dependency. Pair with @lottiefiles/lottie-js: that one for editing, this one for playing.
entries.language_stack: C++ (ThorVG) -> WebAssembly with a TS wrapper
entries.last_activity: v0.79.1 published 2026-08-13 — extremely active (167 versions)
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: ThorVG rasterises paths; text in Lottie is generally pre-outlined, so Arabic renders correctly when outlined and unreliably when it depends on system font shaping.
entries.steal_this_idea: ThorVG itself (MIT, C++ -> wasm) is a complete, permissively licensed 2D VECTOR RASTERISER with anti-aliasing, gradients, clipping, masks and blend modes. If EXELMJ's Canvas2D rendering ever hits a fidelity or performance ceiling, ThorVG is the MIT escape hatch — and it is the same engine LottieFiles chose over their own JS renderer, which is a meaningful endorsement.

entries.name: lottie-web
entries.what_it_is: Airbnb's original Lottie renderer for the web — the reference implementation, with SVG, Canvas and HTML renderers.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, ZERO dependencies, 25.4 MB / 312 files unpacked because it ships every build variant (light/full x svg/canvas/html x min/dev). Pick ONE build (e.g. lottie_svg.min.js) and the actual payload is modest.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Mostly as the correctness reference and as the SVG-renderer option: unlike the ThorVG-based players it can emit an actual SVG DOM, which means a Lottie frame can be captured as SVG and then imported into our editor as real vector nodes — a crude but effective 'flatten animation frame to editable vectors' path that needs no new parsing code at all. Otherwise prefer dotlottie-web for playback.
entries.last_activity: v5.13.0 published 2025-05-21 — maintained but slowing; LottieFiles' ThorVG players are where the momentum is
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Its SVG renderer produces standard SVG text/paths; if a Lottie has live Arabic text it will inherit browser shaping, which is actually correct in Electron.
entries.steal_this_idea: The SVG-renderer-as-vector-exporter trick: render one frame with the SVG renderer, then serialise the resulting DOM subtree. Any format with a DOM-based renderer can be turned into a vector importer this way with almost no code — worth remembering for other formats too.

entries.name: @resvg/resvg-wasm
entries.what_it_is: The Rust `resvg` SVG renderer compiled to WebAssembly — a high-fidelity, spec-compliant static SVG rasteriser (SVG -> PNG) that does not depend on a browser engine.
entries.license: MPL-2.0 — on our allow-list. File-level copyleft: linking is fine, only modifications to resvg's own files must be published.
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, ZERO dependencies, 2.53 MB / 7 files, sideEffects:false, ESM+CJS. Runs in browser, Worker, Node and Electron. Fully offline; fonts must be supplied explicitly as buffers.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Three concrete jobs. (1) Thumbnails: rasterise layer/document previews for the layers panel and file browser off the main thread, without a canvas or a hidden window. (2) Ground truth: when our own Canvas2D renderer disagrees with what a browser shows, resvg is the third opinion that tells us who is wrong. (3) It is what openfig-cli chose for exactly this purpose, which is corroboration rather than guesswork. Notably it renders deterministically and identically on every platform, which our Canvas2D path does not.
entries.last_activity: v2.6.2 published 2024-03-26 (npm metadata modified 2026-01-28) — stable; the native @resvg/resvg-js line is more active
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: IMPORTANT: resvg requires fonts to be loaded EXPLICITLY (it has no system font access in wasm) and its text shaping does support complex scripts via rustybuzz — but only for fonts you feed it. Arabic will render correctly ONLY if we pass an Arabic-capable font buffer. Budget for bundling one.
entries.steal_this_idea: Deterministic cross-platform rasterisation as a TEST ORACLE. Combine with ssim.js (as openfig-cli does) and we get a golden-image regression suite for the design module that does not depend on which machine or GPU runs it — the single most valuable safety net available for a 2900-line hand-written renderer.

entries.name: ase-utils
entries.what_it_is: Encode and decode colour palettes in Adobe's .ase (Adobe Swatch Exchange) binary format — the interchange format Illustrator, Photoshop and InDesign use to move swatch libraries between documents and applications.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package with one dependency pinned to bytebuffer@3.5.4 (ancient — replace it with a few DataView calls when vendoring). The implementation is essentially one small file; vendor it rather than installing it.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Nobody else in eight sweeps surfaced a swatch INTERCHANGE format, and it is the missing piece of the swatches/tokens layer. EXELMJ already has an Illustrator COM bridge, so our users have .ase libraries — brand palettes handed down by clients. Reading and writing .ase means a designer's existing swatch library opens in EXELMJ and our palettes go back to Illustrator. That is a small amount of code for a disproportionately credible feature. Relevant to the CMYK thread too: .ase stores swatches in RGB, CMYK or LAB mode, so it is a second reason we need a real CMYK path.
entries.last_activity: v0.1.1 published 2015-05-21 — LONG DEAD but complete and trivially vendorable; .ase is a frozen binary format so age is not a defect. Verify the encoder against a real Illustrator-produced .ase before trusting round-trip.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Swatch NAMES in .ase are stored as UTF-16BE, so Arabic swatch names are representable — but confirm the implementation reads/writes UTF-16BE correctly rather than assuming ASCII, as older parsers often get this wrong.
entries.steal_this_idea: The .ase format itself (block-structured: colour-group start, colour entries with a 4-char space signature ARGB/CMYK/LAB/Gray, group end). It is simple enough to implement from scratch in an afternoon, and supporting it is a concrete, checkable interoperability win over competitors who only import PNG.

entries.name: ag-psd
entries.what_it_is: A library for READING and WRITING Photoshop .psd/.psb files in JavaScript — layers, groups, masks, layer effects, text layers, and vector path/shape data.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, 2 dependencies (pako, base64-js), 12.9 MB / 2658 files unpacked (source-heavy; the runtime bundle is far smaller). Works in browser and Node. sideEffects:true, so import cost needs measuring.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The sweep covered zero import; PSD is the other file every designer has. Beyond raster layers, ag-psd exposes VECTOR path data and text layers, which means a PSD can contribute editable shapes rather than just a flattened bitmap — and EXELMJ already has raster inpainting and image tracing, so an imported PSD's raster layers land in machinery we already own. It also WRITES psd, which would let us hand work back to a Photoshop-based collaborator.
entries.last_activity: v31.0.2 published 2026-07-02 — actively maintained
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: PSD text layers store the string plus an engine-data blob containing Photoshop's own paragraph/direction settings. Arabic text will come through as logical Unicode, but Photoshop's ME (Middle Eastern) text features live in engine data that is awkward to interpret — plan to import Arabic PSD text as unshaped logical strings and re-run our own bidi/shaping.
entries.steal_this_idea: That a mature binary-format library exposes BOTH a high-level typed document AND the raw unparsed blocks it did not understand, so consumers can round-trip files containing features the library predates. Adopt the same escape hatch in EXELMJ's importers — an 'unknown data' bag attached to each node makes lossless round-trip possible without understanding everything.

entries.name: opentype.js
entries.what_it_is: A pure-JavaScript OpenType/TrueType font parser and writer that exposes glyph OUTLINES as path commands (moveTo/lineTo/curveTo/quadraticCurveTo), advance widths, kerning, and font tables.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, ZERO dependencies, 3.64 MB / 10 files, sideEffects:false, ESM+CJS+UMD. Browser and Node.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The text-to-vector primitive a vector designer cannot do without: 'convert text to outlines' is a core Illustrator operation, and it is also how we guarantee that exported SVG/PDF renders identically on a machine without the font. Since our export stack already speaks bezier paths, glyph outlines drop straight into it. Also useful for the font picker's live preview without touching the DOM.
entries.last_activity: v2.0.0 published — actively maintained project
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: CRITICAL CAVEAT FOR THIS PROJECT: opentype.js has only PARTIAL OpenType layout support. It does not implement full complex-script shaping the way HarfBuzz does, so Arabic contextual forms, ligatures and mark positioning will NOT be produced correctly by asking it to lay out a string. Correct approach for EXELMJ: keep using the platform/Canvas for Arabic SHAPING to obtain the final glyph IDs and positions, then use opentype.js purely to fetch the OUTLINE for each already-resolved glyph ID. Used that way it is exactly right; used as a text layout engine it will silently mangle Arabic.
entries.steal_this_idea: The shaping/outline SPLIT itself. Treat 'which glyphs and where' and 'what shape is glyph N' as two independent problems with two different providers. That separation is what lets an Arabic-first app get correct text-to-outlines without shipping HarfBuzz, and it is worth writing down as an architectural rule in PROJECT_MAP.md.

entries.name: svg-path-commander
entries.what_it_is: TypeScript tools for SVG path data: parse the `d` attribute to a segment array, normalise and absolutise commands, convert arcs and quadratics to cubic beziers, apply transforms (translate/rotate/scale/skew and full matrices) directly to path data, reverse paths, and optimise/round output.
entries.license: MIT
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, ONE dependency (@thednp/dommatrix — a DOMMatrix polyfill so it works outside a DOM), 1.41 MB / 15 files, sideEffects:false, ESM.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The missing utility belt between every importer in this list and our internal shape model. Whether paths arrive from SVG, PDF operator lists, DXF, Lottie or PSD, they arrive in inconsistent forms — relative commands, arcs, quadratics, nested transforms. This normalises all of it to absolute cubic beziers with transforms baked in, which is the single representation our existing curve-fitting and export code already handles. Arc-to-cubic conversion alone is a nasty piece of maths nobody should write twice.
entries.framework_lock: None; the DOMMatrix polyfill dependency means it runs in Node/Worker too
entries.last_activity: v2.3.1 published — maintained
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: N/A — geometry only
entries.steal_this_idea: Defining ONE canonical internal path form (absolute, cubic-only, transforms baked) and forcing every importer to converge on it before touching our code. That decision collapses the combinatorial explosion of N formats x M path features into N small adapters, and it is the difference between an import layer that scales to six formats and one that collapses after two.

domain: In-place source write-back (JS/TS/JSX AST → edit existing files without destroying them), the parallel HTML surgical-edit layer, CSS parse/diff/serialise, and a permissively-licensed framework-free style-inspector / CSS-property-editor panel for the UI builder + AI element picker

entries.name: recast
entries.what_it_is: JS syntax-tree transformer + non-destructive pretty-printer. Parses to an ast-types AST, remembers the original source text for every node, and on print re-emits the ORIGINAL bytes for any subtree you did not touch, pretty-printing only modified subtrees.
entries.license: MIT (verified on npm registry + repo)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `recast` (latest 0.24.0). CJS (`main: main.js`). Deps: tslib, esprima ~4.0.0 (BSD-2), ast-types ^0.16.1 (MIT), source-map ~0.6.1 (BSD-3), tiny-invariant (MIT) — all pure JS, no native bindings. Bundleable into an Electron RENDERER with Vite (the core printer does not need `fs`; only the optional `recast/parsers/*` shims pull in parser packages). NOTE: package.json now declares `engines: node >= 22` on 0.24.0 — Electron 43's bundled Node satisfies this.
entries.last_activity: npm latest = 0.24.0 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08). Previous line was 0.23.11. Exact publish date not verifiable — npm web page returns 403 to fetchers and the GitHub releases page did not render dates.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Irrelevant (operates on source text). Unicode string literals are preserved byte-for-byte on untouched nodes, so Arabic string literals in our generated code survive round-trips.
entries.why_useful_for_us: THE missing piece for deliverable (a). It is the only widely-deployed library whose documented contract is `recast.print(recast.parse(source)).code === source` — i.e. a canvas edit rewrites one JSX attribute and the other 2,000 lines of the user's file come back untouched, comments and all. Also emits character-by-character source maps automatically, so a canvas node can be traced back to file:line.
entries.steal_this_idea: The reprint algorithm itself: keep `node.original` + `node.loc.lines` on every node; at print time diff the new AST against the original AST and, for any node that is deep-equal to its original, splice the original source slice back in verbatim. That single idea is portable to ANY language (we can implement it over oxc/tree-sitter ranges ourselves if we don't want the dep).

entries.name: recast — JSX/TSX reality check (issues #365, #167, #1386)
entries.what_it_is: Verified state of the JSX complaints the critic flagged. #365 'Improve formatting of printed JSX' (opened 2017-01-22) is CLOSED. #167 'Reformatting JSX Children' is still OPEN (enhancement; whitespace-only JSXText literals show up as children and reprint awkwardly). #1386 'Extra parenthesis added to JSX elements containing comments even when AST is not modified' (opened 2024-02-16) is still OPEN and is the serious one — it is a documented violation of the identity guarantee: with comments nested inside JSX, `<List>` comes back as `(<List>` with an UNMODIFIED AST. No maintainer response visible.
entries.license: n/a (issue tracker)
entries.embeddable_how: n/a — this is a risk register entry, not a dependency.
entries.last_activity: #1386 open since 2024-02-16, still open as of this sweep.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: n/a
entries.why_useful_for_us: Directly answers 'is recast safe for our JSX write-back'. Answer: yes for the 90% case, NO as a blind guarantee. Mitigation we should adopt: (1) after every write-back, re-parse the output and assert the AST is structurally equal to the intended AST; (2) keep a byte-diff guard — if recast changed more than the ranges we intended to touch, abort the write and fall back to a magic-string range splice; (3) prefer the babel/TS parser over esprima for TSX.
entries.steal_this_idea: Adopt the 'print → reparse → structural-equality assert → byte-diff guard' loop as a hard invariant of our write-back MCP tool. It converts a probabilistic formatter into a safe one, and it works no matter which printer we end up using.

entries.name: magic-string
entries.what_it_is: String-mutation primitive: you hold the ORIGINAL source, call `.overwrite(start, end, str)` / `.appendLeft` / `.remove`, and it produces the new text plus a correct source map. It never re-prints anything — untouched bytes are literally the same bytes.
entries.license: MIT (verified)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `magic-string` 1.2.0. Exactly ONE runtime dep: `@jridgewell/sourcemap-codec` (MIT). Pure ESM (`dist/index.mjs`). Runs in an Electron renderer, a worker, or Node with zero config.
entries.last_activity: npm latest 1.2.0 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08). Actively maintained (it is Rollup/Vite/Svelte infrastructure).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Offset-based, UTF-16 code-unit indices — safe for Arabic content as long as we take offsets from the same parser that produced them.
entries.why_useful_for_us: This is the correct FOUNDATION for our write-back, more so than any AST printer. Pattern: parse with whatever gives byte ranges (oxc / tree-sitter / TS / parse5 / postcss), compute the exact range of the JSX attribute or CSS declaration the canvas edited, `overwrite()` it, write the file. Formatting preservation is then a mathematical property, not a library promise — nothing outside the edited range can possibly change. It also solves the 'trace a canvas edit back to file:line' requirement in both directions via the generated map.
entries.steal_this_idea: Formatting preservation is a RANGE problem, not a PRINTER problem. Any parser that gives you accurate start/end offsets + magic-string = a formatting-preserving codemod engine, for JS, TS, HTML, CSS, Vue SFC, Svelte, all with one code path. This is the single highest-leverage architectural insight in this sweep.

entries.name: jscodeshift
entries.what_it_is: Meta's codemod runner: recast + a jQuery-like collection API over the AST, plus a parallel file-walking CLI. It is recast with ergonomics and a worker pool, not a different formatting engine.
entries.license: MIT (verified)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `jscodeshift` 17.4.0, engines node>=16, ships a `bin/jscodeshift.js`. Depends on `recast ^0.23.11` plus @babel/core, @babel/register, flow-parser, graceful-fs, tmp, write-file-atomic, neo-async. MAIN-PROCESS ONLY — `@babel/register` hooks require(), it forks worker processes, and it does real fs I/O. Do not try to bundle this into the renderer.
entries.last_activity: npm latest 17.4.0 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: n/a
entries.why_useful_for_us: Useful for BATCH refactors driven from the MCP server ("rename this component everywhere", "add a prop to every call site"), run in the Electron main process or a spawned Node child. It is the wrong tool for a single live canvas edit — for that, call recast/magic-string directly and skip the worker pool.
entries.steal_this_idea: Its `.find(j.JSXAttribute, {name: {name: 'className'}})` collection API — a tiny declarative matcher layer over the AST is exactly the surface our MCP tools should expose to Claude, instead of raw AST node manipulation.

entries.name: ts-morph (+ @ts-morph/bootstrap)
entries.what_it_is: A navigation/manipulation wrapper over the real TypeScript compiler API. Manipulation is implemented as TEXT-RANGE edits against the source file which are then re-parsed, so code you don't touch keeps its exact original text; it does not re-print whole files.
entries.license: MIT (verified)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `ts-morph` 28.0.0 (deps: @ts-morph/common ~0.29.0, code-block-writer ^13). Lighter sibling `@ts-morph/bootstrap` 0.29.0 (MIT) is just the compiler-API setup. RENDERER-CAPABLE: package.json declares a `browser` field that stubs out fs, os, glob, dir-glob, tinyglobby, glob-parent, graceful-fs, fs.realpath, source-map-support to `false`, and the Project can be created with an in-memory file system. That combination is a deliberate browser-support affordance.
entries.framework_lock: None, but TS-only — it does not parse plain JS with Flow, and it is not a general JSX-agnostic tool (though .tsx is fully supported by the TS compiler).
entries.last_activity: npm latest 28.0.0 / @ts-morph/common 0.29.0 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: n/a
entries.why_useful_for_us: Best choice for OUR OWN codebase, which is TypeScript. It gives real type information (which recast/babel cannot), so an MCP tool can answer 'what props does this component accept' before writing an edit. TSX is first-class via the TS compiler, so the recast JSX-comment bug class does not apply. The browser field + in-memory FS means we could even run it in the renderer for preview-only analysis, at the cost of shipping the ~7MB typescript package.
entries.steal_this_idea: Manipulate-by-text-range-then-reparse: instead of maintaining a mutable AST and printing it, apply a text edit and throw the AST away. Formatting preservation falls out for free and you never have to write a printer. Same insight as magic-string, but proven at whole-project scale.

entries.name: @babel/parser + @babel/traverse + @babel/generator
entries.what_it_is: The standard JS/TS/JSX parse-traverse-print trio. Parser and traverse are excellent; the GENERATOR is the weak link — it re-prints from the AST and does NOT preserve original formatting or blank lines (`retainLines` only approximates line numbers, it does not preserve style).
entries.license: MIT (verified)
entries.embeddable_how: npm @babel/parser / @babel/traverse / @babel/generator, now on the 8.x line (@babel/generator 8.0.0 verified). WARNING: @babel/generator 8.0.0 declares `engines: node ^22.18.0 || >=24.11.0` — check Electron 43's bundled Node before upgrading, or pin the 7.x line. All pure JS, so it bundles into a renderer (babel-standalone proves browser viability). Deps of the generator: @babel/types, @babel/parser, jsesc, @jridgewell/gen-mapping, @jridgewell/trace-mapping.
entries.last_activity: @babel/generator 8.0.0 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08). Babel 8 is out.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: n/a
entries.why_useful_for_us: Use @babel/parser as the RANGE PROVIDER (every node carries `start`/`end` offsets and `loc`), then edit with magic-string. Do NOT use @babel/generator for write-back into user source — it will reflow the whole file and destroy their formatting. This is the exact trap the critic identified: Onlook's babel plugin and react-dev-inspector use babel for INSTRUMENTATION (injecting data-attributes at build time), which is fine, but that is not write-back.
entries.steal_this_idea: Babel's build-time JSX instrumentation is still the right mechanism for the element picker: a tiny babel plugin that stamps `data-src="file:line:col"` onto every JSXOpeningElement during dev builds. The picker then reads that attribute off the clicked DOM node and gets file:line for free — no source-map arithmetic, no heuristic selector matching.

entries.name: acorn (+ acorn-jsx)
