entries.what_it_is: Minimal, extremely fast ESTree parser. Zero dependencies, ~ESM+CJS dual, `engines: node >=0.4.0`. Parse-only — no printer, no formatting preservation of its own.
entries.license: MIT (verified)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `acorn` 8.18.0, zero runtime deps, dual ESM/CJS exports. Runs anywhere including a renderer or a web worker. JSX requires the separate `acorn-jsx` plugin; TypeScript is NOT supported at all.
entries.last_activity: npm latest 8.18.0 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: n/a
entries.why_useful_for_us: Only worth it if we need a tiny in-renderer parser for plain JS with `ranges: true, locations: true` feeding magic-string. For our TS/TSX-heavy target it is the wrong pick — use oxc, TS, or babel instead. Included for completeness because the brief asked.
entries.steal_this_idea: Its `onComment` / `onToken` callback design — collecting comments and tokens as side-channels rather than as AST nodes is how you keep a parser fast AND keep enough information to reconstruct formatting.

entries.name: oxc-parser / oxc-transform (Rust + napi)
entries.what_it_is: The Oxidation Compiler's JS/TS/JSX parser and transformer exposed to Node via napi-rs. Extremely fast, full TS+JSX, returns ESTree-shaped AST with byte ranges.
entries.license: MIT (verified on npm for both oxc-parser 0.144.0 and oxc-transform 0.144.0)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `oxc-parser`. ELECTRON-SAFE PREBUILT: YES — optionalDependencies include `@oxc-parser/binding-win32-x64-msvc`, `-win32-arm64-msvc`, `-win32-ia32-msvc` plus darwin/linux variants, all published at the matching version. CRITICAL EXTRA FINDING: `@oxc-parser/binding-wasm32-wasi` 0.144.0 also EXISTS (MIT, deps @napi-rs/wasm-runtime + @emnapi), which means oxc can run in the RENDERER via WASM with no native module at all. `engines: node ^20.19.0 || >=22.12.0`. Native .node binaries would otherwise be main-process-only (Electron ABI rebuild pain); the wasi binding sidesteps that entirely.
entries.language_stack: Rust core, napi/wasm bindings, TS typings via @oxc-project/types
entries.last_activity: 0.144.0 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08). Very fast release cadence.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Returns byte offsets into a UTF-8 buffer — mind the UTF-8-vs-UTF-16 offset conversion if we mix oxc ranges with JS string indices on files containing Arabic. This is a real bug source; oxc exposes utf16 range helpers, verify before use.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Best RANGE PROVIDER for a fast canvas↔code loop: parse a 3,000-line TSX file in ~1ms, get exact ranges, splice with magic-string. oxc-transform is a transpiler (it re-prints) so it is NOT a write-back tool — do not confuse the two.
entries.steal_this_idea: The `@oxc-parser/binding-wasm32-wasi` escape hatch — shipping a wasm32-wasi napi binding alongside native ones so the SAME JS API works in a browser/renderer context. If we ever ship native deps in EXELMJ, copy this packaging pattern rather than forcing main-process IPC.

entries.name: @swc/core / @swc/wasm-web
entries.what_it_is: Rust-based JS/TS compiler with napi bindings. Parses to its own (non-ESTree) AST and can print, but printing is a full re-emit — it is a compiler, not a formatting-preserving editor.
entries.license: Apache-2.0 (verified on npm for both @swc/core 1.15.47 and @swc/wasm-web 1.15.47)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `@swc/core` 1.15.47. Electron-safe prebuilt: YES for Windows — optionalDependencies include `@swc/core-win32-x64-msvc`, `-win32-arm64-msvc`, `-win32-ia32-msvc` at the exact matching version. Still a native .node → main process only, needs the ABI to match Electron's Node. For the renderer, `@swc/wasm-web` 1.15.47 (Apache-2.0, ESM, `wasm.js`) exists and is browser-targeted.
entries.last_activity: 1.15.47 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: n/a
entries.why_useful_for_us: Recommend AGAINST for write-back — it will reformat everything, and its AST is not ESTree so nothing else in the ecosystem interoperates. Genuinely useful only if we need to TRANSPILE the user's project inside the mini-browser (deliverable d) without a full bundler; @swc/wasm-web could do that entirely in the renderer, offline.
entries.steal_this_idea: Nothing for write-back. For the mini-browser: the wasm-web build shows you can run a real TS/JSX transpiler in-page with no Node process, which is how our embedded preview can run TSX projects offline without spawning Vite.

entries.name: @biomejs/wasm-web (Biome)
entries.what_it_is: Biome's workspace API compiled to WebAssembly for the browser. Biome's parser is built on a LOSSLESS CST (rowan-style, like rust-analyzer): every byte of the original file — whitespace, comments, trivia — is represented in the tree, so a serialise of an unmodified tree is byte-identical by construction, not by heuristic.
entries.license: MIT OR Apache-2.0 (dual, verified on npm)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `@biomejs/wasm-web` 2.5.8. `type: module`, entry `biome_wasm.js`, types `biome_wasm.d.ts`. Runs in an Electron RENDERER. Cost: ~45MB unpacked (the wasm blob). Node-side equivalents are `@biomejs/js-api` + `@biomejs/wasm-nodejs` / native `@biomejs/cli-*`.
entries.last_activity: 2.5.8 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08). Very active.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: n/a
entries.why_useful_for_us: The most structurally correct formatting-preservation model available under a permissive licence, and it runs in the renderer. Caveat that keeps it out of first place: Biome's public JS API today exposes format/lint/parse-diagnostics, not a stable 'mutate this CST node and serialise' API — using it as our write-back engine would mean depending on internals. Track it; do not bet the module on it yet.
entries.steal_this_idea: The lossless-CST idea itself. If we build our own tiny write-back engine, model the tree as (green node, trivia) pairs where trivia is attached to tokens — then 'preserve formatting' stops being a feature you implement and becomes something you cannot break.

entries.name: web-tree-sitter
entries.what_it_is: Tree-sitter's incremental parser compiled to WebAssembly with JS bindings. Concrete syntax tree with exact byte ranges for every node, incremental re-parse on edit, and per-language grammars loaded as separate .wasm files.
entries.license: MIT (verified)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `web-tree-sitter` 0.26.12, zero runtime deps, ships both ESM (`web-tree-sitter.js`) and CJS (`.cjs`) plus `web-tree-sitter.wasm`. Runs in an Electron RENDERER with no native module. Grammars (tree-sitter-typescript, -tsx, -css, -html) are separate .wasm files we vendor once — fully offline.
entries.last_activity: 0.26.12 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Byte offsets are UTF-8; the JS binding also exposes point (row/column) positions. Same UTF-8/UTF-16 conversion caution as oxc for Arabic text.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Strongest renderer-side option for the 'canvas edit → exact source range' problem across MULTIPLE languages with ONE dependency: TSX, CSS and HTML all covered by grammars, all in-process, all offline. Pair with magic-string and the formatting question disappears. Also gives us incremental re-parse, so we can keep a live tree in sync with a CodeMirror buffer at 60fps.
entries.steal_this_idea: Incremental `tree.edit({startIndex, oldEndIndex, newEndIndex, ...})` then `parser.parse(newSrc, oldTree)` — reparsing only the damaged region. This is what lets a visual builder keep an authoritative AST alive while the user types, instead of re-parsing the file on every keystroke.

entries.name: @ast-grep/napi
entries.what_it_is: Structural search-and-replace over tree-sitter CSTs using code PATTERNS (`console.log($ARG)` → `logger.debug($ARG)`). Rewrites are range splices into the original text, so everything outside a match is preserved verbatim.
entries.license: MIT (verified)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `@ast-grep/napi` 0.45.1, engines node>=10. Electron-safe prebuilt: YES for Windows — optionalDependencies include `@ast-grep/napi-win32-x64-msvc`, `-win32-arm64-msvc`, `-win32-ia32-msvc`. Native .node → MAIN PROCESS only (renderer would need the ABI rebuilt). No wasi binding listed in the optionalDeps, unlike oxc.
entries.last_activity: 0.45.1 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: n/a
entries.why_useful_for_us: Excellent MCP tool surface: Claude can express a refactor as a pattern + rewrite string instead of writing AST-walking code, and formatting preservation is guaranteed because only matched ranges are replaced. Perfect for 'add a className to every <Button>' style edits driven from chat. Run it in the main process behind an IPC/MCP boundary.
entries.steal_this_idea: Pattern-based rewriting as the AGENT-FACING API. Raw AST manipulation is a terrible interface for an LLM; `pattern` + `rewrite` with `$METAVARIABLES` is compact, reviewable, and inherently non-destructive. Our MCP server should expose this shape even if we implement it ourselves.

entries.name: magicast (unjs)
entries.what_it_is: A proxy-based facade that lets you edit a JS/TS module as if it were a plain JS object (`mod.exports.default.plugins.push(...)`) and write it back with the original formatting, quote style and indentation intact.
entries.license: MIT (verified)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `magicast` 0.5.4. Runtime deps are only @babel/parser, @babel/types, source-map-js — because it now INLINES recast 0.23.18 into its own dist (recast appears in devDependencies and in an `inlinedDependencies` field). Pure JS, ESM, subpath exports `./core` and `./helpers`. Bundleable into a renderer; `loadFile`/`writeFile` obviously need Node fs, but the `parseModule`/`generateCode` core does not.
entries.last_activity: 0.5.4 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Preserves original quote style, so Arabic string literals in config/source are written back unchanged.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The obscure-but-perfect-fit find for one specific job: editing CONFIG and REGISTRY files that our UI builder must maintain (routes lists, component registries, theme objects, vite.config.ts, i18n dictionaries). Doing that through recast by hand is 200 lines; through magicast it is 3. Its 'smart formatting' detection (infers tabs/quotes from surrounding code) is exactly what a generator needs so emitted code matches the user's house style.
entries.steal_this_idea: The `detectCodeFormat()` heuristic — sniff quote style, indentation and semicolon usage from the existing file and apply them to NEWLY inserted nodes. That is the missing half of recast's guarantee: recast preserves old code, this makes new code look like it belongs.

entries.name: esrap
entries.what_it_is: 'Parse in reverse' — a tiny ESTree→string printer by Rich Harris, used by the Svelte 5 compiler. Ships TS and TSX language modules that print @typescript-eslint/types-shaped ASTs. Generates sourcemap mappings when the AST carries `loc` (e.g. acorn with `locations: true`).
entries.license: MIT (verified)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `esrap` 2.3.3. Single runtime dep `@jridgewell/sourcemap-codec` (MIT). Ships raw ESM source (`./src/index.js`, `./src/languages/ts`, `./src/languages/tsx`). Renderer-safe, tiny.
entries.framework_lock: None (it is Svelte-adjacent but has no Svelte dependency)
entries.last_activity: 2.3.3 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: n/a
entries.why_useful_for_us: Not a formatting-PRESERVING printer — but it IS a small, sourcemap-producing TSX printer for code we generate FROM SCRATCH (new component files, new route files), where there is no user formatting to preserve. Much lighter than @babel/generator and it has explicit TSX support, which is where recast is weakest. Good division of labour: esrap for new files, magic-string+ranges for edits to existing files.
entries.steal_this_idea: Its language-module design: the printer core is language-agnostic and TS/TSX are pluggable visitor tables. If we generate for several targets (TSX, plain HTML/JS, maybe Flutter later), a pluggable print table beats one monolithic generator.

entries.name: astring
entries.what_it_is: Tiny, very fast ESTree→JS code generator (~16KB min, ~4KB gzip), zero dependencies, with optional source-map generation.
entries.license: MIT (verified)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `astring` 1.9.0. Zero runtime deps. Exports ESM (`dist/astring.mjs`), CJS (`dist/astring.js`) and a dedicated `browser` build (`dist/astring.min.js`). Trivially renderer-safe.
entries.last_activity: 1.9.0 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08). Mature/low-churn rather than dead.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: n/a
entries.why_useful_for_us: Backup/alternative to esrap for from-scratch generation when we want the absolute smallest renderer bundle. Plain-ESTree only — no TS/JSX out of the box (you supply custom generator entries), which is its main limitation for us.
entries.steal_this_idea: Its generator-as-a-lookup-table design (`{NodeType: (node, state) => ...}`) that you can extend with your own node types. That is how we would print OUR OWN intermediate representation (canvas node tree) without inventing a printer framework.

entries.name: parse5 (+ sourceCodeLocationInfo)
entries.what_it_is: Spec-compliant WHATWG HTML5 parser and serializer. With `sourceCodeLocationInfo: true` every node (except the root) gets a `sourceCodeLocation` — an ElementLocation for non-empty elements and a Location for empty ones — with start/end offsets and per-ATTRIBUTE locations.
entries.license: MIT (verified)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `parse5` 8.0.1. One runtime dep: `entities` ^8.0.0 (BSD-2). ESM, `dist/index.js`. Pure JS, no node builtins → runs fine in an Electron RENDERER.
entries.last_activity: 8.0.1 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Handles `dir="rtl"`, `lang="ar"` and Arabic text as ordinary markup. Serializer escapes only what the HTML spec requires, so Arabic text is not entity-mangled.
entries.why_useful_for_us: This is the HTML half of the write-back answer and it is CLEANER than the JS half: parse5's location info gives us the exact byte range of `<div class="...">` and of the `class` attribute VALUE specifically. Point magic-string at that range and an HTML edit from the canvas is provably surgical — comments, indentation, and even malformed-but-tolerated markup elsewhere in the file are untouched. Do NOT use parse5's own `serialize()` for write-back (it normalises); use it only for read-side analysis.
entries.steal_this_idea: Per-attribute source locations (`sourceCodeLocation.attrs.class`). That granularity is what turns 'edit the HTML' into 'replace 11 bytes'. Anyone shipping an HTML AST without per-attribute ranges has built a code generator, not an editor.

entries.name: htmlparser2
entries.what_it_is: Fast, forgiving streaming HTML/XML parser producing a domhandler DOM. Supports index-tracking options so nodes carry startIndex/endIndex.
entries.license: MIT (verified)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `htmlparser2` 12.0.0. Deps: domutils ^4, domhandler ^6, domelementtype ^3, entities ^8 (all BSD-2/MIT). Exports include a `WebWritableStream` build explicitly for browser/streams usage → renderer-safe.
entries.last_activity: 12.0.0 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: n/a
entries.why_useful_for_us: Lighter, faster alternative to parse5 when we do not need full HTML5 tree-construction spec compliance (e.g. parsing a component template fragment rather than a document). It is the parser posthtml-parser sits on. Its `withStartIndices`/`withEndIndices` domhandler options give the ranges magic-string needs.
entries.steal_this_idea: n/a — pick it or parse5, not both.

entries.name: posthtml + posthtml-parser
entries.what_it_is: PostCSS-style plugin pipeline for HTML: parse to a simple JSON-ish tree (`[{tag, attrs, content}]`), run plugins, render back. posthtml-parser exposes `sourceLocations: true` which attaches a `location` with `start` and `end` LINE/COLUMN to each node.
entries.license: MIT (verified for both `posthtml` 0.16.7 and `posthtml-parser` 0.12.1)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `posthtml` (deps posthtml-parser + posthtml-render), engines node>=12. posthtml-parser wraps htmlparser2 ^9. Pure JS, renderer-safe.
entries.last_activity: posthtml 0.16.7 / posthtml-parser 0.12.1 (registry-verified). Low churn — mature but not abandoned; treat as stable-but-slow.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: n/a
entries.why_useful_for_us: Weaker than parse5 for our purposes for one concrete reason I verified: `sourceLocations` gives line/column, NOT byte offsets, so we would have to convert positions ourselves before splicing. Its real value is the PLUGIN PIPELINE shape — if we want user-extensible HTML transforms in the builder, this is the smallest permissive framework for that.
entries.steal_this_idea: The tree shape `{tag, attrs, content}` — a JSON-serialisable HTML representation is trivially sendable over MCP to Claude and back, unlike a parse5 DOM full of circular parent pointers. Worth adopting as our WIRE format even if parse5 is our parser.

entries.name: unified / rehype / hast (+ rehype-parse, rehype-stringify)
entries.what_it_is: The unified ecosystem's HTML processor: rehype-parse (built on parse5) → hast tree with `position` info → plugins → rehype-stringify. Huge utility ecosystem (hast-util-*, unist-util-visit, property-information).
entries.license: MIT (verified for `rehype` 13.0.2; the whole unified/syntax-tree org is MIT)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `rehype` 13.0.2 (deps unified ^11, rehype-parse ^9, rehype-stringify ^10, @types/hast ^3). Pure ESM, pure JS, renderer-safe. Very granular — you can take just `hast-util-to-html` or `unist-util-visit`.
entries.last_activity: rehype 13.0.2 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: `property-information` correctly handles `dir`, `lang` and other RTL-relevant attributes when converting between HTML attribute names and hast property names.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Good for ANALYSIS and for generating new HTML; BAD as a round-trip write-back path — rehype-stringify normalises quoting, attribute order, self-closing syntax and whitespace, so `stringify(parse(html)) !== html`. Use hast's `position` offsets as the range source and splice with magic-string instead of stringifying. Note also that @compai/css-gui (below) is built on this ecosystem, so if we take css.gui we get unified anyway.
entries.steal_this_idea: `unist-util-visit`'s visitor contract (`visit(tree, test, (node, index, parent) => ...)` with SKIP/EXIT control) — the cleanest tree-walking API in JS. Worth copying for our own canvas node tree.

entries.name: postcss
entries.what_it_is: The CSS equivalent of recast, and the answer to the 'total CSS hole'. Its AST nodes carry a `raws` object which the docs describe as holding the whitespace and characters needed to 'generate byte-to-byte equal node string as it was in the origin input' (raws.before / after / between / semicolon / afterName / left / right), plus a `source` with input file and start/end line+column.
entries.license: MIT (verified)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `postcss` 8.5.26, engines node ^10 || ^12 || >=14. Only three runtime deps — nanoid, picocolors, source-map-js — all pure JS with no node builtins. 24 subpath exports (parser, processor, node types, tokenizer, map-generator). Runs in an Electron RENDERER; there is a long history of postcss running in browsers/playgrounds.
entries.last_activity: 8.5.26 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08). Actively maintained.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Preserves declaration text verbatim, so logical properties (`margin-inline-start`, `padding-inline-end`) and `direction: rtl` survive untouched — important because our Arabic-first UI builder should emit logical properties, not left/right.
entries.why_useful_for_us: THE pick for the CSS write-back hole. `root.toString()` reproduces the input byte-for-byte thanks to raws, so an AI element picker can change `color: red` → `color: blue` in the user's stylesheet and nothing else in the file moves — comments, blank lines and their formatting all intact. Same guarantee class as recast, but without recast's JSX-comment bug. Also gives source maps for canvas→file:line tracing.
entries.steal_this_idea: The `raws` concept: store the INSIGNIFICANT characters on the node instead of throwing them away, keyed by where they sat (before/between/after). It is a cheaper, more debuggable formatting-preservation model than either recast's original-source-diffing or Biome's full lossless CST, and it is easy to reimplement for our own node types.

entries.name: css-tree (csstree)
entries.what_it_is: Detailed CSS parser + walker + generator + LEXER that validates declarations against the real CSS grammar using mdn-data. `positions: true` records `loc` (offset/line/column) on every node. Options: positions, parseValue, parseAtrulePrelude, parseRulePrelude, onComment, onToken, onParseError, context, filename/offset/line/column.
entries.license: MIT (verified)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `css-tree` 3.2.1. Deps: mdn-data 2.27.1 (CC0) + source-map-js ^1.2.1 (BSD-3). Ships dual ESM/CJS with per-feature subpath exports (lexer, parser, walker, generator, tokenizer, definition-syntax) AND an explicit browser build `dist/csstree.esm.js`. Renderer-safe.
entries.last_activity: 3.2.1 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: n/a
entries.why_useful_for_us: Use it for what postcss cannot do: VALIDATE a CSS property/value pair against the spec before we write it (`lexer.matchProperty`), autocomplete allowed values in the style panel, and parse selectors/values into structured pieces. CRITICAL CAVEAT I VERIFIED IN THE DOCS: css-tree's parser 'omits redundant separators, spaces and comments (except exclamation comments)' when building the AST — so `generate(parse(css))` does NOT round-trip and WILL strip the user's comments. Never use css-tree as the write-back printer; use it as an analyser and take `loc` offsets into magic-string.
entries.steal_this_idea: The mdn-data-driven LEXER. `lexer.matchProperty('margin-inline-start', valueAst)` gives you spec-accurate validation and, inverted, the set of legal values for a property — which is exactly the data a style-inspector panel needs to render the right control (length picker vs colour picker vs keyword dropdown) for all ~600 CSS properties without hand-writing a schema.

entries.name: lightningcss / lightningcss-wasm
entries.what_it_is: Rust CSS parser, transformer, minifier and vendor-prefixer with a JS visitor API. It fully re-prints output (that is the point — it minifies and lowers modern syntax), so it does not preserve the user's formatting or comments.
entries.license: MPL-2.0 (verified on npm for BOTH lightningcss 1.33.0 and lightningcss-wasm 1.33.0). MPL-2.0 is file-level copyleft and is explicitly on our allowed list; we can link it without opening our source, but modifications to ITS files must be published.
entries.embeddable_how: npm `lightningcss` 1.33.0 — native napi with prebuilt Windows bindings (`lightningcss-win32-x64-msvc`, `lightningcss-win32-arm64-msvc`) plus darwin/linux/android/freebsd; one dep `detect-libc`; engines node>=12; native .node → MAIN PROCESS only. VERIFIED ALTERNATIVE: `lightningcss-wasm` 1.33.0 exists (MPL-2.0, dep `napi-wasm`) with conditional exports — node paths (`wasm-node.mjs/.cjs`), a browser default (`index.mjs/.cjs`), and the raw `.wasm` exported — so it RUNS IN THE RENDERER offline.
entries.last_activity: 1.33.0 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Notably good at logical properties and can LOWER `margin-inline-start` to physical properties for old targets — useful if our exported projects must support old browsers while we author RTL-correctly.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Wrong tool for write-back, right tool for the PREVIEW pipeline: in the embedded mini-browser (deliverable d) we need to take the styles the canvas produced, autoprefix and lower them, and inject them live — lightningcss-wasm does that in-renderer with no Node process. Its visitor API is also the fastest way to statically extract every colour/font/spacing token from a user's stylesheet for a design-token panel.
entries.steal_this_idea: Its JS `visitor` API over a Rust AST (`{ Rule(rule){...}, Declaration(decl){...} }`) — a well-designed FFI boundary where the fast path stays in Rust and only nodes you asked for cross into JS. If we ever put oxc/tree-sitter behind IPC, copy this selective-visitation design instead of shipping whole ASTs across the boundary.

entries.name: @adobe/css-tools
entries.what_it_is: A maintained, TypeScript-rewritten fork of the classic reworkcss/css parser+stringifier. Produces a small, plain-JSON CSS AST with `position` info (start/end line+column) on nodes, and a stringifier with a compress option.
entries.license: MIT (verified)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `@adobe/css-tools` 4.5.0. ZERO runtime dependencies. Dual exports: ESM `dist/esm/adobe-css-tools.mjs` and CJS `dist/cjs/adobe-css-tools.cjs`, with .d.mts types. Renderer-safe, tiny.
entries.last_activity: 4.5.0 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08). Kept alive because @testing-library/jest-dom depends on it.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: n/a
entries.why_useful_for_us: The obscure-but-fitting lightweight option: when we only need to read a stylesheet into JSON, find a rule, and know where it is in the file — with zero dependency surface — this beats pulling in postcss's plugin machinery. Good for the AI element picker's read path (which rule matched, at which line). I did NOT independently verify from source that `position` is populated by default in 4.5.0 (the reworkcss lineage has always had it, and the docs describe a `silent`/`source` option set) — verify before relying on it.
entries.steal_this_idea: Its API minimalism: `parse(css) -> {type:'stylesheet', stylesheet:{rules:[...]}}` as plain JSON. A CSS AST that is JSON.stringify-able crosses the MCP boundary to Claude for free; postcss nodes do not (circular parent refs, class instances).

entries.name: stylis
entries.what_it_is: A ~5KB CSS preprocessor (nesting, vendor prefixing, scoping) built as a middleware pipeline. It is the engine inside emotion and styled-components. Compiles CSS → CSS; it is not an editor and keeps no formatting.
entries.license: MIT (verified)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `stylis` 4.4.0. ZERO runtime dependencies. `import` → `./index.js` (ESM), `require` → `./dist/umd/stylis.js`. Runs anywhere, including the renderer. Notable: `stylis-plugin-rtl` (MIT, community) provides RTL flipping on top of it.
entries.framework_lock: None (framework-agnostic, though CSS-in-JS libraries are its main consumers)
entries.last_activity: 4.4.0 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: DIRECTLY RELEVANT TO EXELMJ: the `stylis-plugin-rtl` middleware (used by MUI for Arabic/Hebrew) auto-flips physical properties (left↔right, padding-left↔padding-right, transforms) at compile time. That is a ready-made LTR→RTL mirroring stage for styles our builder emits.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Not for write-back. Two real uses: (1) live style injection in the mini-browser preview — take the canvas's style object, run it through stylis, inject one <style> tag, no build step; (2) the RTL flipping plugin, which is otherwise a chunk of work we would have to write ourselves for an Arabic-first builder.
entries.steal_this_idea: The RTL-flip middleware as a PIPELINE STAGE rather than a property-by-property special case in the editor. Author everything LTR-logically, flip at emit time — the style panel stays simple and RTL correctness becomes one deterministic pass.

entries.name: postcss-selector-parser + @bramus/specificity + specificity
entries.what_it_is: The cascade/specificity helper layer the sweep was missing. postcss-selector-parser 7.1.5 (MIT, deps cssesc + util-deprecate) parses a selector string into a manipulable node tree. @bramus/specificity 2.4.2 (MIT, dep css-tree ^3) computes (a,b,c) specificity per the current spec including :is()/:where()/:not() and ships subpath exports for core/sort/compare/filter/util. keeganstreet's `specificity` 1.0.0 (MIT, dep css-tree ^2.3.1) is the older, simpler equivalent.
entries.license: MIT for all three (each verified on the npm registry)
entries.embeddable_how: All npm, all pure JS, all renderer-safe. @bramus/specificity declares a `browser` export condition explicitly. Note the css-tree major mismatch: @bramus/specificity wants css-tree ^3, keeganstreet's specificity wants ^2 — pick ONE to avoid two copies of css-tree in the bundle. Prefer @bramus/specificity.
entries.last_activity: postcss-selector-parser 7.1.5, @bramus/specificity 2.4.2, specificity 1.0.0 (all registry-verified as of 2026-08).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: n/a
entries.why_useful_for_us: Required by BOTH the style-inspector panel and the AI element picker, and named by no previous sweep. When the picker reports 'this element's colour comes from these 4 rules', we must sort them by origin → specificity → source order to show which one WINS and therefore which one to edit — that is precisely the DevTools Styles-pane behaviour (winning declaration on top, overridden ones struck through). Without specificity computation the panel would edit the wrong rule and appear to do nothing.
entries.steal_this_idea: The compare/sort exports: @bramus/specificity ships `compare(a,b)` and `sortAsc/sortDesc` as first-class API, not just a calculator. That is the exact primitive the style panel consumes — do not just compute (a,b,c), expose an ordering.

entries.name: Chrome DevTools frontend + chii + chobitsu (the real Styles pane, offline)
entries.what_it_is: The genuine article for the missing style-inspector panel. `chrome-devtools-frontend` (npm 1.0.1676824, BSD-3-Clause, ~68MB unpacked, 4,761 files) IS the Elements panel + editable Styles pane + Computed pane + box model. `chobitsu` 1.8.6 (MIT) is a pure-JS in-page implementation of the Chrome DevTools Protocol (DOM, CSS, Overlay domains) so the frontend can drive an ordinary web page with no browser debugger attached. `chii` 1.15.5 (MIT) is the packaging: a local koa+ws server that serves the DevTools frontend plus a `target.js` you inject into the page.
entries.license: BSD-3-Clause (devtools-frontend, Chromium Authors) + MIT (chii) + MIT (chobitsu). All permissive, all verified.
entries.embeddable_how: Two ways. (1) Full chii: run `chii start -p 8080` as a local Node process from Electron's main process, inject `target.js` into the preview iframe/webview, open the DevTools UI in a second frame — entirely localhost, no cloud. (2) Leaner: embed `chobitsu` alone in the preview page and speak CDP to it from OUR OWN panel UI, skipping the 68MB frontend. chobitsu's deps: licia, devtools-protocol, luna-dom-highlighter, html2canvas, core-js, axios (axios ^0.27 is old — audit or shim it).
entries.language_stack: chii: Node (koa/ws) + prebuilt DevTools frontend. chobitsu: TypeScript, browser.
entries.framework_lock: None. The DevTools frontend is vanilla TS/Lit and self-hosting; chobitsu is framework-free.
entries.last_activity: chii 1.15.5, chobitsu 1.8.6, chrome-devtools-frontend 1.0.1676824 (all registry-verified as of 2026-08). devtools-frontend is continuously released from Chromium.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: DevTools UI itself is LTR-only; it would sit as an LTR tool panel inside our RTL app. It correctly inspects RTL pages (shows direction, logical properties, and the box model of RTL layouts).
entries.why_useful_for_us: This closes the panel hole with the highest-fidelity option available under a permissive licence, and it simultaneously serves deliverables (c) and (d): the element picker IS DevTools' inspect mode (`Overlay.setInspectMode` over CDP), and the styles panel IS the real Styles pane with live editing. Everything runs on localhost with no account. The cost is bundle size and the fact that we would be driving a UI we do not control — which is why option (2), chobitsu + our own panel, is probably the right call: we get the CDP DOM/CSS domain implementation (the hard part: matched rules, inherited rules, computed styles, specificity ordering) and render our own Arabic-first RTL panel on top.
entries.steal_this_idea: The CDP `CSS.getMatchedStylesForNode` RESPONSE SHAPE — {inlineStyle, attributesStyle, matchedCSSRules[{rule, matchingSelectors}], pseudoElements, inherited[]} — is a battle-tested, JSON-serialisable contract for 'everything a style panel needs about one element'. Adopt it verbatim as the payload our element picker sends to Claude over MCP; it is already the format every DevTools-like UI understands, and chobitsu gives us a working implementation to copy from.

entries.name: eruda
entries.what_it_is: A self-contained, in-page developer console for mobile browsers: Console, Elements (with a DOM tree, a styles/computed section and a box-model diagram), Network, Resources, Sources, Info. Injected as a single script into any page; no extension, no debugger, no server.
entries.license: MIT (verified)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `eruda` 3.4.3, single UMD bundle, `eruda.init()`. Vanilla JS/TS — no framework. Drop it into the preview iframe of our mini-browser and it just works, offline. Plugin API for custom tools.
entries.last_activity: 3.4.3 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08). Same author as chii/chobitsu/luna, all actively maintained together.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: UI is LTR; would be a floating tool overlay rather than part of our RTL chrome. Inspects RTL/Arabic content correctly.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The pragmatic middle answer to the panel hole: a WORKING, MIT, framework-free Elements+Styles inspector that is ~1MB rather than 68MB and needs no server. For deliverable (d) — a mini-browser that runs our projects — dropping eruda into the preview frame gives the user a real inspector on day one. And because it is MIT and vanilla, we can lift its Elements panel implementation directly rather than depending on the whole bundle.
entries.steal_this_idea: Its Elements panel is the reference implementation of 'style inspector with no browser privileges': it reads `getComputedStyle()` for the computed pane and walks `document.styleSheets` → `CSSRule.selectorText` → `element.matches(selectorText)` to find matched rules, then orders them by specificity. That is ~300 lines and needs no CDP at all. If chobitsu is too heavy, THIS is the algorithm to copy.

entries.name: luna component family (luna-dom-viewer, luna-box-model, luna-dom-highlighter, luna-object-viewer, luna-data-grid, luna-setting, luna-toolbar)
entries.what_it_is: The 49-component vanilla-JS UI toolkit that eruda and chobitsu are built out of, published as ~49 INDIVIDUAL npm packages. Directly relevant members: luna-dom-viewer (DOM tree navigator), luna-box-model (CSS box-model metrics widget — verified on npm as `luna-box-model` 1.0.1, MIT, dep licia), luna-dom-highlighter (the blue/green/orange element overlay), luna-setting (a settings/property-row panel), luna-toolbar, luna-data-grid, luna-object-viewer.
entries.license: MIT (verified on the repo and on luna-box-model's npm record)
entries.embeddable_how: npm per component (`npm i luna-dom-viewer`), each shipping its own JS + CSS file. Framework-free vanilla classes (`new LunaDomViewer(container, opts)`); CDN or bundler. Shared dep: `licia` (MIT utility library, same author).
entries.framework_lock: NONE — this is the key property. No React, no Vue, which matches EXELMJ's hand-written vanilla TS design module exactly.
entries.last_activity: luna-box-model 1.0.1 registry-verified; the monorepo is actively maintained (it backs eruda 3.4.3 and chii 1.15.5, both current).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Component CSS is authored LTR; each component is a small isolated stylesheet so RTL-adapting them is a contained job (and they are MIT, so we can fork the CSS).
entries.why_useful_for_us: This is the best ANSWER TO THE EXACT GAP: 'a permissively-licensed, framework-free style-inspector PANEL'. Nobody ships a complete one — but luna ships the PARTS, individually installable, MIT, vanilla, no framework lock: DOM tree + element highlighter + box-model diagram + property-row panel. We assemble those four into our style inspector and only have to write the CSS-declaration list ourselves (using css-tree's lexer for value validation and @bramus/specificity for ordering). Nothing else found in this sweep matches EXELMJ's vanilla-TS constraint this well.
entries.steal_this_idea: The packaging strategy itself: one monorepo, one component per npm package, each shipping its own CSS, all framework-free. It is why eruda/chii can share a devtools UI without a framework. If we build our design-module panels this way, the same panels serve the UI builder, the vector designer AND the element picker without a component framework.

entries.name: GrapesJS Style Manager
entries.what_it_is: A full web-builder framework whose `StyleManager` module is a genuine, production-grade CSS property editor panel: property sectors (typography/decorations/dimension/flex...), typed controls (integer+unit, colour, select, composite, stack for shadows/gradients), computed-value display, per-state styling (:hover, :active), and a SelectorManager that decides WHICH rule the edit lands in (class vs id vs inline).
entries.license: BSD-3-Clause (verified on npm — permissive, allowed)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `grapesjs` 0.23.5, `dist/grapes.mjs` (ESM) / `dist/grapes.min.js`. Deps bundled in: backbone 1.4.1, underscore, backbone-undo, codemirror 5.63, html-entities, promise-polyfill. Runs entirely in the browser/renderer, fully offline, no account. The Style Manager is not separately published — to use it alone you would fork/vendor it out of the BSD-3 source (legal, just work).
entries.framework_lock: No React/Vue requirement (that is the point), but it DOES drag in Backbone+Underscore, so it is 'framework-free' only in the sense of not forcing YOUR framework.
entries.last_activity: 0.23.5 (registry-verified, current as of 2026-08). Actively developed (the paid Studio SDK funds the OSS core; the core repo stays BSD-3).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: GrapesJS has documented RTL usage and its canvas can host an RTL document; the panel chrome itself is LTR and would need CSS work.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The single most complete permissive CSS-property-editor panel that exists. Even if we reject GrapesJS as a whole (it would fight our hand-written designApp.ts), its Style Manager property-type TAXONOMY is a spec we should copy wholesale rather than invent. Its SelectorManager also solves a problem no one else addressed: when the user edits a style on the canvas, which selector should receive it?
entries.steal_this_idea: The SelectorManager's 'state + selected classes → target rule' resolution. Editing a style is ambiguous (inline? the element's class? a new class?) and GrapesJS makes that choice EXPLICIT in the UI — the user sees and picks the target selector before editing. Our AI element picker must do the same, otherwise Claude will silently write inline styles that override the user's stylesheet forever.

entries.name: @compai/css-gui (css.gui)
entries.what_it_is: A visual toolkit for editing element styles: an `<Editor>` component that AUTO-GENERATES the right control for each of ~280 CSS properties (length+unit sliders, colour pickers with culori, keyword selects, composite editors for shadows/gradients/transitions), theme-aware, driven by a JSON style object.
entries.license: MIT (verified on npm for @compai/css-gui 0.0.247)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `@compai/css-gui`. HARD REACT LOCK: peerDependencies react >=18 and react-dom >=18, and it pulls ~40 runtime deps including theme-ui, @emotion/react, 10 @radix-ui packages, downshift, @use-gesture/react, culori, csstype, plus the whole unified/rehype/mdast stack. EXELMJ has React 19 present (for Univer), so it is technically installable in the renderer — but this is a heavy, opinionated dependency to bolt onto a vanilla-TS design module.
entries.framework_lock: React 18+ required. This is the disqualifier for us.
entries.last_activity: 0.0.247 (registry-verified as of 2026-08). Version scheme suggests continuous auto-publishing; the project has not had a stable 1.0 and appears quiet — treat maintenance as uncertain.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: No RTL affordances noted; panel is LTR.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The closest thing to a drop-in 'CSS property editor panel' package on npm, and MIT — so it belongs in the answer. Recommendation: DO NOT take the dependency (React lock + 40 deps + uncertain maintenance), but DO mine its `data/properties` control mapping, which is the hard-won part: a table of ~280 CSS properties → control type → valid units/keywords. That table is what our own vanilla panel needs and it is MIT-licensed.
entries.steal_this_idea: The property→control mapping table (280 properties, each with a control type, unit set and default). Combined with css-tree's mdn-data lexer for validation, that gives us a complete style panel spec without hand-designing 280 widgets. This is the single most reusable artefact in the project.

entries.name: tweakpane (+ lil-gui)
entries.what_it_is: Compact, dependency-free floating property panes. Tweakpane 4.0.5 (MIT, written in TypeScript, ZERO runtime deps) binds a JS object to typed controls — number+slider+step, colour (rgb/hsl/hex with alpha), point2d/3d, select, text, checkbox — with folders, tabs, monitors/graphs, blade API and a plugin system. lil-gui 0.21.0 (MIT, zero deps, ESM+UMD) is the smaller dat.GUI successor.
entries.license: MIT (both verified on npm)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `tweakpane` 4.0.5 (`dist/tweakpane.js` + types) or `lil-gui` 0.21.0 (`dist/lil-gui.esm.js` / `.umd.js`). Zero dependencies each. Pure browser DOM — drops straight into an Electron renderer next to our existing hand-written panels.
entries.framework_lock: NONE. Vanilla DOM, no framework at all.
entries.last_activity: tweakpane 4.0.5, lil-gui 0.21.0 (both registry-verified as of 2026-08).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: LTR-authored but tiny CSS surfaces; both are themeable via CSS custom properties, so an RTL/Arabic skin is a small job (unlike theming a React design system).
entries.why_useful_for_us: The pragmatic vanilla answer to 'we need a property panel and nothing permissive exists'. Neither knows anything about CSS — but combined with the css.gui property table (control type per property) and css-tree's lexer (valid values per property), tweakpane's blade/plugin API can RENDER a full CSS style inspector with zero framework dependencies and zero new widget code. This is the lowest-risk path for EXELMJ specifically, and it serves the vector designer (b) and the UI builder (a) with the same panel code.
entries.steal_this_idea: Tweakpane's plugin contract: a control plugin declares `{id, type, accept(value, params), binding:{reader, writer, constraint}, controller}`. Declarative accept+reader/writer means adding a new CSS property type (say `<length-percentage>`) is ~30 lines and the pane handles layout, undo-friendly change events and theming. That contract is worth copying even if we write our own pane.

entries.name: @medv/finder
entries.what_it_is: CSS selector generator: given a DOM element, produces the shortest selector that uniquely identifies it, with configurable attribute/class allow-lists, seed elements and an optimisation pass.
entries.license: MIT (verified)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `@medv/finder` 4.0.2. ZERO runtime dependencies. Browser-only, ~2KB. Drops into the preview iframe or the renderer directly.
entries.last_activity: 4.0.2 (registry-verified as of 2026-08).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: n/a
entries.why_useful_for_us: Required by deliverable (c). The AI element picker must send Claude a STABLE, human-readable selector for the clicked element — not `body > div:nth-child(3) > div > div:nth-child(2)`. finder produces `.card > .title`-quality output and lets us blacklist generated class names (CSS-modules hashes, Tailwind JIT classes) so the selector survives a rebuild. Pair it with the babel `data-src` instrumentation above: selector for the runtime, data-src for the file:line.
entries.steal_this_idea: Its cost function: score candidate selector parts (id < class < attribute < nth-child) and search for the cheapest UNIQUE combination, rather than greedily walking up the tree. That is why its output is readable. Also its `idName`/`className`/`attr` predicate hooks — letting the CALLER decide which identifiers are stable is what makes it work across frameworks.

entries.name: code-inspector-plugin / @code-inspector/core
entries.what_it_is: Build-plugin + runtime pair: at dev-build time it stamps source file/line/column onto DOM elements; at runtime, alt-click (or a toggle) on any element in the page opens the user's IDE with the cursor on the exact JSX/template line that produced it.
entries.license: MIT (verified on npm for code-inspector-plugin 2.0.7)
entries.embeddable_how: npm `code-inspector-plugin` 2.0.7 — a meta-package pulling @code-inspector/core, /vite, /webpack, /esbuild, /turbopack, /mako (all 2.0.7). We would use `@code-inspector/vite` since EXELMJ is on Vite 8. The build plugin runs in Node; the injected runtime overlay runs in the page. Local only, no cloud.
entries.framework_lock: None — supports Vue 2/3, React, Preact, Svelte, Solid, Astro, Qwik via the same instrumentation.
entries.last_activity: 2.0.7 (registry-verified as of 2026-08).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: n/a
entries.why_useful_for_us: This is the WORKING, MIT, framework-agnostic implementation of the click-element→file:line half of deliverable (c) — the same idea as react-dev-inspector but not React-locked, which matters because our builder should be able to target vanilla TS and Vue as well as React. Instead of opening VS Code, we redirect its resolved {file, line, column} into our MCP server so Claude receives 'the user clicked THIS element, which is src/design/panel.ts:412'. That closes the loop between the picker, the AST write-back layer and the AI.
entries.steal_this_idea: Its resolution chain: build-time attribute stamp → runtime overlay reads the attribute → local server resolves it to an absolute path → editor/agent opens it. Every link is trivial; the value is that it avoids source-map math entirely. Also note it strips the injected attributes in production builds — do the same so our instrumentation never ships in the user's exported project.

domain: RTL/Arabic verification pass + licence and CDP architecture gates for the EXELMJ design / UI-builder / element-picker / MCP module

entries.name: GrapesJS
entries.what_it_is: Visual web page builder / drag-drop UI editor with an iframe canvas. The sweep's #1 ADOPT candidate for the visual UI-builder.
entries.license: BSD-3-Clause (npm `grapesjs` 0.23.5). NOTE: not MIT as often assumed — still permissive, still fine.
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, plain UMD/ESM bundle, mounts into any DOM node. Framework-free.

entries.last_activity: 2026-08-11 (npm modified). Very active.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: VERDICT: RTL is still NOT supported in 0.23.x, and I can now say precisely where. (1) Issue #1122 ('[Feature request] Support RTL', opened 2018-05-20) was CLOSED 2018-05-23 with label `outdated` — never implemented, no linked PR. (2) Issue #4015 ('BUG: Drag and drop not working well in case of RTL', opened 2021-12-15) was closed 2023-08-10 as `inactive` — a stale-bot close, not a fix; repro was `editor.Css.setRule('.gjs-wrapper', {direction:'rtl'})` breaking column drop positions. (3) Issue #2851 reported Style Manager breaking under `html{direction:rtl}`. DIRECT SOURCE INSPECTION (decisive, beats the issue tracker): I downloaded grapes.min.css (61 KB) and grapes.min.js (1.15 MB) from jsDelivr. The editor CSS contains ZERO `[dir=rtl]` selectors, ZERO `:dir()` pseudo-classes, ZERO logical properties (no margin-inline/padding-inline/inset-inline), and 23 physical `margin-left/right` + `padding-left/right` declarations. In the JS, all 15 `rtl` occurrences belong to the BUNDLED CODEMIRROR (`CodeMirror-rtl`, `doc.direction`, `setDirection`, UBA level ordering) plus one CSS-keyword autocomplete list — i.e. GrapesJS has no first-party RTL code at all; the only RTL in the bundle is inherited from a vendored dependency. SPLIT ANSWER to the question asked: the CANVAS/iframe document IS fixable via supported config (see steal_this_idea); the EDITOR CHROME is not, and needs rtlcss/postcss-rtlcss post-processing of grapes.min.css. Drag-drop math in RTL remains unverified-broken (#4015 never fixed).
entries.steal_this_idea: The working canvas-RTL workaround is a documented config option, not a hack. Canvas config defaults are `frameContent: '<!DOCTYPE html>'` and `frameStyle: 'body { background-color:#fff } ...'`. I confirmed in the bundle that frameContent is written verbatim into the iframe via `doc.open(); doc.write(frameContent); doc.close()` on frame load, and frameStyle is injected as a `<style>` into the frame head. So `canvas: { frameContent: '<!DOCTYPE html><html dir="rtl" lang="ar">', frameStyle: 'body{direction:rtl} @font-face{...Arabic...}' }` makes the edited document genuinely RTL with an embedded offline Arabic font. Steal this pattern for EXELMJ's own mini-browser/preview iframe regardless of whether GrapesJS is adopted: own the iframe's doctype+html attributes rather than trying to patch direction in after load.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Downgrade from ADOPT to ADOPT-WITH-FORK. For an Arabic-RTL-FIRST app, shipping GrapesJS means shipping an LTR-only editor chrome. Budget a real task: run rtlcss or postcss-rtlcss over grapes.min.css at build time to emit an RTL chrome stylesheet, and independently verify the sorter/drag-drop geometry under RTL since #4015 was never fixed. The canvas side is a 2-line config fix.
