entries.rtl_arabic_notes: RISK RESOLVED — RTL IS SHIPPED. Issue #146 'RTL Support' was filed 2026-04-10 by user mosaaleb explicitly for an Arabic app ('the CSS relies on physical directional properties rather than logical ones') and is now CLOSED. I verified the fix landed by downloading dist/basecoat.cdn.min.css (218 KB) and grepping it: logical properties dominate — margin-inline-start x15, padding-inline-end x14, padding-inline-start x13, inset-inline-end x9, margin-inline-end x7, border-inline-start x4, inset-inline-start x4; text-align:start x7 and text-align:end x1. Six `[dir=rtl]` selectors exist, written defensively as `:where(:dir(rtl),[dir=rtl],[dir=rtl] *)` so both the modern pseudo-class and the attribute selector match. Icon mirroring is handled by a `[data-rtl-flip]` opt-in attribute that applies `rotate:180deg` (used on breadcrumb and dropdown-menu chevrons), and `.sidebar nav ul ul` gets an RTL-specific 1px translate correction. RESIDUAL BUGS I FOUND (small, patchable, worth reporting upstream): (a) `.btn[data-icon=inline-end]` variants still use physical `padding-right` at all four sizes (default/xs/sm/lg) — should be `padding-inline-end`; (b) three `.sidebar nav` rules use `text-align:left` — should be `text-align:start`. Everything else is clean. The remaining physical left/right declarations are intentional: `.sidebar[data-side=left|right]` and `[data-tooltip][data-side=left|right]` are explicit physical placements that also ship logical `inline-start`/`inline-end` siblings.
entries.steal_this_idea: The `:where(:dir(rtl),[dir=rtl],[dir=rtl] *)` triple-selector idiom. `:where()` keeps specificity at zero so it never fights the base rule, and covering both `:dir()` and `[dir]` handles the inheritance gap (see the ':dir() semantic-only' entry). Also steal the `data-rtl-flip` opt-in attribute: mirroring icons wholesale is wrong (a magnifier or a play button must not flip, a chevron must), so an explicit per-element opt-in beats a blanket `transform:scaleX(-1)` on all icons — directly applicable to EXELMJ's toolbar.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Upgrade to ADOPT, RTL risk closed. This is now one of the few component layers in the whole sweep with deliberate, verified, shipped RTL. Only caveat: it depends on the `dir` ATTRIBUTE being present (see the ':dir() semantic-only' entry) — CSS `direction:rtl` alone will not trigger it.

entries.name: @zumer/snapdom
entries.what_it_is: DOM-to-image capture engine: clones an element with computed styles, pseudo-elements and fonts, exports to SVG/PNG/JPG/WebP/canvas/Blob. Candidate for capturing elements in the AI element picker.
entries.license: MIT (verified in npm registry metadata for 2.24.1).
entries.embeddable_how: npm package `@zumer/snapdom`, ZERO runtime dependencies, pure browser Web APIs. Drop straight into the Electron renderer.
entries.last_activity: 2.24.1, npm modified 2026-08-10 — four days before this sweep. Very active.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: RTL-SAFE BY ARCHITECTURE — this was the right thing to check and it passes. Mechanism verified by reading the dist bundle: snapdom clones the subtree with `cloneNode(true)` (so the `dir` attribute and lang are preserved verbatim), inlines computed styles, and embeds the result in an SVG `<foreignObject>` which the browser then lays out and rasterizes. Because layout and text run through Chromium's own engine (HarfBuzz), Unicode bidi reordering and Arabic contextual shaping are done by the browser — snapdom never reimplements text layout, so there is no code path that could produce reversed or disconnected Arabic. Beyond that, the author has demonstrably thought about RTL: the bounding-box code contains `direction === 'rtl' ? Math.min(n.left, n.right - scrollWidth) : n.left`, an explicit RTL-aware overflow-geometry correction, and it also special-cases `writingMode` starting with `vertical`/`sideways`. Zero Arabic/RTL/bidi issues are open on the tracker — which here reads as 'no bugs' rather than 'untested', given the explicit RTL code. THE ONE REAL ARABIC RISK IS FONTS, NOT TEXT: `embedFonts` defaults to FALSE. With it off, the rasterized SVG has no access to page fonts and Arabic will fall back or render as tofu. EXELMJ must pass `embedFonts: true` and ship a self-hosted Arabic face (e.g. @fontsource/noto-sans-arabic, listed separately).
entries.steal_this_idea: The `<foreignObject>` + `cloneNode(true)` capture strategy itself is the lesson for any RTL-first app: never reimplement text layout, hand the markup back to the browser and let its shaper do bidi and Arabic joining. Any capture/export path in EXELMJ that rasterizes text itself (rather than delegating to the browser or to HarfBuzz) is a latent Arabic bug. Also steal the RTL overflow-geometry line — measuring scroll overflow from `right - scrollWidth` instead of `left` is exactly the bug class that breaks RTL canvases.
entries.why_useful_for_us: CONFIRMS ADOPT. Best-in-class choice for capturing a picked element as an image to feed an AI, and safe for Arabic content provided embedFonts is enabled. Zero deps and offline-clean.

entries.name: modern-screenshot
entries.what_it_is: Successor to html-to-image / dom-to-image: renders a DOM node to PNG/JPEG/SVG/canvas. The designated fallback if snapdom fails.
entries.license: MIT (verified in npm registry metadata for 4.7.0).
entries.embeddable_how: npm package, browser-side, no native deps.
entries.last_activity: 4.7.0, npm modified 2026-04-16. Maintained but less active than snapdom.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: RTL-SAFE BY THE SAME ARCHITECTURE, BUT LESS RTL-AWARE THAN SNAPDOM. Verified by reading the dist bundle: it also uses SVG `<foreignObject>` and `cloneNode(true)`, so bidi and Arabic shaping are again delegated to Chromium and cannot be mangled. However — and this is the concrete difference from snapdom — grepping the entire bundle for `direction`, `unicode-bidi` and `writing-mode` returns ZERO hits. There is no RTL-aware overflow/geometry correction anywhere. So for a simple element it is fine, but for an element with horizontal scroll overflow in an RTL container, expect clipping or offset errors that snapdom explicitly corrects for.
entries.steal_this_idea: Its value is as a differential test oracle, not as a library: capture the same Arabic RTL element with both snapdom and modern-screenshot and diff the output. Divergence localises whether a capture bug is in EXELMJ's markup or in the capture library's geometry math — cheap regression harness for a subsystem that is otherwise hard to unit-test.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Keep as fallback, but rank strictly below snapdom for an RTL-first app. Prefer snapdom as primary.

entries.name: @svgedit/svgcanvas
entries.what_it_is: The headless SVG editing engine extracted from SVG-Edit — selection, path editing, transforms, undo/redo history, layers, sanitize, coords/units math, with no editor UI. The only mature headless SVG editing engine the sweep found.
entries.license: MIT — VERIFIED CLEAN. This is the blocker resolution.
entries.embeddable_how: npm package `@svgedit/svgcanvas` 7.4.2, or vendor the 43-file source tree directly (it ships uncompiled ESM under core/ and common/ plus a prebuilt dist).
entries.language_stack: Vanilla ESM JavaScript, ships its own .d.ts. Vite build config included.
entries.framework_lock: None — genuinely headless, no DOM chrome, no jQuery in this package.
entries.last_activity: 7.4.2, npm modified 2026-07-11. Active.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Not RTL-specific — it manipulates SVG geometry, not text layout. Its `core/text-actions.js` handles SVG text editing, so Arabic text INSIDE edited SVG will depend on the browser's SVG text shaping (Chromium handles this correctly for `<text>` with a proper font). Not independently verified for Arabic text editing caret behaviour — treat SVG text editing in Arabic as unproven.
entries.steal_this_idea: Its `core/` module split is the reusable design: recalculate.js (transform flattening), coords.js, math.js, path-actions.js, history.js + historyrecording.js (command-pattern undo), sanitize.js. Even if never adopted wholesale, `recalculate.js` (collapsing nested SVG transform matrices back into element attributes) and the history/historyrecording command pair are the two hardest parts of a vector editor and are worth reading before EXELMJ writes its own — designApp.ts already has undo/redo and shapes and would otherwise reinvent transform flattening.
entries.why_useful_for_us: BLOCKER CLEARED — this was the single licence question gating the only mature headless SVG engine available. I downloaded and unpacked the actual published tarball (svgcanvas-7.4.2.tgz, 43 files) and grepped the entire package for `LGPL`, `GPL` and `General Public`: ZERO matches, grep exit code 1. Every source file under core/ and common/ carries an `MIT` licence header. package.json declares plain `"license": "MIT"` with ZERO dependencies and ZERO peerDependencies. The LGPL fragment in the ROOT svgedit package.json does not reach this subpackage. Safe to vendor or npm-install into EXELMJ.

entries.name: svgedit (root package) — LGPL forensics
entries.what_it_is: The full SVG-Edit application (editor UI + canvas). Investigated only to identify which vendored file carries the LGPL-3.0-or-later fragment declared in its composite licence string.
entries.license: Root npm `svgedit` 7.4.2 declares `(MIT AND Apache-2.0 AND ISC AND LGPL-3.0-or-later AND X11)` — a composite covering vendored third-party files.
entries.embeddable_how: DO NOT link the root package into EXELMJ. Use @svgedit/svgcanvas instead. Reference/inspiration only for the root editor UI.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Editor chrome is LTR-oriented; not evaluated further because the root package is not a link candidate.
entries.steal_this_idea: The `licenseInfo.json` + `filesByLicense` convention itself. SVG-Edit ships a machine-readable map from licence SPDX string to the exact file paths it covers, and declares `bundledRootPackages` separately. That is exactly what let me resolve this blocker in one file read instead of auditing a whole repo. EXELMJ should adopt the same file for its own vendored third-party code (it already vendors a potrace-like tracer and an Illustrator COM bridge) — it turns a future licence audit from days into minutes.
entries.why_useful_for_us: QUESTION ANSWERED DEFINITIVELY. I unpacked the published svgedit-7.4.2.tgz and read package/licenseInfo.json (856 bytes). Its `filesByLicense` map states verbatim: `"LGPL-3.0-or-later": ["src/editor/jspdf/jspdf.plugin.svgToPdf.js"]`. That is the ONE and ONLY LGPL file — a vendored jsPDF SVG-to-PDF plugin, living under src/editor/ (the UI package), NOT under packages/svgcanvas. The same map shows `"X11": ["src/editor/jspdf/jspdf.min.js"]` (X11 is MIT-equivalent, permissive), `"(MIT OR GPL-2.0)": ["src/editor/jquerybbq/jquery.bbq.min.js"]` and `"(MIT OR GPL-2.0-or-later)": ["src/editor/extensions/ext-server_moinsave.js"]` — both DUAL-licensed, so the MIT option can simply be elected. docs/versions/6.0.0.md confirms the composite string was introduced precisely to enumerate bundled terms. CONCLUSION: the LGPL contamination is confined to a PDF-export plugin that EXELMJ does not need (it already exports PDF via pdf-lib), and it is absent from @svgedit/svgcanvas entirely.

entries.name: chrome-devtools-mcp
entries.what_it_is: Official Chrome DevTools MCP server — exposes CDP-backed browser inspection and automation as MCP tools.
entries.license: Apache-2.0 (verified in npm registry metadata for 1.7.0).
entries.embeddable_how: Local Node process via npx; two bins (`chrome-devtools`, `chrome-devtools-mcp`). Speaks MCP over stdio, so Claude can drive it directly.
entries.last_activity: 1.7.0, npm modified 2026-08-10. Very active.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Transport layer — direction-agnostic. It inspects whatever the page renders, so Arabic content is reported as-is.
entries.steal_this_idea: `--wsEndpoint` + `--wsHeaders` (custom JSON headers on the CDP WebSocket handshake) is the pattern for authenticating an MCP server against a debug port you do not want world-open. An Electron app that opens a CDP port opens it to every local process; a header-gated ws endpoint plus binding to 127.0.0.1 is the minimum hardening for EXELMJ's element-picker bridge.
entries.why_useful_for_us: CLAIM CONFIRMED — the 'point an MCP server at our Electron WebContentsView' plan is viable. README verified: it ships `--browserUrl` / `--browser-url` / `-u` ('Connect to a running, debuggable Chrome instance (e.g. http://127.0.0.1:9222)') AND `--wsEndpoint` / `--ws-endpoint` / `-w` ('WebSocket endpoint to connect to a running Chrome instance'), plus `--wsHeaders` and `--autoConnect`. Two caveats: (1) README states it targets 'current stable Chrome or newer' — Electron 43 ships Chromium 150, which satisfies this; (2) `--autoConnect` specifically requires Chrome 144+ and resolves via user-data-dir, so for Electron prefer explicit `--browser-url`/`--wsEndpoint`.

entries.name: @playwright/mcp
entries.what_it_is: Microsoft's Playwright MCP server — accessibility-tree-driven browser automation exposed over MCP.
entries.license: Apache-2.0 (verified in npm registry metadata for 0.0.79).
entries.embeddable_how: Local Node process via npx `playwright-mcp`. MCP over stdio.
entries.last_activity: 0.0.79, npm modified 2026-08-13 — one day before this sweep. Extremely active.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Direction-agnostic transport. Its accessibility-tree snapshot mode returns text content, which for Arabic is returned in LOGICAL order (as the DOM stores it) — this is correct and is what you want to feed an AI, unlike a pixel screenshot.
entries.steal_this_idea: Two things. (a) `--device` ('device to emulate, for example: iPhone 15') and `--viewport-size` ('1280x720') are exactly the desktop/tablet/mobile viewport switcher EXELMJ wants for its mini-browser — copy the named-device-preset model rather than hardcoding three pixel widths. (b) Its accessibility-tree snapshot instead of a screenshot is the better element-picker payload: cheaper than an image, already in logical order, and it survives Arabic without any shaping concerns.
entries.why_useful_for_us: CLAIM CONFIRMED. README verified: `--cdp-endpoint` exists ('CDP endpoint to connect to.'), alongside `--cdp-header` ('CDP headers to send with the connect request, multiple can be specified') and `--cdp-timeout` (default 30000ms). Also `--isolated`, `--browser` (chrome/firefox/webkit/msedge), `--extension` and `--endpoint`. So both MCP candidates can attach to an existing Chromium debug port — the architecture plan holds for either.

entries.name: Electron 43 — webContents.debugger vs DevTools (HARD CONSTRAINT)
entries.what_it_is: Not a library — the platform constraint governing the AI element picker. Electron 43 ships Chromium 150.0.7871.46 / V8 15.0 / Node 24.17.0 (43.2.0: Chromium 150.0.7871.129, Node 24.18.0).
entries.license: Electron is MIT.
entries.embeddable_how: Built in — `webContents.debugger.attach()` / `.sendCommand()` / `.detach()` / `.isAttached()`, plus the `'detach'` and `'message'` events.
entries.last_activity: Electron 43 current; 43.2.0 released.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: N/A — platform layer.
entries.steal_this_idea: Design around the exclusivity instead of fighting it: run the previewed project in its OWN WebContentsView, own the CDP session on THAT view exclusively, and never call openDevTools on it — open DevTools on the host UI webContents instead, which is a different target and therefore unaffected. Better still, consider skipping CDP for the picker entirely: an injected content script doing hover-highlight + click capture + getComputedStyle + selector generation gives the same result with no debugger session, no DevTools conflict, no experimental-domain risk, and works identically offline. Reserve CDP for what only CDP can do.
entries.why_useful_for_us: CRITICAL CONSTRAINT CONFIRMED — this changes the element-picker design. Electron's official debugger docs state verbatim that the `'detach'` event fires when 'the debugging session is terminated. This happens either when `webContents` is closed **or DevTools is invoked for the attached `webContents`**.' So webContents.debugger and DevTools are MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE on the same webContents: opening DevTools force-detaches your CDP session. Corroborated by electron/electron issue #8336 ('DevTools connection failed when another debugger is already attached to this target'). The docs do NOT document a specific 'Another debugger is already attached' throw string for attach(), so wrap attach() in try/catch and treat the 'detach' event as the authoritative signal. Chromium version (150) is high enough for every CDP and CSS feature relied on elsewhere in this sweep.

entries.name: CDP Overlay domain — Overlay.setInspectMode
entries.what_it_is: The Chrome DevTools Protocol domain that powers DevTools' own element inspector — hover highlighting and click-to-inspect.
entries.license: Protocol spec (Chromium, BSD-3-Clause).
entries.embeddable_how: Via webContents.debugger.sendCommand('Overlay.setInspectMode', ...) in Electron main, or through either MCP server.
entries.last_activity: Current (tip-of-tree protocol).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: N/A.
entries.steal_this_idea: The `inspectNodeRequested` event is the whole picker in one primitive: setInspectMode('searchForNode') makes Chromium draw the highlight overlay and do hit-testing for you, then fires inspectNodeRequested with the backendNodeId on click. That is native-quality hover highlighting (including margin/padding/border box shading via HighlightConfig) for free — far better than a hand-rolled outline div, which is what a naive picker builds and which breaks on transforms, shadow DOM and iframes.
entries.why_useful_for_us: CLAIM CONFIRMED, WITH ONE CAVEAT. `Overlay.setInspectMode` still exists, unrenamed, in the current protocol: signature 'Enters the "inspect" mode. In this mode, elements that user is hovering over are highlighted.', params `mode` (enum: searchForNode, searchForUAShadowDOM, captureAreaScreenshot, none) and optional `highlightConfig`. It is NOT deprecated. Events `inspectNodeRequested` and `nodeHighlightRequested` both present. CAVEAT: the ENTIRE Overlay domain is marked EXPERIMENTAL, so it carries no stability guarantee across Chromium upgrades — pin behaviour with a smoke test that runs on every Electron bump. (By contrast `Overlay.setShowHitTestBorders` IS deprecated and 'no longer has any effect'.) Combined with the previous entry: setInspectMode works, but only while DevTools is closed on that webContents.

entries.name: Zag.js (@zag-js/*)
entries.what_it_is: Headless UI component state machines (finite-state-machine driven) for React/Vue/Solid/Svelte AND vanilla JS. Provides behaviour + a11y, no styling.
entries.license: MIT (verified in npm registry metadata for @zag-js/slider 1.43.0).
entries.embeddable_how: npm, per-component packages (`@zag-js/slider`, `@zag-js/menu`, …). Vanilla JS adapter available — no framework required.
entries.language_stack: TypeScript, ships ESM + CJS + .d.ts per component.
entries.framework_lock: None — explicitly framework-agnostic, vanilla adapter supported.
entries.last_activity: 1.43.0, npm modified 2026-08-01. Very active.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: RTL IS FIRST-CLASS AND REAL — but incomplete for keyboard. Every machine context accepts `dir: 'ltr' | 'rtl'` as a documented prop ('the document's text/writing direction'), consistent across Switch, Tour, Select, Tooltip, Menu and others. I verified this is not merely declarative by unpacking @zag-js/slider 1.43.0 and reading dist: `slider.machine.js` derives `isRtl: ({prop}) => prop('orientation')==='horizontal' && prop('dir')==='rtl'`; `slider.dom.js` inverts pointer-to-value mapping with `return dir === 'rtl' || invertX ? 1 - percent.x : percent.x`; `slider.style.js` uses isRtl in 13 places to swap range start/end anchoring (`[isRtl?'right':'left']`) and to flip thumb transforms (`isRtl ? 'translateX(50%)' : 'translateX(-50%)'`). GAP I FOUND: keyboard is NOT mirrored. `slider.connect.js` maps `ArrowLeft() → send({type:'ARROW_DEC'})` and `ArrowRight() → ARROW_INC` UNCONDITIONALLY, and `slider.machine.js` handles ARROW_DEC with a plain `decrementThumbAtIndex` with no isRtl branch. Per WAI-ARIA, a horizontal RTL slider should have ArrowRight DECREASE. So Zag's slider is geometry/pointer-correct but keyboard-inverted in Arabic. Other components not individually audited — assume the same pattern needs spot-checking.
entries.steal_this_idea: Modelling `isRtl` as a DERIVED value inside the state machine (`computed('isRtl')`) rather than as scattered CSS or ad-hoc checks. Direction becomes a single machine input that every geometry and style calculation reads from one place, so RTL cannot drift out of sync between pointer math, styles and behaviour — the exact failure mode that makes RTL retrofits so expensive. This is the single most transferable architectural idea in this sweep for EXELMJ's canvas: put `dir` in the design-document model, derive everything.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Strong ADOPT for interactive widget behaviour in an RTL-first app — it is one of the very few libraries where RTL is a modelled input rather than a stylesheet afterthought. Ship it, but add keyboard-direction tests for any horizontal-axis widget (slider, and check carousel/splitter similarly).

entries.name: Web Awesome (@awesome.me/webawesome) / Shoelace
entries.what_it_is: Web-component UI library, successor to Shoelace (the Shoelace repo now redirects to Web Awesome). Framework-agnostic custom elements built on Lit.
entries.license: MIT (verified in npm registry metadata for @awesome.me/webawesome 3.11.0). Free core is MIT; a paid Pro tier exists but is not required.
entries.embeddable_how: npm; custom elements registered globally, usable from vanilla HTML in the Electron renderer. Note it pulls a real dependency tree (lit, @floating-ui/dom, @lit/context, marked, nanoid, @ctrl/tinycolor).
entries.framework_lock: None for consumption (custom elements work anywhere), but Lit is a hard runtime dependency you are shipping.
entries.last_activity: 3.11.0, npm modified 2026-07-30. Very active.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: GENUINE, DESIGNED-IN RTL — the strongest of any component library checked. Direction is handled centrally by @shoelace-style/localize (a declared dependency of webawesome 3.11.0, `^3.2.3` — verified in the package's dependency list, so the RTL machinery ships with the MIT core, not the Pro tier). Components resolve direction via `LocalizeController.dir()` returning 'ltr'|'rtl', style themselves with the `:dir(rtl)` pseudo-class, and — notably — animations accept an `rtlKeyframes` property that is automatically substituted when the component's directionality is RTL. Historical issue #2188 ('RTL-/LTR-detection leads to hard errors in older browsers') was about `:dir()` being unsupported in old engines; this is MOOT for EXELMJ, since Electron 43 ships Chromium 150 and `:dir()` has been Baseline-widely-available since Dec 2023. PR #768 shows community RTL work landing as far back as the Shoelace era.
entries.steal_this_idea: `rtlKeyframes`. Nearly everyone remembers to mirror static layout and forgets to mirror MOTION — a drawer that slides in from the left, a toast that flies in from the right, an accordion chevron that rotates the wrong way. Making the animation keyframe set a first-class direction-aware property (rather than patching transforms at call sites) is the clean fix, and EXELMJ's design module has panels and drawers with exactly this problem.
entries.why_useful_for_us: ADOPT-worthy for RTL correctness specifically. If the Lit dependency tree is unacceptable for a vanilla-TS app, take basecoat-css instead and steal the rtlKeyframes idea — but note Web Awesome is the reference implementation of doing RTL properly in components.

entries.name: @shoelace-style/localize
entries.what_it_is: Zero-dependency micro-library for localizing custom elements — the direction/locale engine extracted from Shoelace/Web Awesome. 89 commits, ~60 stars: exactly the obscure-but-fitting profile.
entries.license: MIT (verified in npm registry metadata for 3.2.3; zero dependencies confirmed).
entries.embeddable_how: npm, ~tiny, zero deps. BUT architected around Lit's Reactive Controller pattern — usable standalone only if you write your own adapter around its core direction/locale resolution.
entries.framework_lock: Soft lock to Lit's controller pattern; the underlying detection logic is framework-free and easy to lift.
entries.last_activity: 3.2.3, npm modified 2026-07-22. Active.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: This IS the RTL mechanism. It resolves the document locale from `<html lang="...">`, allows any element to be scoped by setting its own `lang`, and stays reactive via a MutationObserver watching `lang` changes on `<html>`. `LocalizeController.dir()` returns 'ltr'|'rtl' and `.lang()` returns the locale. This is precisely the piece an English-only sweep would have skipped as 'just an i18n helper' while it is in fact the direction backbone of the whole Web Awesome component set.
entries.steal_this_idea: The MutationObserver-on-`<html>` reactive direction pattern. EXELMJ needs a live Arabic/English toggle; the naive implementation re-renders everything on toggle. Instead, observe `dir`/`lang` on the document element once, expose a single reactive `dir()` accessor, and let every component read from it — direction changes then propagate automatically with no re-mount and no prop drilling. Combine with Zag's derived-`isRtl` idea and you have a complete direction architecture: observe once at the document, derive everywhere.
entries.why_useful_for_us: High-value small steal. Even if EXELMJ adopts neither Web Awesome nor basecoat, this ~single-file pattern is the right foundation for its Arabic/English direction switching, and it is MIT with zero dependencies so it can be vendored outright.

entries.name: VvvebJs
entries.what_it_is: Drag-and-drop page builder JavaScript library — the main GrapesJS alternative in the sweep.
entries.license: Apache-2.0 (verified in npm registry metadata for 2.0.9).
entries.embeddable_how: npm `vvvebjs` or vendor the source; jQuery/Bootstrap-flavoured, iframe canvas.
entries.framework_lock: None strictly, but Bootstrap-oriented component set.
entries.last_activity: 2.0.9, npm modified 2026-06-30. Active.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: NO RTL SUPPORT — worse than GrapesJS. I downloaded libs/builder/builder.js (135 KB) from the master branch and grepped for `rtl`, `direction`, `dir=` and `getAttribute('dir')`: exactly ONE match, and it is a false positive (a `rtL` substring inside an identifier). Zero direction handling, zero dir-attribute plumbing, and — unlike GrapesJS — I found no equivalent of a `frameContent`/`frameStyle` config hook to inject `dir="rtl"` into the canvas iframe, so even the canvas-side workaround that rescues GrapesJS is not obviously available here. No RTL-related issues surfaced.
entries.steal_this_idea: Mainly a negative result worth recording: it demonstrates the sweep's structural blind spot. VvvebJs scores well on every English-language criterion (permissive Apache-2.0, active, offline, framework-free, embeddable) and would rank highly on a popularity/features matrix — yet it is the WORST candidate of the shortlist for an Arabic-first app. Any future sweep for this project must make 'grep the actual shipped bundle for dir/rtl/logical-properties' a mandatory column, not an afterthought.
entries.why_useful_for_us: REJECT for EXELMJ. Retrofitting RTL here means patching the builder core with no upstream config seam, versus GrapesJS where the canvas is a config option and only the chrome CSS needs post-processing. GrapesJS is strictly the better RTL bet of the two.

entries.name: bidi-shaper
entries.what_it_is: Logical→visual Unicode BiDi (UAX #9) reordering PLUS Arabic contextual shaping, purpose-built for renderers OUTSIDE the browser layout engine: PDF, canvas, WebGL, SVG, terminals, games. Created 2026-07-03 — brand new and near-invisible.
entries.license: MIT (verified in npm registry metadata for 0.1.2; zero dependencies confirmed).
entries.embeddable_how: npm `bidi-shaper`, ZERO dependencies. Pure JS, drop into renderer or main process.
entries.last_activity: 0.1.2, published 2026-07-03 (created same day). Brand new — version 0.1.x, so API stability is unproven.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: THIS IS THE SINGLE MOST ON-TARGET FIND OF THE SWEEP FOR EXELMJ. It does exactly the two things Arabic needs and that no browser-bypassing renderer gets for free: (1) full UAX #9 bidi reordering, (2) Arabic contextual shaping into initial/medial/final/isolated presentation forms, including mandatory lam-alef ligatures. Verified API surface: `render(text, options)` → visual-order string; `analyze(text, options)` → shaped text plus embedding levels AND an index mapping; `shape()` (shaping only); `reorder()` (reordering only); `getEmbeddingLevels()`; `detectDirection()`. Documented example: `render('مرحبا بالعالم')` → `'ﻢﻟﺎﻌﻟﺎﺑ ﺎﺒﺣﺮﻣ'`. Repo existence confirmed by direct fetch.
entries.steal_this_idea: `analyze()` returning an INDEX MAPPING between logical and visual order alongside the shaped glyphs. That mapping is what makes caret placement, text selection, and hit-testing possible in a canvas text editor — you can convert a click at visual position N back to a logical character offset. Every hand-rolled Arabic canvas editor gets this wrong by shaping and discarding the mapping, which is why selection jumps around. EXELMJ's designApp.ts has text boxes with 'Arabic bidi runs' already; this is the missing primitive for correct caret/selection in them.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Directly plugs EXELMJ's real exposure. Its Canvas and SVG and PDF export paths bypass the browser's layout engine, so Chromium's shaper does NOT help there — Arabic will come out disconnected or reversed unless something does UAX#9 + shaping explicitly. Adopt with caution given 0.1.x maturity: pin the version, and validate against bidi-js for reordering agreement before trusting it.

entries.name: naqqash
entries.what_it_is: Arabic text shaping specifically for PDF generation — converts raw Arabic Unicode into correctly joined presentation forms, ~9KB, with a dedicated pdf-lib adapter. Created 2026-04-03. Arabic-authored, essentially undiscoverable in English search.
entries.license: MIT (verified in npm registry metadata for 0.2.0).
entries.embeddable_how: npm `naqqash`, plus a `naqqash/pdf-lib` subpath adapter.
entries.last_activity: 0.2.0, published 2026-04-03. New, early-stage (0.2.x).
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Handles Arabic contextual joining (isolated/initial/medial/final), lam-alef ligatures (لا، لأ، لإ، لآ), diacritics/harakat preservation, and Farsi characters — without HarfBuzz, Puppeteer or WASM. API: `shapeArabicText(text)` → shaped string for PDFs; `shapeArabic(text)` → array of original/shaped codepoints; `shapeArabicVisual(text)` → shaped AND reversed for Canvas/WebGL; `drawArabicText(page, text, x, y, opts)` → pdf-lib adapter with font/size/color/align/wordWrap/lineHeight; utilities `isArabicLetter()`, `isDiacritic()`, `getJoiningType()`. IMPORTANT LIMITATION, stated by the author: it does NOT implement the bidi algorithm — it must be paired with bidi-shaper or bidi-js for mixed Arabic/Latin/digit runs. DISCREPANCY I FOUND: the README and npm description both claim 'zero deps', but the published package.json declares `"@pdf-lib/fontkit": "^1.1.1"`. Not a blocker (fontkit is permissive and EXELMJ already ships pdf-lib) but the claim is inaccurate — flag it.
entries.steal_this_idea: The `drawArabicText(page, text, x, y, {font, size, align:'right', wordWrap})` adapter shape. Rather than exposing shaping as a string transform the caller must remember to apply, it wraps pdf-lib's drawText so Arabic is correct BY DEFAULT at the call site. Wrapping the risky primitive instead of documenting it is the right ergonomics for a codebase where one forgotten call produces silently broken Arabic invoices — and the example in its own README is literally `'فاتورة ضريبية مبسطة'` (simplified tax invoice).
entries.why_useful_for_us: Near-perfect fit: EXELMJ already exports PDF via pdf-lib, and this is a pdf-lib-native Arabic shaper. Pair with bidi-shaper (or bidi-js) for the bidi half. Early-stage, so pin the version and test against real invoice text with mixed Arabic/Latin/digits.

entries.name: bidi-js
entries.what_it_is: Reference-quality JavaScript implementation of the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm (UAX #9). By the author of troika-three-text; it is the bidi engine used inside several 3D/canvas text stacks.
entries.license: MIT (verified in npm registry metadata for 1.0.3).
entries.embeddable_how: npm `bidi-js`. One dependency (`require-from-string`).
entries.last_activity: 1.0.3, npm modified 2023-07-31. STALE by date — but UAX#9 is a frozen algorithm, so low churn is expected and is not a red flag here.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Pure bidi ONLY — reordering and embedding levels. It does NOT do Arabic contextual shaping, so on its own it produces correctly-ordered but disconnected Arabic letters. Must be paired with a shaper (naqqash, bidi-shaper, or harfbuzzjs). Its production credibility is high: I confirmed @shotstack/shotstack-canvas depends on `bidi-js ^1.0.3` alongside harfbuzzjs, i.e. a commercial text-layout engine uses exactly this pairing.
entries.steal_this_idea: The bidi/shaping SEPARATION itself is the architectural lesson, and the pairing evidence proves it is the industry pattern: bidi-js (order) + harfbuzz/shaper (glyph forms) are distinct stages. Teams that conflate them ship the classic bug where text is either correctly ordered but disconnected, or correctly joined but reversed. EXELMJ should model these as two explicit pipeline stages in its canvas text path, which also makes each independently testable.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The conservative, battle-tested choice for the bidi half — use it as the correctness oracle against which to validate the newer bidi-shaper. If bidi-shaper's 0.1.x reordering disagrees with bidi-js, trust bidi-js.

entries.name: harfbuzzjs
entries.what_it_is: Official minimal HarfBuzz build for JavaScript (WASM) — the same industry-standard shaping engine Chromium, Android and LibreOffice use, exposed to JS.
entries.license: MIT (verified in npm registry metadata for 1.6.0; zero dependencies confirmed).
entries.embeddable_how: npm `harfbuzzjs`, WASM binary loaded at runtime. Works in Electron renderer or Node main. Ship the .wasm locally for offline use.
entries.language_stack: C++ compiled to WebAssembly + JS glue.
entries.last_activity: 1.6.0, npm modified 2026-08-09 — five days before this sweep. Actively maintained under the official harfbuzz org.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: The ground-truth Arabic shaper. Unlike lookup-table shapers (naqqash, arabic-persian-reshaper) which map to Unicode presentation forms, HarfBuzz does real OpenType shaping — it reads the font's own GSUB/GPOS tables, so it handles font-specific ligatures, proper mark positioning for harakat, and calligraphic Naskh/Ruq'ah features that presentation-form substitution simply cannot express. This matters for EXELMJ specifically because it is a DESIGN tool: designers will load real Arabic display fonts whose behaviour lives in OpenType tables. Heavier than the alternatives (WASM payload) and needs font binaries supplied.
entries.steal_this_idea: Tiered shaping strategy: presentation-form substitution (naqqash, ~9 KB) is fine for plain UI labels and simple invoice text, but any user-supplied Arabic display font in the design canvas needs real OpenType shaping. Decide the tier per text-run based on whether the font has meaningful GSUB coverage, rather than committing the whole app to one shaper — this keeps the common path light and the design path correct.
entries.why_useful_for_us: The correctness ceiling for Arabic in EXELMJ's vector/canvas designer. Heaviest option, so treat as the high-fidelity path, not the default. Being under the official harfbuzz org with an August 2026 release makes it the lowest-risk long-term dependency of all the Arabic tooling here.

entries.name: rtlcss
entries.what_it_is: The canonical framework for transforming a stylesheet from LTR to RTL (used by Bootstrap's own RTL build).
entries.license: MIT (verified in npm registry metadata for 4.3.0).
entries.embeddable_how: Node build-time tool / CLI / PostCSS-compatible. Never ships to the client.
entries.last_activity: 4.3.0, npm modified 2024-08-27. Stable/mature rather than abandoned — it tracks a slow-moving problem.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: This is the concrete remediation for the GrapesJS finding. GrapesJS's grapes.min.css has 23 physical left/right declarations and zero logical properties; rtlcss is the standard way to mechanically produce an RTL variant of a third-party stylesheet you do not control. Supports value/directive control comments (`/*rtl:ignore*/`) for the cases that must not be flipped — e.g. code snippets, logos, LTR-locked numeric fields.
entries.steal_this_idea: `/*rtl:ignore*/` control directives. Automatic flipping is right ~95% of the time and catastrophically wrong for the rest (a code editor pane, a Latin brand mark, an LTR-locked URL field). An in-stylesheet escape hatch lets you automate the bulk and hand-annotate the exceptions — essential when the stylesheet is vendored and regenerated on every dependency bump, which is exactly the GrapesJS situation.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Build-step answer to 'GrapesJS chrome is LTR-only'. Run it over grapes.min.css to emit grapes.rtl.css, load conditionally. Turns the GrapesJS RTL verdict from a blocker into a build task.

entries.name: postcss-rtlcss
entries.what_it_is: PostCSS plugin that emits BOTH LTR and RTL rules into one stylesheet, rather than generating two separate files.
entries.license: Apache-2.0 (verified in npm registry metadata for 6.0.0).
entries.embeddable_how: PostCSS plugin in the Vite 8 build — EXELMJ already runs Vite, so this is a config-level addition.
entries.last_activity: 6.0.0, npm modified 2026-03-29. Actively maintained — notably fresher than rtlcss.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Strategically better than rtlcss for an app that switches language at RUNTIME, which EXELMJ does (Arabic first, English second, user-togglable). Because both direction variants live in one stylesheet scoped by `[dir]`, flipping direction is a single attribute change on `<html>` with no stylesheet swap, no flash, and no reload. rtlcss's two-file model forces you to swap the loaded stylesheet on toggle.
entries.steal_this_idea: The single-stylesheet, `[dir]`-scoped output strategy. It converts direction from a BUILD-TIME variant into a RUNTIME attribute, which is the correct model for a bilingual desktop app with a language switcher — and it composes perfectly with the MutationObserver-on-`<html>` pattern from @shoelace-style/localize: set `dir` once on the root, and both CSS and component behaviour follow.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Preferred over rtlcss for EXELMJ's own source given the runtime language toggle and existing Vite pipeline. Use rtlcss only for one-off transformation of vendored third-party CSS like GrapesJS's.

entries.name: postcss-logical
entries.what_it_is: PostCSS plugin letting you author in CSS logical properties and values, transforming them for compatibility.
entries.license: MIT-0 (verified in npm registry metadata for 9.0.0) — MIT-0 is MIT without the attribution requirement, i.e. maximally permissive.
entries.embeddable_how: PostCSS plugin in the Vite build.
entries.last_activity: 9.0.0, npm modified 2026-01-14. Active, maintained under the csstools org.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: The prevention strategy rather than the cure: authoring in `margin-inline-start` / `padding-inline-end` / `inset-inline-*` / `text-align: start|end` means new EXELMJ CSS is direction-correct with no flipping step at all. This is precisely the discipline basecoat-css adopted to close its RTL issue. Largely unnecessary for compatibility in Electron 43 (Chromium 150 supports logical properties natively) — its value is as a lint/authoring convention, not a polyfill.
entries.steal_this_idea: Enforce it as a rule, not a tool: ban physical `left`/`right` in new CSS and require logical equivalents. The basecoat audit above is the proof this works — its remaining RTL bugs were exactly and only the handful of places where physical properties survived (`padding-right` on button icons, `text-align:left` in the sidebar). A lint rule would have caught both.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Cheapest possible RTL insurance for the ~2900-line designApp.ts and its stylesheets. Prevents the next RTL retrofit from ever being needed.

entries.name: :dir() is SEMANTIC-ONLY — direction:rtl will not trigger it (GOTCHA)
entries.what_it_is: Not a library — a CSS behaviour that silently breaks RTL adoption of basecoat-css, Web Awesome and anything else built on :dir(). Worth its own entry because it would have caused a false 'this library's RTL is broken' verdict.
entries.license: N/A (web platform).
entries.embeddable_how: N/A.
entries.last_activity: Baseline widely available since December 2023.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: MDN states verbatim that `:dir()` 'uses only the _semantic_ value of the directionality, i.e., the one defined in the document itself. It doesn't account for _styling_ directionality, i.e., the directionality set by CSS properties such as `direction`.' CONSEQUENCE FOR EXELMJ: if the app switches to Arabic by setting CSS `direction: rtl` (which is the intuitive move, and is exactly what GrapesJS issues #2851 and #4015 did — `editor.Css.setRule(..., {direction:'rtl'})`), then EVERY `:dir(rtl)` rule in basecoat-css and every Web Awesome component's RTL styling will SILENTLY FAIL TO MATCH. The `dir` ATTRIBUTE must be set: `<html dir="rtl" lang="ar">`. Note also `:dir()` differs from `[dir=…]`: `:dir()` matches INHERITED/calculated directionality, while `[dir=…]` matches only elements carrying an explicit attribute — which is why basecoat writes `:where(:dir(rtl),[dir=rtl],[dir=rtl] *)` to cover both. COMPATIBILITY IS A NON-ISSUE HERE: Baseline-widely-available since Dec 2023 (Chromium 120+), and Electron 43 ships Chromium 150, so Shoelace issue #2188 about old-browser `:dir()` failures does not apply to EXELMJ.
entries.steal_this_idea: Make `dir="rtl" lang="ar"` on the root element the SINGLE source of truth for direction across the whole app — document iframe, editor chrome, and exported artefacts alike — and never express direction with CSS `direction` alone. This one rule simultaneously satisfies basecoat's `:dir()`, Web Awesome's LocalizeController, @shoelace-style/localize's MutationObserver, postcss-rtlcss's `[dir]` scoping, and GrapesJS's `frameContent` injection. Every RTL mechanism in this sweep keys off the same attribute — which is why getting it wrong breaks all of them at once, invisibly.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Highest-leverage single finding in the pass. It is a one-line implementation detail that determines whether four separately-verified RTL mechanisms work or silently no-op, and it explains why several GrapesJS RTL bug reports used an approach that could never have worked.

entries.name: arabic-persian-reshaper
entries.what_it_is: Small Node module reshaping Arabic/Persian characters into presentation forms for environments without automatic shaping.
entries.license: MIT (verified in npm registry metadata for 1.0.1; zero dependencies confirmed).
entries.embeddable_how: npm `arabic-persian-reshaper`, zero deps, tiny.
entries.last_activity: 1.0.1, npm modified 2022-04-11. STALE — no releases in ~4 years.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Presentation-form substitution only, with explicit Persian/Farsi letter coverage (پ چ ژ گ) which pure-Arabic shapers sometimes miss. No bidi. Older and less capable than naqqash or bidi-shaper; included for completeness as the long-standing prior art in this niche. Two even older siblings exist (`arabic-reshaper` 2016, `js-arabic-reshaper` 2017) and are effectively abandoned — noted so they are not mistaken for live options.
entries.steal_this_idea: Its joining-type tables are the readable reference implementation of Arabic shaping — short enough to actually read end-to-end, which the WASM alternatives are not. Useful for understanding what naqqash/bidi-shaper are doing before trusting either, and for writing test fixtures.
entries.why_useful_for_us: Low priority — superseded by naqqash (newer, pdf-lib adapter, diacritics) and bidi-shaper (adds bidi). Listed so the option space is complete and so its staleness is on record rather than rediscovered later.

entries.name: @shotstack/shotstack-canvas
entries.what_it_is: Self-contained text layout and animation engine for Node and Web built on HarfBuzz — surfaced while searching for HarfBuzz/bidi canvas stacks.
entries.license: UNVERIFIED — the npm registry metadata returns NO license field for 2.10.3. Must be treated as licence-unknown until the repo LICENSE file is read. Do NOT link it into EXELMJ on the strength of this entry.
entries.embeddable_how: npm, but pulls a heavy native/binary dependency tree.
entries.language_stack: TypeScript/Node with native and WASM deps.
entries.last_activity: 2.10.3, npm modified 2026-06-19. Active.
entries.rtl_arabic_notes: Its dependency list is the useful intelligence, and it independently corroborates the recommended architecture: it depends on `bidi-js ^1.0.3` AND `harfbuzzjs 0.4.12` AND `fontkit ^2.0.4` together. That is a commercial text-layout engine converging on exactly the bidi-engine + HarfBuzz-shaper + font-parser split recommended in the bidi-js entry above. Its own Arabic quality is unverified.
entries.steal_this_idea: Read its dependency manifest as a validated bill of materials for correct international text layout: bidi-js (UAX#9 order) + harfbuzzjs (OpenType shaping) + fontkit (font parsing/metrics). If EXELMJ builds its own canvas text pipeline, that trio is the proven composition — and it is reassuring that an independent commercial product arrived at the same answer.
entries.why_useful_for_us: REJECT as a dependency: no declared licence, plus `ffmpeg-static`, `@resvg/resvg-js` native binaries and `canvas`/@napi-rs/canvas make it heavy and hostile to a clean offline Electron bundle. Valuable ONLY as architectural corroboration.
